articles.summary: NATO’s top general lays out plan to fight Russia — with or without America  POLITICO.euNato’s supreme commander warns Moscow against attacks in Europe  Financial TimesNATO Details Plan to Shield Ukraine’s European Allies From Russia  The New York TimesNATO general sets out tough military response to any 'foolish' Russian attack  ReutersNATO says will do ‘anything and everything’ if alliance is attacked  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
NATO’s top commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich on Monday vowed to block, blunt and break any Russian attack as part of a new “Theory of Victory,” and underlined that alliance troops would fight even if U.S. forces were engaged elsewhere.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum, Grynkewich outlined how the 32-member alliance would respond to an invasion of NATO territory as concerns grow that Russia could be capable of attacking a NATO member by the end of the decade.
“Our alliance exists to preserve peace,” he said, “but let there be no doubt: should war come, we will block, blunt any attack, and then, if it does not cease, we will break the forces conducting aggression against us.”

articles.title: Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones - Euromaidan Press
articles.summary: Ten casualties to one, by a NATO official’s count: Russia’s September in Ukraine’s kill zones  Euromaidan Press
articles.full_text:
Russia suffered vastly more casualties than Ukraine in September, a senior NATO military official told Bloomberg. Ukraine’s General Staff put the month’s Russian toll only slightly lower.
September’s toll lands on a recruitment system that was already falling short. Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) estimated that Russian losses outran new contracts in June and July, when monthly losses ran lower. In August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, citing military intelligence, warned that Russia is preparing a mass call-up after its parliamentary elections. That vote ended on 20 September.
Where the numbers come from
Russian casualties passed 50,000 in September, up to 28,000 of them killed, the official said. Ukraine’s losses over the same month came to about 5,000, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. Russia does not release casualty figures, Bloomberg noted. In late August, Pavlo Palisa, deputy head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, put Russia’s July losses at 43,000 killed and wounded. Bloomberg could not confirm his figures.
To push forward, Russia keeps feeding troops into “kill zones,” the official said. These are stretches of ground saturated with armed drones, mines, and artillery fire. Maksym, call sign Rumyn, is a deputy company commander in the 46th Airmobile Brigade’s drone battalion. In April, he said the zone once ran 3–5 km deep and is now several times larger.
Ukraine suffered 10 times fewer casualties than Russia in Vivaldi counteroffensive, veteran says. Ukraine’s innovations in drone and ground robot tactics are changing frontline warfare
Rising stakes for Moscow
Russia’s defense spending is expected to near $199 billion this year, Bloomberg reported, citing two sources close to the government. That is about 40% above the plan the government set in late 2025.
Russian President Vladimir Putin would struggle to wind down the invasion without a political cost, Martin Jäger said last week. He heads Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND).

articles.title: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback - AOL.co.uk
articles.summary: ‘We still love you’: NATO envoy seeks to reassure Europe over US military pullback  AOL.co.uk
articles.full_text:
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker told European Commissioner for Defence Andrius Kubilius that Washington remains committed to Europe’s defence, amid an ongoing US military review withdrawing thousands of troops and key strategic assets from the continent.
“We still love you,” Whitaker said at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday in the Polish capital.
“I keep telling our European allies… the United States isn't stepping back.”
His remarks came during a panel on NATO 3.0 — a US-backed model that calls for Europe to take the lead with its conventional defences as American forces draw down from the continent and shift their attention elsewhere.
Kubilius said NATO 3.0 did not mean the United States was saying, “We don’t love you anymore, Europeans, so you should do your own job”. Rather, he argued, Europe needed to develop the capabilities to deter aggression on its own territory.
“Europe needs to take responsibility in our hands,” he said.
Kubilius has previously estimated that replacing US strategic military assets could cost Europe up to €500 billion. Experts have also suggested that Europe could need 300,000 additional troops to defend itself against Russia in a scenario in which Washington continues to withdraw its military support.
Since Donald Trump returned to the White House, Washington has sought to redirect military resources towards other regions, including the Indo-Pacific, to counter China’s growing influence.
The Pentagon’s review of US military deployments in Europe is expected to conclude by December, with its findings to be presented to US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth. The assessment could pave the way for further reductions in America’s military presence on the continent.
However, separate force reductions are already under way. In May, for example, the Pentagon ordered the withdrawal of approximately 5,000 troops from Germany and cancelled a planned deployment of a long-range fires battalion.
Whitaker said he did not want to “preview” further measures under the review because “it is not ready”, but argued that Washington’s push for a more European NATO was “working”.
“The proof is in where we're sitting today, here in Poland, spending 4.7% on core defence and leading really the alliance to a stronger, more capable military,” he said.
Allies agreed to raise their core defence spending target from 2% to 3.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035 at the 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, alongside a further 1.5% for broader security and defence spending.
"That is what the United States is expecting from all of its allies," Whitaker said of the overall 5% defence spending target.
Poland is among NATO’s highest spenders on core defence as a share of GDP, according to the alliance’s latest estimates.
The effort to increase defence spending also comes as the European Union seeks to strengthen its military capabilities by 2030, amid warnings from European intelligence agencies that Russia could pose a more direct threat to NATO in the coming years.
But the rearmament drive is facing significant hurdles. A leaked version of the European Defence Agency's landmark report — aiming to assess the progress — reveals major capability gaps, most notably in drone defences and maritime warfare.

articles.title: EU AI Act Readiness: A Practitioner's Guide for Corporate Leaders - The National Law Review
articles.summary: EU AI Act Readiness: A Practitioner's Guide for Corporate Leaders  The National Law Review
articles.full_text:
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) is the world’s first horizontal AI law, and it already applies in part. Prohibition of certain AI practices and AI literacy requirements have been enforceable since February 2025, and obligations for providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models have applied since August 2025. The Article 50 transparency requirements became legally enforceable on August 2, 2026. The heaviest obligations for high-risk AI systems will apply from December 2, 2027, for the use cases listed in Annex III and from August 2, 2028, for AI embedded in products regulated under Annex I. The July 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI deferred several key obligations for high-risk systems beyond their original August 2026 and August 2027 deadlines. However, that deferral only provides additional runway to in-scope organizations. The underlying obligations have not changed, and the time the regulator has provided should be used productively towards EU AI Act readiness in the coming weeks and months.
This guide provides a short overview of the Act for corporate leaders and executives and addresses common misconceptions in Part I. Part II sets out ten concrete steps towards EU AI Act readiness. Part III closes by introducing some technology platforms that can help practitioners get started and lead through the process.
PART I: THE EU AI ACT IN BRIEF
The Act regulates AI by risk: the higher the potential harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, the heavier the obligations. It entered into force on August 1, 2024, and its obligations phase in through 2028. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), in force since July 27, 2026, mainly moved the high-risk deadlines back and simplified some procedures; the Act’s core requirements are unchanged.
The EU AI Act categorizes AI systems into four risk tiers:
- Prohibited practices (Art. 5). The regulation places an outright ban on certain prohibited practices that are detailed in Article 5. These prohibited practices include manipulative or exploitative techniques, social scoring, emotion recognition in workplaces and schools, untargeted scraping of facial images, and most real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes. The Omnibus added AI that generates non-consensual intimate imagery or child sexual abuse material.
- High-risk AI systems (Art. 6, Annexes I and III). Under the EU AI Act, "high-risk" AI systems are the primary focus of the regulation and are subject to the strictest compliance, design, and monitoring obligations in Articles 8 to 27. Because these systems pose a significant threat to health, safety, or fundamental rights, they are highly regulated throughout their entire lifecycle. The Act classifies high-risk AI systems into two main groups: (1) Annex I addresses product safety and includes AI that functions as a safety component in products already covered by existing EU harmonization laws, such as medical devices; (2) Annex III sets out certain specific sensitive use cases with critical societal impact, such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment and worker management, access to essential services such as credit scoring and life/health insurance pricing, law enforcement, migration and justice.
- Limited risk (Art. 50). Limited risk systems, also referred to as systems with specific transparency risk, are not subject to the heavy compliance burden of high-risk AI systems, but they are required to adhere to mandatory transparency obligations under Article 50. These requirements are designed to prevent deception and ensure users are aware they are engaging with artificial intelligence. For example, chatbots must disclose that users are dealing with AI; synthetic audio, image, video and text must be machine-readably marked; deepfakes and certain AI-generated public-interest text must be labeled.
- Minimal risk. Most AI falls into the minimal risk category. This includes, e.g., AI systems used for spam filters, inventory forecasting, or product recommendation engines. The Act does not require specific obligations beyond AI literacy (Art. 4), but encourages organizations to voluntarily follow codes of conduct and adhere to best practices for these systems.
General Purpose AI models (GPAI)
General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models, such as large language models (LLMs) and foundational models, are regulated through a separate, two-tiered framework based on their capabilities and potential impact. Rather than categorizing them strictly by their end-use case (like the risk tiers for standard AI systems as shown above), the Act evaluates the core engines of GPAI models based on their generality and capabilities. All GPAI model providers must meet baseline obligations: technical documentation, information for downstream providers that integrate the model, a copyright policy and a public summary of training content (Art. 53). Models with systemic risk face additional obligations on top of these, including model evaluations, adversarial testing, serious-incident reporting and cybersecurity protection (Art. 55). Systemic risk is presumed where training compute exceeds 10²⁵ floating-point operations (FLOPs) (Art. 51(2)) but is also open to designation by the Commission based on capabilities or impact.
The organization’s role determines its duties
The Act assigns obligations by role and distinguishes between providers and deployers. Article 3 defines a provider as an organization that develops an AI system or has it developed and places it on the market or puts it in service under its own name or trademark. Providers bear most of the Act’s regulatory weight. A deployer is an organization that uses an AI system under its authority in a professional context. Most corporate organizations are deployers for most systems. They become providers when they build their own AI systems, including systems only used internally. They also become providers and inherit the regulation’s strict and costly compliance obligations applicable to providers if they white-label or substantially modify the AI or repurpose a system into a high-risk use case (Art. 25).
Penalties
The EU AI Act imposes significant penalties for violations. Fines reach up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover for prohibited practices, and up to €15 million or 3% for most other breaches, including high-risk and transparency obligations. Supplying incorrect or misleading information to authorities can cost up to €7.5 million or 1% (Art. 99).
Common misconceptions
As a General Counsel, I frequently hear misconceptions about the Act. This is not surprising, primarily due to the law’s unprecedented regulatory structure, its extraterritorial reach, and the complex realities of modern software supply chains. Because regulating artificial intelligence merges product safety laws with data privacy concepts, organizations and the public frequently misinterpret how the rules apply in practice. This section directly addresses some of the misconceptions I hear most frequently:
| Misconception | What the Regulation Says | 
| “We’re headquartered outside the EU, so the EU AI Act doesn’t apply to our organization.” | According to Article 2, the EU AI Act applies wherever AI is placed on the EU market or its output is used in the EU. The Act is extraterritorial, so it can apply to businesses anywhere in the world whose AI systems are offered in the EU or whose AI outputs are used in the EU. | 
| “We’re not a tech company and we only buy AI, so the EU AI Act is the vendor’s problem.” | Companies often assume that because they did not build a foundational model from scratch, they are merely "deployers" facing minimal operational duties. However, standard software development practices, such as fine-tuning a third-party open-source model for a specific use case, embedding it into a SaaS platform, or white-labeling it, can legally make the company a "provider." If the resulting system is high-risk, this triggers the heaviest compliance burdens, including risk management systems and conformity assessments. In addition, deployers have their own duties, including AI literacy (Art. 4), transparency (Art. 50), and for high-risk systems, human oversight, monitoring, log retention, worker information and in some cases a fundamental rights impact assessment (Arts. 26–27). | 
| “Our pre-deployment testing and software audit already satisfy EU AI Act compliance.” | Businesses frequently attempt to manage AI using traditional IT or GDPR compliance frameworks, treating it as standard software. The AI Act, however, treats high-risk AI more like physical machinery or medical devices. Because AI models evolve, drift, degrade, and adapt over time, particularly the high-risk obligations under the Act are designed as lifecycle obligations and specifically require continuous risk management, post-market monitoring, audit trails and incident reporting, as well as human oversight. This creates a heavy operational lift that static compliance checklists cannot handle. | 
| “The EU AI Act has been delayed, and we don’t have to prioritize it yet.” | The Act did not take effect all at once. Its phased rollout - banning prohibited systems first, enforcing AI literacy and GPAI rules by 2025, and shifting high-risk obligations to December 2027 and August 2028 through the Digital Omnibus regulation - created immense confusion. Companies often conflate future deadlines with immediate legal liabilities, or conversely, assume they can wait to comply when certain rules are already active and enforceable. | 
PART II: TEN STEPS TOWARDS EU AI ACT READINESS FOR LEADERSHIP
As shown in Part I above, the EU AI Act introduces a complex matrix of obligations that requires organizations to fundamentally shift how they govern technology. These ten steps provide a practical roadmap for leadership to operationalize compliance, moving from initial accountability and inventory to robust life

articles.title: China-EU trade deal: Europe targets China's USD 7.5 billion hybrid car boom with export curbs - https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.summary: China-EU trade deal: Europe targets China's USD 7.5 billion hybrid car boom with export curbs  https://internationalfinance.com/
articles.full_text:
China’s recent agreement with the European Union (EU) has imposed new restrictions on EV manufacturers from the world’s largest auto market by limiting hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc.
The timing of the deal couldn’t have been worse for the Chinese automakers, who have been ramping up hybrid shipments exempt from EU tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, with sales growth slowing at home.
Take the latest China Passenger Car Association data, for example, in which China’s domestic car sales extended their decline for a 12th successive month.
Passenger vehicle sales fell 28.1% from a year earlier to 1.63 million units in September, worsening from a 23.7% decline in August, the association noted.
In that background, exports have remained a key growth driver, with automakers looking overseas to cushion the impact of a sluggish home market.
Some 923,000 vehicles were shipped in September, showing a jump of 73.2% year-on-year, compared to a 77.5% rise in August.
Now what is there in the China-EU deal? As per the European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, Beijing would cut exports of hybrid cars to the bloc by more than half, with the EU successfully forcing the Xi Jinping administration to address the ballooning trade deficit with the bloc.
In H1 2026, China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to USD 7.5 billion from USD 2.5 billion a year earlier. The figure, published by the China Customs Department, was nearly nine times the USD 845 million exported in all of 2021.
In 2024, the EU imposed additional tariffs on Chinese EVs. Automakers from the world’s second-largest economy, since then, have increasingly turned to plug-in hybrids, which are exempt from the extra duties.
The decision was a masterstroke, as weak charging infrastructure in parts of Europe also supported demand for plug-in hybrids, marketed for their long range and strong fuel economy.
SAIC, BYD, and Chery accounted for more than 90% of Chinese hybrid sales volume in the EU, while hybrids represented more than half of their European sales, according to Jefferies.
While Sefcovic said on Friday the agreement would cut the imports of “several million cars over four years,” Brussels and Beijing have yet to disclose how the arrangement will be implemented.
As per China’s Commerce Ministry, the arrangement will allow continued export growth and guarantee Beijing a quota no smaller than that granted to any other source of imports.
Investors and analysts view the agreement as a de-escalation of trade tensions and a potential indication that tariffs on Chinese hybrids may be temporarily suspended.
“Overall we believe it is a risk-relief rally story…as the implementation rules, volume caps, price floors, and carve-outs are still pending technical negotiation,” Citi analysts said.
The rapid market proliferation of Chinese hybrids has increasingly challenged European manufacturers, including Volkswagen, long the region’s leading plug-in hybrid seller, said Li Yanwei, an analyst at the China Automobile Dealers Association.
BYD, China’s largest hybrid vehicle exporter to Europe, apart from being considered Tesla’s global rival, sold more plug-in hybrids than fully electric models in the first eight months of the year.
As per Li’s calculations, the Seal U SUV emerged as BYD’s best-selling model.
Together with Chery, SAIC, and Geely, the company has narrowed the gap with Volkswagen, which still commanded a 31.8% share of the EU plug-in hybrid market.
Jefferies analysts see the China-EU deal as signaling “tariff risk off, quota risk on,” potentially pushing Chinese automakers towards higher-priced models, increasing pressure on German premium brands, and accelerating plans to build more vehicles in Europe.
What is there in the deal?
Sefcovic said that the “shared understanding” would “moderate” China’s export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU while also cutting the imports of several million cars over four years, following the two-day talks with the Xi administration.
Sefcovic and Chinese officials, including Commerce Minister Wang Wentao, were involved in intense discussions over the last three months, which came after years of disputes between Beijing and Brussels over soaring Chinese exports, including cars.
EU leaders will discuss the outcome at Brussels this Thursday to determine whether the agreement marks the start of a rebalancing of the bloc’s trade deficit with China, a figure that has swelled to over 1 billion euro (USD 1.12 billion) a day.
Sefcovic called the deal an “excellent result” achieved by the two sides.
However, the agreement is just the beginning. It is a crucial first step—but only a first step—in the process of rebalancing,” he told reporters in Beijing.
Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee, told the media that the hybrid deal should be used as a model to extend similar measures to other sectors as well, apart from the necessity of the EU deploying trade defence measures more effectively.
Chinese Commerce Minister Wang told Sefcovic that China was not the root cause of the EU’s problems but a partner in solving them, according to the Chinese ministry.
The two sides also reached an understanding to reduce Chinese import duties on approximately four billion euros worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil, and footwear.
The deal also included the smoothening of China’s granting of export licences for rare earths and permanent magnets.
China’s and the EU’s dispute over cheap Chinese EV exports has clouded bilateral ties over the past two years and led to EU tariffs in 2024. China’s retaliatory measures against EU beverages, animal protein, and dairy, as well as restrictions on exports of rare earths and critical minerals, hit the bloc severely.
China and the EU will now continue discussions on price undertakings as an alternative to tariffs.
While German auto industry group VDA welcomed the agreement, it maintained a cautious tune by stating that it was too early to determine if the deal would address unfair competition.
Mercedes-Benz said the deal showed constructive dialogue was the right way to address challenges, and it should provide greater predictability.
Matthias Schmidt, a European autos research analyst, said countries like Germany had thought themselves immune to the threat from Chinese car companies but were waking up and asking Brussels to step in.
“The result is this statement from Sefcovic today,” he said on Friday.
“Now Berlin is asking London to join them, and Brussels, given the UK accounts for 30% of Western Europe’s new Chinese car sales,” Schmidt added further.
As part of Friday’s agreement, China’s commerce ministry said it also would continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets through a “green channel” mechanism.
The focus is on the trade imbalance
As per the UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totalled USD 560 billion in 2025, up from USD 517 billion in 2024.
Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose about 10% from a year earlier, while shipments to Hungary jumped 43%.
China, on the other hand, imported USD 268.3 billion worth of European goods, down from USD 269.4 billion in 2024, led by purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France.
While Beijing has been using exports aggressively to flood its relatively cheap, state-subsidized goods that its own domestic population can’t absorb, the EU is torn between welcoming those imports to ease living costs and keeping them out to rebuild its own factories.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, in September, warned the European Parliament about the trade gap reaching a “tipping point” and that the 27-member bloc would use all the tools at its disposal to rebalance the relationship.
“China and the EU will keep exploring the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods and continue dialogue on market access for medical devices,” the Chinese ministry said.
“Sefcovic and Wang are set to meet again in March 2027, with a video conference call in January,” the department concluded.

articles.summary: Global Market: Eurozone bond yields ease as Russia-Ukraine energy truce lifts sentiment  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Germany’s 10-year government bond yield, the euro zone benchmark, fell 2.5 basis points to 3.46%, while the two-year German yield, more sensitive to monetary policy expectations, declined 2 basis points to 3.07%.
Also Read | Global Market: South Korean shares fall nearly 2% as Middle East tensions weigh on sentiment
According to Reuters, Trump announced the agreement in a post on Truth Social on Sunday, saying Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy-related ceasefire. The development helped ease concerns about potential disruptions to energy supplies and their implications for inflation.
Investors have also increasingly bet that tensions in the Middle East will remain contained, reducing the risk of a sharp energy price spike ahead of the November US midterm elections. Lower energy prices could help temper inflationary pressures, although uncertainty surrounding geopolitical developments continues to influence the outlook for European monetary policy, the report stated.
Also Read | Once-hot AI trade leaves Korean stocks struggling for buyers
ECB rate expectations remain elevated
Money markets were pricing in a European Central Bank deposit rate of 2.73% by December, compared with the current rate of 2.50%. Expectations pointed to the rate reaching 3.22% by late 2027, indicating that investors continued to anticipate tighter monetary policy over the longer term.
French, Italian bond spreads narrow
Risk premiums on French and Italian government debt also eased on Monday, reflecting a modest improvement in investor sentiment.
The yield spread between French government bonds, known as OATs, and German Bunds narrowed by 1 basis point to 136.50 basis points. The spread, which measures the additional yield investors demand to hold French debt over German government bonds, had climbed to 158.67 basis points in early October, its highest level since November 2011, the report stated.
Italy’s yield spread over German Bunds stood at 109 basis points, down from 129.74 basis points reached earlier this month.
The narrowing spreads suggest some easing in pressure on French and Italian debt, although both countries’ borrowing costs remain subject to fiscal concerns, political uncertainty and broader movements in euro zone bond markets.
Investors will continue to monitor geopolitical developments, energy prices and central bank rate expectations for clues about the direction of European government bond yields in the coming weeks, the report stated.

articles.full_text:
The EUR/USD pair gains ground to near 1.1165 during the early Asian trading hours on Tuesday. Nonetheless, the potential upside for the major pair might be limited amid growing fiscal and political instability in France. All eyes will be on the key US inflation reports later this week.
Worries about France’s ability to rein in its budget deficit and a sharp bond market selloff last week elevated fears of a potential sovereign debt crisis in the Eurozone. Citi analysts believe growing fiscal risks in France could prompt the European Central Bank (ECB) to pause interest rate hikes after December, or earlier if financial stress spreads across the Eurozone.
Elsewhere, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for November 29 after parliament rejected two of his minority government's housing decrees.
On the US front. Cleveland Federal Reserve (Fed) President Beth Hammack said on Monday that the Federal Reserve should move "relatively quickly" to a restrictive policy to control inflation she sees as more broad-based.
The US Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation report is due on Wednesday, followed by the Producer Price Index (PPI) and Retail Sales data on Thursday. These reports could provide further direction on the Federal Reserve’s policy path.
“I don’t think [the reports] are going to show any signs of easing in inflation, and they would probably lean bearish for the metals market,” said Jim Wyckoff, a market analyst at American Gold Exchange.
Euro steadies as OAT/Bund spread stagnates and EUR/USD shorts build
Analysts at Societe Generale observe that the “stagnation of 10y OAT/Bund spread around 137bp removed a source of weakness for EUR/USD and EUR/G10,” even as they caution that it remains “unclear what can drive the spread back to the mean around 110bp.” At the same time, positioning has turned notably bearish, with the bank highlighting that “EUR/USD short positions are the highest since Dec-24,” underscoring the potential for a sharp repositioning should market drivers shift.
Hammack leans hawkish as Fed rhetoric flags risk of entrenched inflation
Fed’s Hammack delivers a notably more hawkish tone, with the 8.4/10 FXS Speechtracker score standing above the 7.5/10 historical average, underscoring a stronger bias toward tighter policy relative to the established baseline. The emphasis that “interest rates need to be higher,” alongside concerns about an inflationary mindset, broad price pressures, and neutral financial conditions, points to a preference for maintaining or increasing restrictiveness, albeit via smaller, more frequent tweaks to the policy rate. Hammack’s focus on demand-side pressures from AI, sustained growth, and a steady job market reinforces the case for tight monetary policy until inflation convincingly returns to the 2% target.
The FXS Fed Sentiment Index rose by 0.59 points to 138.92, firmly in hawkish territory and consistent with the elevated FXS Speechtracker score. This move signals that Fed communication is skewing more toward tightening risks, supporting expectations that the Dollar could remain underpinned as markets price in a higher-for-longer rate stance.
Technical Analysis: EUR/USD keeps a bearish vibe under the 100-day SMA
In the daily chart, EUR/USD extends a bearish near-term tone as spot holds below the 100-day simple moving average (SMA) and even beneath the Bollinger middle band. Price is only modestly above the lower Bollinger band, while the Relative Strength Index (14) sits in oversold territory, hinting that while downside pressure dominates, the sell-off is becoming stretched.
On the topside, initial resistance is located at the Bollinger middle band near 1.1320, followed by the 100-day SMA at 1.1485 and the upper Bollinger band around 1.1540, where any recovery would likely stall unless buyers regain broader control. On the downside, the lower Bollinger band at 1.1105 offers the next notable support, and a decisive break beneath this floor would open the door to a continuation of the downtrend toward fresh lows.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)
Euro FAQs
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

articles.summary: Russia is building jet drones that fly 800 kilometers per hour, and Ukraine says it is already working on how to stop next generation  Euromaidan Press‘A life-or-death race’: the volunteers protecting Kyiv’s skies from new jet-powered drones  The GuardianRussia’s Jet-Powered Shahed Drones Can Hit 600 KM/H. Ukraine Is Scaling Up Ways to Take Them Down  UNITED24 MediaDrone attack damages houses and cars in Lviv region  UkrinformRussia attacked Lviv overnight...
articles.full_text:
Aviation is one of the most effective ways to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones. Its effectiveness continues to grow due to pilots’ skill and better coordination, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara says, Glavcom reports.
Russia’s jet-powered Gerans fly several times faster than the propeller Shaheds Ukraine learned to shoot down, and they remain the main challenge for its air defense. Ukraine downs more than 90% of the slow drones but only about 55% of the jet ones.
“Due to them, our aviation now uses fewer munitions per aerial target. We plan to improve this further,” Khmara states.
Air defense works as a layered system because no single type of weapon is enough, he explains. The layers run from surface-to-air and shoulder-fired missiles to turrets, electronic warfare, interceptor-drone crews, and small-scale air defense, topped by aircraft including Mirage and F-16 jets.
Scaling what works against jet drones
Ukraine already has combat results against the jet drones, Khmara notes. In one engagement, five Bars interceptors destroyed five aerial targets, a 100% hit rate in that case, and the task now is to raise the overall destruction rate and quickly scale the solutions that prove themselves.
Heavy-caliber turrets are adding to that. Their number in service already runs into the hundreds, he adds.
“This direction is being scaled, and systems with greater range are being worked on. In parallel, surface-to-air and shoulder-fired missile systems are also proving effective,” he says.
Preparing for the next generation
Ukraine is also looking past today’s threats, the minister stresses. The ministry is working to supply interceptor drones, aviation and its munitions, missile and artillery systems, turrets and electronic warfare gear, and to plan several steps ahead with enough stock in reserve.
“We also know what solutions Russia is developing, which concern jet drones with a speed of 800 kilometers per hour. We are working on finding countermeasures to the next generation of threats,” Khmara says.
Producers have been tasked with offering proposals and prototypes, he concludes.

U.S. Envoy to NATO Matthew Whitaker told member states to modernize their military infrastructure in order to move their troops from Western to Eastern Europe.
Whitaker spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Monday where he advised NATO’s members that they must refashion their military infrastructure in order to move troops and equipment from the West to the East “where we would expect any future conflicts,” Politico reported. The envoy also asserted that Europe comes fourth in American defense priorities after homeland security, the Western Hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific.
Though he did not explicitly confirm any American troop drawdown, he emphasized that Washington is reassessing its military priorities.
The U.S. Mission to the North Atlantic Treaty Organization did not immediately respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.
“Superpowers and great global powers have mostly had challenges when they get overextended,” Whitaker said, emphasizing that President Donald Trump wants U.S. allies to be “capable and not dependent,” according to Politico. Under the ongoing U.S. force posture and basing review, outdated military bases, fuel supply chains and agreements governing the stationing of American troops in Europe will be scrutinized.
Whitaker also criticized countries falling short of their spending goals and sent a “very strong message” to political leadership in the Czech Republic, the outlet reported. The European country’s current defense budget is 1.8% of its GDP, 0.2% below the current 2% NATO standard.
This comes as European officials warn that Russia could be ready to attack a NATO country by 2030, according to Politico.
Since Trump has returned to office, the administration has changed its position on troop reallotment in Europe several times.
“The United States isn’t stepping back. We’re just asking you to step forward,” Whitaker told NATO countries, according to Politico.
Whittaker previously served as acting U.S. Attorney General for several months from late 2018 to early 2019 during the first Trump administration.

articles.title: Adieu aux ‘Enfants Rouges’: Tears and shock as fire destroys Paris’s oldest covered food market - France 24
articles.summary: Adieu aux ‘Enfants Rouges’: Tears and shock as fire destroys Paris’s oldest covered food market  France 24Fire destroys Marché des Enfants Rouges, ‘coolest market in Paris’  The GuardianOldest food market in Paris destroyed by fire  The TelegraphInferno destroys 400-year-old Paris landmark – what we know  The IndependentOldest covered food market in Paris destroyed in fire  Sky News
articles.full_text:
A devastating blaze destroyed the French capital’s oldest covered food market in the early hours of Monday, stripping Paris of a cherished venue popular with locals and tourists alike. Traders and residents said the destruction of the Enfants Rouges market, named after a 16th-century orphanage, had left them feeling “orphaned” themselves.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
New Yorkers Lorrie and Ricky so enjoyed discovering the Marché des Enfants Rouges (Red children’s market) a few days ago, that they decided to pay another visit to its celebrated food stalls before leaving the French capital.
But when they approached the centuries-old venue on Monday morning, they were greeted by police cordons, fire trucks and a foul, acrid smell hanging over this picturesque neighbourhood in central Paris.
“It was such a lovely place, so charming – and now it’s gone,” said Ricky, gazing at the blackened entrance to the Enfants Rouges. “It’s tragic.”
Read moreFire destroys Paris's oldest covered food market
A spectacular blaze tore through the iconic covered market overnight, gutting its iron and glass roof and torching all 17 food stalls. Video footage on social media showed huge flames and billowing smoke rising above the venue, hemmed in between buildings on the northern edge of the Marais district popular with tourists.
After touring the site, Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the market had been “completely destroyed”. He thanked firefighters who battled the blaze for over two hours – for ensuring that it did not spread to surrounding buildings in the densely populated area known for its cozy cafes and stylish boutiques.
There were no casualties aside from a firefighter who suffered “minor injuries”, Grégoire told reporters. It was the only consolation for shopkeepers huddled together on a sidewalk – many in tears as they listened to accounts of the devastation wrought by the flames.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
“We’re all a big family, and now we’ve been orphaned,” said Ahmed Ouaddi, whose Moroccan couscous stall had been a fixture of the market for decades. “Our livelihoods have gone up in smoke.”
‘Heart and soul’ of the neighbourhood
Founded in 1615 during the reign of Louis XIII, the Enfants Rouges was the oldest covered market still in operation in Paris. It owed its name to a nearby 16th-century orphanage whose young residents wore red clothing, a symbol of Christian charity at the time.
A buzzing hub for locals and tourists alike, the market offered fresh produce and specialties from around the world. The industry magazine Food & Wine ranked it fifth worldwide for street food this year, after other eating spots in London, Bangkok, Mexico City and France’s culinary capital – Lyon.
To those nostalgic for the Paris of old, it provided a small taste of what the historic Les Halles, the city’s sprawling central market, was like before it was gutted and turned into a giant mall in the 1970s.
In recent years, the Enfants Rouges had become too touristy – and pricey – for many Parisians, in step with the area’s rapid gentrification. But it remained “the heart and soul” of the neighbourhood, said Ouaddi.
“It was the oldest and prettiest market in Paris. We all loved it and we’re all in shock today,” said local pharmacist Virginie Prulhière, still shaken from the blaze, her voice breaking as she gazed at the fire truck parked where her partner’s stall would normally be standing.
“It was also a symbol of resistance, because people here fought to preserve it,” she added, referring to a grassroots campaign in the 1990s against plans to tear down the market and replace it with an underground carpark and housing units.
‘The Enfants rouges will survive’
Residents looked on in disbelief Monday morning as firefighters accompanied the Paris mayor and other officials to inspect the smouldering ruins. Some asked why it had not been possible to save at least part of the structure, noting that the nearest fire station is located just minutes away.
Local authorities said the fire broke out at 3am (01:00 GMT) but the fire brigade did not receive a call until over an hour later. More than 150 firefighters and dozens of vehicles were mobilised to battle the blaze. Their efforts were hampered by the layout of the market, surrounded by buildings on all sides and accessible only through alleyways too narrow for most vehicles.
The cause of the blaze is not yet known.
Read moreSounding the fire alarm: Why French firefighters are on strike
“Luckily, no one was hurt, and that’s the most important thing,” said Alexis Abbou, the market’s manager, striving to remain upbeat as he sought to console its shopkeepers and caterers. “We’ll start all over again and rebuild this wonderful place,” he added.
Paris Mayor Grégoire promised to find a temporary relocation for the traders “so they can resume their business as soon as possible”. In a post on X, Serge Papin, the minister for small businesses and tourism, said the French state would “stand alongside Paris City Hall to help with reconstruction”.
Ariel Weil, mayor of the third arrondissement (district) that housed the market, also recalled the fight to save the market in the 1990s, as he vowed to restore it to its former glory.
“The Enfants Rouges survived a threat to replace it with a carpark,” he said. “It will survive this fire, too.”

articles.summary: EUR/USD consolidates at the lows as France's budget and US CPI remain in focus  investingLive
articles.full_text:
Summary
- The US dollar remains supported by risk-off flows amid French fiscal concerns, despite a dovish repricing of Fed expectations. Markets will focus on Wednesday’s US CPI report, with hotter core inflation potentially reviving rate hike bets and boosting the greenback. Meanwhile, the euro’s outlook hinges on developments in France, where the proposed deficit reduction to 5.0% of GDP could help stabilise bond markets, although parliamentary risks remain. US-Iran negotiations and energy prices will also influence inflation expectations and central bank policy.
The US dollar has been supported recently despite a dovish repricing triggered by Fed’s Williams and Fed’s Jefferson comments that pushed back against expectations of a rate hike in October.
The main reason were risk-off flows into the greenback due to European debt concerns. The focus has been particularly on France, where political uncertainty and concerns over the country's large fiscal deficit have recently pushed French government bond yields higher and widened the spread over German Bunds to its highest level since the eurozone debt crisis.
A stabilization in French spreads could allow some of the euro's risk premium to unwind and trigger a pullback in the US dollar, while further widening and contagion to other countries would likely keep the greenback supported.
Moreover, the US-Iran negotiations continue to be at a stalemate but at least Trump ruled out new strikes before the November elections last week. This week, we also have the US CPI report on the agenda, which could trigger big moves in the markets.
A hotter than expected core CPI could bring a rate hike in October back on the table and give the US dollar a boost. A soft report, on the other hand, will likely weigh on the greenback in the short-term on a fall in Treasury yields.
On the EUR side, the probabilities of an ECB rate hike in October have faded following the sharp widening in the French-German bond spread, as policymakers are likely to remain cautious about adding further pressure to already fragile financial markets.
However, markets still expect the ECB to raise rates in December, reflecting persistent inflationary pressures due to higher energy prices. In terms of economic data, the latest Eurozone CPI showed headline inflation surging to 3.8% in September from 3.2% in August, largely due to higher energy prices. Core inflation remained relatively contained, edging up to 2.5% from 2.4%.
Looking ahead, energy prices and developments in the Middle East will remain important drivers of the inflation outlook. Any sustained decline in energy prices could reduce near-term inflation pressure and give the ECB more room to delay further tightening. This would also be positive for the euro on improved risk sentiment and lower Fed rate hike expectations.
The euro will also remain sensitive to developments in the bond market, particularly the French-German spread. France’s government has proposed a 2027 budget targeting a deficit of 5.0% of GDP, supported by spending restraint and higher tax revenues. This is lower than the previously 5.4% and helped ease market concerns somewhat. However, the plan still faces parliamentary hurdles, and Eurozone finance ministers and the ECB have urged France to pass a credible budget to restore market confidence.
Traders will keep a close eye on France where improvements would be positive for the euro, while negative outcomes will likely continue to weigh on the single currency.

The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep pushing into new lows. articles.title: David McNamara: France faces its Waterloo on bond markets - Irish Examiner
articles.summary: David McNamara: France faces its Waterloo on bond markets  Irish Examiner
articles.full_text:
European bond markets have continued to be roiled by ongoing political uncertainty in recent days, driving a steepening in yield curves, widening spreads for troubled sovereigns, and a depreciation in the euro.
Given the relatively muted trends in headline inflation versus the previous shock in 2022, current market pricing for central bank rates has fallen a little in recent weeks. Nevertheless, inflation worries have driven both the front end and long end of the curve since the US-Iran war began.
However, underlying this inflationary catalyst, markets are also pricing in greater risk premia on governments with poor records of delivering deficit reduction. France, Italy and the UK continue to stand out, enduring significant increases in borrowing costs, while also seeing spreads widen to safe haven assets such as German bunds.
Indeed, political uncertainty in Europe is also now providing a further leg-up to yields. A snap election called in Spain and street protests in France seeking greater public spending, despite the challenging fiscal arithmetic, are adding to political angst which was already high following the recent regional German elections.
French bonds now consistently trade wider than their Italian counterparts, with the 10-year trading between 130-140 basis points (bps) above the German equivalent compared to around 100bps for Italy.
At face value, the widening looks overdone, with both France and Italy running similarly sized deficits of around 5% of GDP, with Italy far surpassing France on its overall debt metric of nearly 140% of GDP versus 118% for its Gallic neighbour.
However, the direction of travel matters for markets. French fiscal policy has become completely unanchored since president Macron lost his majority in parliament a few years ago, whereas the political picture in Italy appears more stable.
There is also a significant risk of a victory for the populist right in the French presidential election next year, which, with a firmly anti-EU outlook, might further weaken EU cohesion at a time of geopolitical uncertainty.
The widening in spreads also brings the focus back on the ECB’s role, risking a politicisation of the institution. In 2022, the ECB tweaked the rules around its Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme to provide greater “flexibility” in how it reinvested the proceeds from the programme.
In practice, this allowed the ECB to intervene to underpin the Italian bond market. The central bank subsequently created the Transmission Protection Instrument, which is a reserve ‘bazooka’ that can, in the ECB’s words, “be activated to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across the euro area”.
On paper, France would fail the criteria for use of the tool, given it requires compliance with the EU fiscal framework, but with its perception as “too big to fail”, there could be increasing pressure on the ECB to act if the situation deteriorates further in the coming weeks.
Looking further ahead, political instability may remain a driver of bond market volatility over the coming year. Alongside the French presidential vote, elections are due across Europe in 2027, including in Italy and Greece.
- David McNamara is chief economist at AIB

articles.full_text:
The EU has significantly increased defence spending, including €8.8 billion for the European Defence Fund and €1.7 billion for military mobility. Member states' defence investments rose by 158.7% between 2021 and 2026, according to the European Council.
Yet, according to the European Commission, Europe lacks a mechanism for rapid crisis response and coordinated defence efforts.
Proposed by the Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen this September, the European Security Council (ESC) would be Europe's first permanent crisis-management forum, keeping security and defence on the agenda year-round.
The Security Council wants to improve operational unity, speed coordination, strengthen strategic direction, and unify crisis responses across member states.
The ESC reflects a broader effort to strengthen Europe's defence and strategic autonomy as concerns over Russian hybrid attacks, airspace violations, cyberattacks, and sabotage grow. Strained US ties and repeated threats to cut NATO funding have also pushed the EU to develop alternatives and rely more on its own security capabilities.
Related
The proposal would bring together EU leaders and international partners, including Ukraine, Canada, Norway, and the UK. Through the emergency security protocol, modelled on NATO's Article 4, members could call consultations when they believe their security, territorial integrity, or political independence is threatened, and plan a coordinated response.
The Commission's idea echoes a 2018 proposal by French President Emmanuel Macron and former German Chancellor Angela Merkel for an ESC, set out in the Meseberg Declaration, "Renewing Europe's promises of security and prosperity".

Dunlop Aircraft Tyres automating EUDR compliance process
12 Oct 2026
Share:
Osapiens AI platform to help build 'defensible' due diligence for natural rubber supply
Mannheim, Germany – Dunlop Aircraft Tyres Ltd (DATL) has selected German software company osapiens to ensure EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) compliance for its natural rubber (NR) supply.
In a 5 Oct statement, osapiens said its AI platform – osapiens HUB – will build “a defensible EUDR due diligence process,” for DATL and offer “a more resilient view of where its natural rubber originates, across a large and fragmented upstream supply chain.”
According to osapiens, NR presents “one of the most complex compliance challenges” under EUDR.
This, it explained is because the regulation extends accountability beyond a company's direct suppliers to the origin of the raw material itself.
“For tire manufacturers, that origin is a large, fragmented network of upstream sources with limited digital records. At that scale, manual review is no longer a viable compliance approach,” said osapiens.
Stephan de Barse, Chief Revenue Officer, osapiens explained, NR compliance is complicated “because the real risk sits many tiers upstream, well beyond what any manual process can reasonably track.”
Dunlop's decision, De Barse said, “shows where the market is heading: toward AI that doesn't just detect risk, but resolves it, automatically and defensibly, at the scale a global supply chain demands.”
According to osapiens, the AI platform can automate deforestation and legality risk assessments “down to the individual plots where its rubber originates.”
The platform then embeds that due diligence directly into Dunlop's existing workflows, making EUDR compliance “a built-in capability” for the tire maker.
The system documents all the checks, pieces of evidence and decisions throughout the process, providing a “clear, defensible record” to present for regulatory reporting, customer requests or internal governance.
Furthermore, AI agents will be employed to work on cases where a standard process can't resolve issues, such as incomplete data or added complexity further upstream.
“Rather than chasing that risk manually across a large, fragmented upstream supply base, the company [DATL] now has a single, continuously updated view of its natural rubber supply chain,” concluded osapiens.

articles.title: Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Trump turns the screws on Kyiv as EU budget talks hit a wall  Euronews.comAnalysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections  BBCTrump insists energy ceasefire holds as Ukraine reports new Russian strikes  Al JazeeraZelenskyy vows to retaliate if Russian strikes on Ukraine’s power grid continue  The GuardianWhy Moscow is staying tight-lipped on Trump's energy ceasefire  BBC
articles.full_text:
Good morning. It’s Monday. I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: Europe braces as Trump turns up the heat on Zelenskyy, and Ireland’s EU budget compromise falls dead on arrival.
Kyiv under pressure: For Ukraine, the past few days have brought back the distinct taste of the Oval Office showdown: public pressure on President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, accusations that Ukraine is obstructing peace and a growing fear (again) that the aim is not compromise, let alone a just peace, but to force Ukraine to surrender, our correspondent Sasha Vakulina writes this morning.
Blindsided: US President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire on attacks against energy infrastructure. There was just one rather significant problem: at least one of those parties appeared unaware of the agreement.
“If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins,” Zelenskyy said in response. Ukraine, he added, was ready.
It was not entirely clear Moscow got the memo either, Sasha explains.After Trump’s announcement, Russia struck a thermal power plant in Kharkiv, before targeting several other power plants overnight. And that was only Sunday.
Diesel deal rattles Europeans: On Friday, Trump had also announced a deal with Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports, without informing Ukrainian or European negotiators who were in Miami for talks. It’s seen as an effort to bring down soaring diesel and gasoline prices, a major issue for American voters, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
Zelenskyy did not mince his words, branding the deal “weak” and warning it would hand Putin “billions” more to wage war. Trump told him he “better damn well stop” striking Russian refineries, before taking it further and saying Ukraine needed a “new leader”. Putin’s leadership, notably, did not come up for discussion.
Rallying around Zelenskyy: There is another irony for Trump: publicly berating Zelenskyy has hardly proven an effective way of weakening him at home - quite the opposite. EU leaders have also been rallying behind the Ukrainian leader – and Zelenskyy is now expected to join leaders when they gather for a summit in Brussels this Thursday and Friday, sources have told Euronews.
Hard reckoning: News of the Trump-Putin diesel deal and the subsequent energy ceasefire is also set to dominate the conversation today in Brussels and Luxembourg, where foreign ministers are gathering, Jorge Liboreiro writes.
Once again, the EU finds itself scrambling to close ranks behind Zelenskyy and push back, with calculated criticism, against Trump’s Russian-friendly diplomacy.
The US Treasury’s sanctions waiver to enable the diesel sales, set to last until April 2027, has particularly enraged Europeans, who see their own sanctions regime undermined by Trump’s out-of-the-blue decisions. It must be noted that the majority of vessels that Russia uses to trade its refined oil products are subject to the G7 price cap ($100 per barrel).
Foreign ministers will today make clear their pressure campaign on Moscow will continue unabated by formally blacklisting more than 1,600 people and companies accused of enabling the war, a record number in one go.
“We are of course continuing our path,” Kallas said on sanctions upon arriving in Luxembourg this morning. “Our message is clear. If we want to end this war, the only way we can do this is putting more pressure on Russia, and we would call on the US to put the sanctions in place so we can finish this war,” she added.
More is needed: Russia’s all-out escalation has forced EU officials and diplomats to admit that their multibillion-euro support for Ukraine will fall short next year. But there are no easy solutions, Jorge writes in his in-depth analysis.
Warsaw watches: The mounting tensions have also raised the stakes of the Warsaw Security Conference kicking off this morning, with President Zelenskyy expected to address delegates from Kyiv in around an hour.
Our chief EU editor Maria Tadeo, on the ground in the Polish capital, reports that security is tight and the mood tense after Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that a man had been arrested on suspicion of plotting to assassinate him and his defence minister. More from our Warsaw colleagues.
Dead on arrival: Meanwhile, a new pitch to trim down the EU’s next long-term budget – known as the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – tabled by Ireland over the weekend has been met with immediate pushback from the so-called frugal countries, which are demanding a much smaller spending pot.
“The size of the new proposal is not a basis for agreement. The EU budget must be affordable for those who bear the brunt of financing it,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in a statement on Saturday.
Dutch directness: Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen was even more blunt. “The Netherlands cannot accept this proposal. At this rate, there will be no deal by the end of the year,” he said in a statement. Sweden also rejected the proposal, insisting that the “overall volume” needs to come down.
Ireland, which currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, on Saturday pitched €141 billion in cuts to the previous proposal in an attempt to appease the frugals. The country’s EU affairs minister, Thomas Byrne, described the proposal as a “compromise designed to act as a catalyst” for wrapping up negotiations by the end of this year – a prospect that now looks increasingly remote.
Crunch time: EU leaders are set to tackle the budget issue when they gather for talks in Brussels on Thursday and Friday – and European Council President António Costa is pushing for a swift compromise. There has been a political push to wrap up the budget negotiations before the end of 2026 to prevent talks from being torpedoed by elections in major EU economies including France, Italy and Poland next year. My colleague Luca Bertuzzi has more.
Oil prices tumble as stocks rise after Trump touts 'energy ceasefire'
Most stock markets rose early Monday as oil prices tumbled after US President Donald Trump announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which offset a fresh wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, my colleague Angela Barnes reports.
Both main crude contracts sank more than 1% following the announcement, reversing an initial spike that came in response to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia at the weekend.
At least a dozen people were killed at Riyadh's international airport Saturday - the deadliest attack on Saudi soil for more than a decade - and another one died following a second strike on Sunday.
The Iran-backed group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the past 24 hours and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom's transit hubs, calling them "a theatre of operations for our forces".
"The market is no longer paying full geopolitical premium on every headline, and that is probably the most useful signal in the morning price action," wrote SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes.
He added: "The physical market remains tight enough to keep Brent above $100, but futures are refusing to treat every new escalation as the start of another straight-line inflation shock."
Angela hasthe details.
More from our newsrooms
Tens of thousands urge EU for climate action at Brussels demonstration. Ahead of a major UN summit, thousands of protesters marched through the streets of Brussels demanding greater action to combat climate change. Euronews’ Evelyn Ann-Marie Dom was on the ground and spoke to protesters and organisers.
Macron's popularity hits lowest level since 2017 as Bardella and Le Pen also lose ground. Some 82% of French people now disapprove of the French President, while the far-right National Rally’s Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella’s ratings were also weakened by Mediapart's revelations about antisemitic texts attributed to Bardella. Alexander Kazakevich hasmore.
North Korea fires 'several ballistic missiles' into Sea of Japan, Seoul's military says. North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles off its east coast, Seoul's military said on Monday, after weeks of mounting friction over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border that divides both countries. Gavin Blackburn hasthe details.
We're also keeping an eye on
- Warsaw Security Conference kicks off. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to give the opening address from Kyiv. Speakers include Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and European Commissioner for Defence, Andrius Kubilius.
- EU foreign affairs and environment ministers gather for talks in Luxembourg.
- European Commission Vice-Presidents Stéphane Séjourné and Roxana Mînzatu to address the European Parliament’s employment committee.
That’s it for today. Sasha Vakulina, Jorge Liboreiro and Luca Bertuzzi contributed to this newsletter.

articles.title: Oil Prices Jump 2% on Saudi Attacks as OPEC Sees Demand Rebound - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
articles.summary: Oil Prices Jump 2% on Saudi Attacks as OPEC Sees Demand Rebound  Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.comOil prices fall as traders assess Russian diesel supply prospects and Saudi-Houthi conflict  CNBCOil falls as Russia diesel supply prospects counter Gulf supply risks  ReutersEnergy prices rise after Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ fails to move Russia or Ukraine  NBC NewsOil Prices Rebound Amid Persistent Middle East Supply Risks  WSJ
articles.full_text:
Oil prices climbed to their highest levels in nearly two weeks on Monday morning as fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and oil tankers near the Strait of Hormuz put Middle East supply risks back at the center of the market, outweighing President Donald Trump's announcements of additional Russian diesel supplies and a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire.
West Texas Intermediate was trading at $93.78 per barrel, up $1.93, or 2.10%, on Monday morning, while Brent crude rose $2.09, or 2.00%, to $106.80 per barrel, according to Oilprice.com data.
The renewed buying followed a weekend of attacks on Saudi Arabia, including a Houthi strike on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. Further attacks were reported Sunday, while two tankers were struck near Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz.
The tanker attacks threaten to interrupt the recovery in Gulf oil exports, which reached 81% of prewar levels in September. Crude and condensate shipments had recovered to 91%, but refined-product exports remained at just 60%.
Goldman Sachs raised its December Brent forecast to $90 per barrel from $85, estimating that geopolitical risks are currently adding just over $20 per barrel to oil prices.
The price increase comes as OPEC has sharply reduced its expectations for global oil demand growth this year. OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais said Monday that the producer group now expects demand to grow by just 400,000 barrels per day in 2026, down from the 1.4 million bpd it forecast at the beginning of the year.
OPEC expects much of the demand deferred during this year's disruptions to return in 2027. The group had already cut its 2026 growth estimate to 380,000 bpd in September, meaning Monday's 400,000-bpd figure is actually a slight increase from last month's forecast even though it represents a 1-million-bpd reduction from OPEC's outlook at the beginning of the year.
The International Energy Agency expects an even deeper demand hit this year, forecasting a 2.5-million-bpd decline in global consumption in 2026 followed by a 2.6-million-bpd rebound in 2027.
Additional Russian barrels could put some downward pressure on fuel prices. Trump said Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons, or roughly 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with additional supplies to follow. Moscow has also partially lifted restrictions on diesel exports, allowing another 500,000 tons, or about 3.7 million barrels, onto the international market.
Trump also announced Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of violating the agreement on Monday.
In the Gulf of Mexico, Shell, Chevron and BP were preparing to restore offshore production after Hurricane Isaias disrupted operations over the weekend.
By Charles Kennedy for Oilprice.com
