articles.summary: Live at the 2026 Paris Motor Show: all the cars that matter  Auto ExpressThe star cars and concepts at the 2026 Paris motor show  The TimesWhy Chinese EVs cost $11,000 less to build than European rivals, and why tariffs won’t close the gap  Automotive NewsEurope’s car manufacturers fight back in Paris  The EconomistParis motor show: Macron urges EU preference amid Chinese competition  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
Paris Motor Show 2026 live: Stunning new Alfa Romeo, Citroen 2CV reborn and more
Car brands from all over the world have taken over Paris and let their imaginations run wild...
The 2026 Paris Motor is underway and proving why it is one of the most important events in the world of cars. After months of build-up, we’ve got our first looks at the reborn Citroen 2CV, next-generation Vauxhall Astra and Smart’s return to the city car sector, with plenty more still to come.
French firms Citroen, Peugeot, Renault, Alpine and DS are putting on quite a show for their hometown fans, unveiling a wild variety of fresh and exciting concepts that preview everything from affordable hatchbacks and family-friendly people carriers to a rally-inspired hyper-hatch and a spectacular sports car Porsche would be jealous of.
Alongside the imaginative show car designs from them, Alfa Romeo, Fiat and others, are some cars you’ll actually be able to buy soon. The new Volkswagen ID. Tiguan – the car formerly known as the ID.4 – made its public debut in Paris, as did the eagerly anticipated successor to the iconic Smart ForTwo, the very petite new Smart #2. China is making its presence known as well, with brands like Geely and Omoda showing off some fresh metal.
Auto Express is on the ground in Paris to see all the exciting new models Europe’s car brands and others have brought along to the show, and speak to some of the most influential figureheads in the automotive industry. Let's get stuck in…
Paris 2026 top car reveals
- Citroen 2CV - French icon is finally reborn, and as charming as ever.
- Volkswagen ID. Tiguan - VW’s electric family SUV has a new look, new interior and a new yet familiar name.
- Vauxhall STX - our first look at the next-generation Vauxhall Astra, and the future of the estate car.
- Smart #2 - pint-sized electric city-slicker will the smallest car in Europe.
- Alpine A310 Vision - Villainous-looking sports car designed to encroach on Porsche and Ferrari’s territory.
- Renault E-Space - Could this be the family bus that makes MPV cool again?
- Peugeot E-T16 - Rally legend reimagined as electric hyper-hatch to take on Renault’s Turbo 3E.
- Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso - drop-dead gorgeous coupe previews the next generation of Alfas.
- DS F3VER - First look at the next-generation DS No3 hatchback focused on Parsian luxury.
- Renault 8 Gordini - jaw-dropping two-door coupe is a rear-wheel drive piece of modern art.
Paris Motor Show 2026: all the big car reveals from A to Z
Here you'll find all of the major new car reveals at Paris 2026, along with information on what the top brands are up to at the show.
Aion
Chinese brand Aion is making its debut at Paris this year, and is showing off two new additions to its line-up. The first being the Aion GS7: a huge SUV with plug-in hybrid power looking to take on the Land Rover Discovery. The other model remains a mystery for now, though the UK managing director, Jon Wakefield, previously hinted to us a “fettled” version of something in the current line-up is on the way. Stay tuned for that.
If you thought's Aion's new UT was a little too tame, the Chinese brand has decided to beef up the electric hatch. Not in a power sense, but the new UT Cross gets a jack-up ride height and wider tyres.
Alfa Romeo
Despite what it might look like, the jaw-dropping Alfa Romeo Cuorerosso is not supposed to be a sneak peek of the long-awaited, next-generation Guilia saloon. However, the hot red four-seat coupe does show us where the Italian brand is heading, with its design set to inform the entire raft of new models Alfa Romeo is working on, and a hybrid-assisted V6 engine under its long, sculpted bonnet.
Alpine
The next-generation Alpine A110 isn’t launching until late next year, sadly. We do now, however, have a good idea of what it will look like and how the iconic sports car’s design is evolving thanks to a dramatic, if slightly abstract, sculpture. If you can’t see the vision don’t worry, because Alpine’s design boss gave Auto Express a sneak peek recently.
The wild, rather villainous-looking Alpine A310 Vision is not just a pie-in-the-sky concept; it’s a statement of intent for the brand’s low-volume, big-money and extreme ‘special projects’. The two-seater, seventies-inspired speculator also demonstrates just how flexible Alpine’s new electric sports car architecture is, in allowing for this car’s outrageous proportions. Sadly, there are no plans to put it into production, but hopefully that will change.
Audi
The innovative if unconventional Audi A2 hatchback from the noughties is back, reborn as Audi’s entry-level EV to take on the likes of the Cupra Born and Volvo EX30. We’ve seen the car already and even had a chance to drive a prototype, but this will be the first chance for the public to have a poke around. It’s perfect time too, as the radical hatchback has just gone on sale, with prices starting from only £30,700.
BYD
BYD covers almost every area of the car market, and now the Atto 8 is coming to take on large seven-seat SUV rivals like the Kia EV9 and new Skoda Peaq.
Prices are yet to be announced, but the Chinese electric SUV will come with BYD’s latest EV technology, including a WLTP range of up to 405 miles and Flash Charging which can boost the 115kW battery from 10 to 97 per cent in nine minutes.
Barely a year has passed since the launch of the BYD Dolphin Surf, but the Chinese brand has just treated its dinky city car to a raft of updates. Amongst some fancy new paint colours and interior upholstery, the Active trim gains larger 16-inch alloy wheels as standard. Most notably, the infotainment screen has grown from a 10.1-inch unit to 12.8-inches.
The Shark pick-up truck is aimed squarely at hunting down rivals like the Ford Ranger, Toyota Hilux and Mitsubishi L200.
It will be going on sale in ‘select markets’ in the next three months, with a ‘wider rollout’ in the first half of 2027. The Shark will cost from £47,290, which is a little more than the entry-level Ford Ranger PHEV when VAT is applied, but the BYD has a higher specification.
Citroen
The iconic Citroen 2CV is coming out of retirement after a nearly 40-year hiatus. France’s post-war hero is returning as a £13k EV - so it’s one for the masses, like the original ‘Deux Chevaux’ - and is leading the charge for a new simpler and cheaper breed of small electric cars coming out of Europe. It’s due to hit the streets in 2028, but this concept model unveiled in Paris will give us plenty to talk about until then.
Retro Citroen vans have a broad range of admirers, whether they be rural farmers on the continent or coffee vendors in the city. The new 2CV Fourgonnette is lined up to be a more modestly-sized option in the electric van world, but its charm factor is undeniably massive.
Cupra
Following on from the Leon and Formentor, the Cupra Raval is the latest of the brand's cars to be given the Abt treatment. The new VZ Abt trim level will be available in the UK from November and features new bucket seats, a Sennheiser sound system and an updated ambient-lighting system. In addition to the trim level, the Custom Cupra by Abt pack has also been revealed, and that adds plenty of sporty touches, such as front and rear splitters, side skirts and a roof spoiler. The pack is only available on the new VZ Abt trim.
Dacia
Revealed back in September but making its public debut in the French capital, the second-generation Dacia Spring is set to cost quite a bit more than the outgoing EV. However, this new one has more style, more range, a nicer interior and should drive better too, so you should be getting your money’s worth with this one.
At the other end of Dacia’s line-up is the new Striker: a jacked-up family estate car that’s part of the value-focused brand’s assault on the critical C-segment market, meaning it’s a rival to top-sellers like the Skoda Octavia, Citroen C5 Aircross and Nissan Qashqai. It’s also the biggest Dacia launched to date, has bold looks, lots of space inside and should start from less than £25,000. Definitely one to check out, we think.
DS
Earlier this year, we learned that the DS3 hatchback was getting a reboot, with the faltering French premium marque going back to where it all began in 2010. The all-new DS No3 will be part of a big renaissance plan for the company, and before it arrives, the DS F3VER shows us what to expect, including surprisingly sporty looks and the latest tech from Stellantis underneath.
Fiat
The new Fiat Grizzly is the next addition to the Italian outfit’s Panda-inspired line-up, following from the wonderfully charming Grande Panda supermini. Both the SUV and more rakish Fastback versions of the mid-size crossover are on display, giving people their first opportunity to poke around the fresh Skoda Karoq and Nissan Qashqai competitors. Both will be available with hybrid and electric power when they launch soon.
The Fiat Multiplay concept is what happens when the Italians push the idea of a multi-purpose vehicle further than your typical SUV. It’s designed to be highly modular, giving customers the ability to transform their car from a seven-seater people carrier to a double-cab pick-up truck with just the push of a button. We love the idea, even if we don’t know if, how or when we could see anything close to a production version.
With the 500e, Grande Panda and Topolino already on its books, Fiat’s no stranger to building modern electric cars with highly unique designs. The Multiplina is a tribute to the original Mulitpla — the very first example, not the one from the 1990s. While this concept was originally called Quattrolino, Audi’s legal team had other ideas.
Ford
The Ford Ranger has won our coveted Pick-up of the Year award on several occasions, so there’s no doubting its capabilities as a workhorse. However, if you prefer a bit of visual drama to go with your truck’s durability, the MS-RT Champion Edition might be the one for you. There’s no performance upgrades, but a range of motorsport-ins

articles.title: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties - Maritime Gateway
articles.summary: India–EU FTA could strengthen Czech investment and manufacturing ties  Maritime Gateway
articles.full_text:
Summary
Czech companies are seeking joint ventures, investment and technology partnerships in India, with the India–EU trade agreement expected to support deeper commercial ties. Czech minister Karel Havlíček outlined opportunities in engineering, construction, energy and transport during a business forum in New Delhi. The agreement is not yet in force.
Czech delegation looks beyond export sales
The India–EU FTA could create opportunities for Czech investment and joint ventures in India, according to Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Addressing the CII-organised India–Czech Republic Business Forum in New Delhi on 12 October, Havlíček said Czech businesses were interested in establishing partnerships and investing locally alongside their export activities.
He identified construction, energy, transport and research and development as areas for cooperation. He also highlighted Czechia’s engineering capabilities, including aircraft manufacturing.
The minister linked the delegation’s interest in local partnerships with India’s manufacturing strategy. His remarks describe prospective business opportunities, rather than a quantified investment commitment or a confirmed portfolio of new projects.
Business mission covers three Indian centres
The forum forms part of a Czech business mission scheduled for 12–15 October, covering Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai.
Ahead of the visit, the Czech Ministry of Industry and Trade said the mission would support companies entering the Indian market and those seeking to expand existing operations.
The programme also included a planned roundtable with Invest India focused on developing bilateral investment opportunities. Direct business contacts and meetings were identified as important elements of the delegation’s approach.
The mission places the minister’s comments within a broader effort to develop commercial relationships. For participating companies, the immediate focus is identifying partners and market opportunities while the trade agreement progresses through its approval process.
The visit’s stated objectives combine market entry, business expansion and investment cooperation, extending the engagement beyond the promotion of finished-product exports alone.
Negotiations concluded, implementation still pending
India and the European Union concluded FTA negotiations on 27 January 2026. The European Commission subsequently put forward a proposal for a Council decision authorising signature.
Negotiating an agreement, signing it and bringing it into force are separate stages. The EU process requires the relevant Council decisions and European Parliament consent, while India must also complete its approval requirements.
Consequently, the agreement’s tariff preferences should be understood as forthcoming provisions, rather than benefits already available to shipments.
The talks began in 2007, were suspended in 2013 and resumed in 2022. Separate negotiations on investment protection and geographical indications were also launched alongside the renewed FTA process.
That distinction is relevant to the investment discussion: the trade agreement and the separate investment protection negotiations address related but different aspects of the commercial relationship.
Industrial tariff reductions underpin the opportunity
The negotiated agreement envisages eliminating or reducing tariffs on 96.6% of EU goods exports to India by value. The European Commission estimates eventual annual duty savings of approximately €4 billion for European products.
Industrial goods feature prominently. Tariffs on machinery, chemicals and pharmaceuticals are to be mostly eliminated, while automobile and component provisions include phased reductions.
These changes provide a commercial backdrop to Czech interest in engineering and industrial cooperation. Lower trade barriers could support cross-border equipment and component supply, although individual benefits will depend on product coverage and implementation schedules.
The agreement also includes provisions on intellectual property and services, including maritime transport. Such commitments extend its scope beyond merchandise tariffs and could support businesses combining technology, equipment and services.
The Commission’s projections concern the overall EU–India relationship; they do not establish a specific increase in Czech exports or investment.
Indian exporters also stand to gain
The agreement provides reciprocal opportunities for Indian businesses. India’s commerce ministry says more than 99% of Indian exports by trade value will gain preferential access to the EU.
Engineering goods, textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products and other labour-intensive sectors are among the areas identified for improved access.
The framework also covers rules of origin, customs and trade facilitation, regulatory cooperation and technical barriers to trade. These provisions matter to manufacturers seeking to build supply relationships across the two markets.
For ports, freight forwarders and logistics providers, any resulting expansion in industrial trade could create additional demand for cargo movement. Its scale will depend on implementation and actual business decisions.
The Czech delegation’s engagement therefore represents an effort to develop partnerships ahead of the agreement’s application, with investment and manufacturing cooperation central to the discussion.
FAQs
What opportunities are Czech companies exploring?
Joint ventures, investment and cooperation in engineering, construction, energy, transport and research and development.
Who outlined these opportunities?
Czech First Deputy Prime Minister and Industry and Trade Minister Karel Havlíček.
Is the India–EU FTA already in force?
No. Negotiations have concluded, but the agreement must complete signature and approval procedures before taking effect.
Were specific Czech investment commitments announced?
The reported remarks did not provide a quantified investment package.
How could Indian exporters benefit?
The agreement envisages preferential EU market access across a broad range of Indian exports, subject to its provisions and implementation.

articles.title: Ukraine’s Strikes on Yandex Data Centers, Explained - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Ukraine’s Strikes on Yandex Data Centers, Explained  The Moscow TimesUkraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant  BBCUkrainian strikes on data centres and Russian bot activity in freefall  Euronews.comRussia's Yandex says data centre in Vladimir area shut down after drone attack  ReutersZelenskyy Says Yandex Strikes Crippled Pro-Kremlin Bots But Tech Experts Question Evidence  Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty
articles.full_text:
A wave of attacks against the Russian internet giant Yandex has sent shockwaves across the country in recent days and caused major disruptions to daily life.
Yandex, often referred to as the “Russia’s Google,” provides a range of digital services used by millions of Russians every day. Russian-language media reported widespread outages across the company’s products over the weekend, with people unable to access certain websites and applications.
The attacks, which Kyiv says are a retaliation for Russia’s strikes against similar targets, represent a new phase in Ukraine’s air campaign against Russia. Ukraine has increasingly sought to undermine Russia’s economy by striking infrastructure vital to some of its largest businesses in recent months, but this is the first time that targeting their data centers has become part of that strategy.
What happened?
On Oct. 9, Yandex, Russia’s largest technology company, announced that two of its data centers had been struck by drones, one in the city of Sasovo southeast of Moscow and the other in the Kaluga region southwest of the capital. A third facility in the suburbs of Vladimir east of Moscow would be hit before the weekend was through.
Serious damage was reported at all three locations. In a statement posted on Friday, Yandex said that operations at its Sasovo facility were “completely halted” while part of the infrastructure in Kaluga was “disabled.” The Vladimir facility, meanwhile, was taken completely offline on Sunday, according to the company.
“Yandex teams are working around the clock to ensure our services remain operational and to help those affected by the incident,” the company said after the two initial strikes. “This is our top priority right now, but unfortunately, it’s not easy.”
The effects of the attacks were not limited to the data centers they targeted. Nine people were injured in the Kaluga region, while about 1,600 customers were left without electricity in the Vladimir region, the heads of each region said. Neither explicitly mentioned the Yandex facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that the attacks were retaliation for Russia’s own strikes against its data centers. Indeed, last month, Moscow struck such facilities in the Kyiv region, causing temporary internet outages for roughly 100,000 households.
Moscow claimed that the data centers it struck were used by Ukrainian military intelligence bodies.
What is Yandex?
To understand the impact these attacks are having on regular Russians’ lives, consider what would happen if Google suddenly went offline.
Gone would be access to the company’s flagship internet browser, but also to its many other essential services: maps, payment, email and its virtual workspace, to name a few.
Like Google, Yandex is a company whose tendrils have stretched to nearly every corner of the Russian technology market since its founding in the 1990s. However, in Russia, its monopoly over digital services is arguably even larger.
While apps like Yandex Maps and Yandex Pay might be expected offerings of Russia’s largest technology company for people in the West, something like the widely used taxi and food delivery app Yandex Go rolls the function of Uber and DoorDash into one. In Russia, they’re all managed by the same company.
What’s more, Yandex offers a cloud computing service that provides digital infrastructure for some of Russia’s largest companies. According to the Yandex Cloud website, the platform has more than 64,000 customers.
How disruptive are the attacks?
As with any other major player in the technology industry, data centers form the backbone of all of these operations.
Understandably, after some of them were hit, people quickly began flagging issues. Russian-language media reported over the weekend that many Yandex apps had gone down temporarily but had been restored. Others were still experiencing interruptions or complete outages on Monday.
Yandex itself urged some users to switch to alternative platforms during the outages. Taxi drivers told the exiled outlet Vyorstka that they received a notification from Yandex advising them to switch to Google Maps or Waze while the company was fixing its servers.
Separately, the websites of other companies that use Yandex’s cloud services were reportedly impacted, including grocery giant Magnit, fast-food chain Vkusno i Tochka and household appliance retailer M.Video, the Kommersant newspaper reported, citing publicly available outage data.
Yandex’s operations outside of Russia also appear to have been affected. According to The Times of Central Asia, users in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan have reported difficulties accessing the company’s apps. Similar outages were noted in the Armenian capital Yerevan, forcing users to book their taxis with a local competitor, which was in turn strained by the surge in traffic.
Particularly disruptive for Russians was the attacks’ effect on digital financial services. Yandex is so integrated into everyday payments that when its digital wallet application, Yandex Pay, went down, it warranted its own explanation from company leadership.
“All your money is safe,” Dima Pirogov, CEO of Yandex’s FinTech Division, said in a statement posted to the company’s social media platforms on Sunday. “The money itself isn’t stored in the data center. That’s where the servers that power our services are located.”
“We can’t yet give you a precise timeline for restoration,” Pirogov added, “but we promise: we won’t stop until the service is restored.”
How are officials reacting?
President Vladimir Putin has so far not commented on the attacks. That’s not unusual — Putin is rarely the first one to telegraph the Kremlin’s reaction to such developments.
Some hints have emerged, however, that the Kremlin is taking the situation seriously.
On Monday, Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev told a State Duma committee that his office was working with the Defense Ministry on measures to protect data centers, a sign that officials are worried about the effect of further attacks.
“The scale of the attacks — which we were all monitoring in real time — was unprecedented,” Shadayev said, adding that “the entire industry is now helping to resolve” the chaos they caused.
As two major questions vex Yandex — how to restore service completely and how to repair damaged infrastructure — the company could be grappling with the fallout from the attacks for a while.
According to a source who spoke to Kommersant, delivering replacement equipment to the damaged facilities could take as long as six months.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

articles.title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest - The Guardian
articles.summary: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest  The GuardianDeloitte helped in falsifying documents to evade tax on Abramovich’s wealth, BBC finds  BBCAbramovich’s close associate misled UK court in £1bn oil-fields case, documents suggest  BBCAbramovich aides accused of hiding mansions and jets to avoid tax  The TelegraphAbramovich’s inner circle presented high court with sham documents and misleading testimony...
articles.full_text:
Aides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets.
New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents.
The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate.
Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers.
The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak, more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.
The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union.
From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion.
This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier.
Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed.
The disappearing $2bn
A crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era.
The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money.
By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC.
One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn.
The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus.
But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest.
The gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it was sanctioned by the UK in 2023, along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth.
“It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in an August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous.
The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree.
“Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote.
Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide.
Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later.
The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts.
History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability.
Andrew Mitchell KC, a leading expert in financial crime and tax law, described the scheme as a “blatant move to protect from legitimate taxation assets which should otherwise have been subject to tax”. This, he claimed, would amount to “straightforward” tax evasion.
Abramovich’s lawyers said: “Any suggestion that our client evaded tax, or sought to deceive the Cypriot authorities, is denied, and publication of the same would be defamatory of him. If an arrangement was proposed by professional advisers of Deloitte’s standing, it would have been entirely proper for companies linked to our client (in which he was not involved on a day-to-day basis) to rely on it.”
The oligarch’s signature
It was not the first time that Abramovich’s subordinates appear to have resorted to backdating to solve a money problem for their boss.
In 2000, Tenenbaum and Ioannides, then still working for Deloitte Cyprus, met in London to discuss a delicate matter.
Abramovich, it seemed, wanted to extract almost $100m from Cypriot companies that held stakes in Sibneft.
According to Ioannides, it was essential that any transaction couldn’t reveal these Cyprus companies and that the money had to appear “earned”. The logic for these conditions was not explained.
Deloitte Cyprus’s solution was a complicated but seemingly bogus arrangement, directly involving Abramovich, that appears to have relied on falsified, backdated consultancy agreements.
These agreements appeared to show that Abramovich’s Sibneft-owning companies had paid an intermediary business $98m for “consultancy services”, namely advice on share purchases.
That intermediary had then supposedly passed on 99.9% of the money to Abramovich, as “commission” for having acted as its “agent”.
But the share purchases in question had already happened a year earlier, meaning the intermediary company had to be at least a year old too, if backdated deals involving it were to appear legitimate.
Ioannides found a suitable Cypriot off-the-shelf company called PB Mediapower Enterprises.
With Tenenbaum’s authorisation, directors of Deloitte Cyprus signed the backdated documents and incorporated their content into PB Mediapower’s annual accounts.
Abramovich’s commission was then converted into promissory notes – effectively IOUs – which he cashed in over the following three years.
The leaked files contain 50 such notes. Unlike much of the paper trail tracing the Abramovich fortune, which kept his name out of it, each of the applications for repayment of the notes bore his signature.
Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied that they had participated in any improper backdating or falsification of documents. Both also stressed that they relied on specialist advice from professional advisers such as Deloitte Cyprus as well as Cypriot corporate advisers.
The ghost house
One of Abramovich’s most prestigious assets was the Fyning Hill estate in West Sussex, an imposing mansion set in 424 acres of South Downs countryside.
The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, reportedly flew in for lunch here during his first UK state visit in 2003.
Two years later, accounts show, the estate was listed among $650m of luxury assets – including a London penthouse, French chateau, helicopters, jets, yachts and a supercar – all held in a Cypriot company, Amiscan Investments.
New Cypriot disclosure rules, introduced in 2003, meant that these would have to be included in Amiscan’s accounts.
But by the time those accounts were filed, this vast billionaire’s toybox had vanished, thanks to Abramovich’s squad of financial fixers.
In an October 2005 email, sent to Tenenbaum, Ioannides suggested it might be “more prudent not to disclose” them.
Files show that Abramovich aides, including Ioannides, worked together to backdate contractual agreements, giving the false impression that Amiscan’s assets had been shifted to its BVI shareholder, Kelvedon Worldwide, at the start of 2003.
Deloitte Cyprus staff took part in discussions about this disappearing act, emails show.
Yet the auditor signed off Amiscan’s accounts, now showing no trace of three properties and a fleet of luxury vehicles.
Lawyers for Abramovich and Tenenbaum denied wrongdoing of any sort, including improper backdating, falsification, or any sort of tax evasion. They each also said that their clients could not recall the context or detail of documents more than 20 years old, which had not been provided to them by the Guardian.
Both said their clients had relied on expert advice, including from Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus, also answering on behalf of Taliotis and Charalambous, said that it “acts in compliance with applicable laws”. It said the correspondence were more than 20 years old and no longer accessible, meaning it could not comment on whether the material was complete or accurate.
A lawyer for Demetris Ioannides said he was unable to comment for personal reasons.
Lawyers for Tenenbaum said that documents could sometimes be backdated for legitimate reasons, such as to show when a transaction became effective.

articles.full_text:
RECCESSARY’s “ASEAN Weekly” highlights Southeast Asia’s new energy and carbon market updates. (Image: RECCESSARY)
 This week in ASEAN, high financing costs remain a major barrier to renewable energy development, according to a new ASEAN energy report. Meanwhile, Energy Tech Summit Asia, held in the region for the first time, brought together industry leaders and investors to discuss rising AI power demand, grid infrastructure and financing challenges facing climate technologies. Here are the key ASEAN stories from Oct. 5–11.
High financing costs hinder Southeast Asia’s energy transition, ASEAN report finds
ASEAN’s energy demand continues to grow, but the region faces an annual investment gap of around USD 405 billion through 2060. Renewables currently account for less than 15% of the energy mix, well below the region’s target.
Meanwhile, geothermal development has emerged as a key topic at the ASEAN Energy Business Forum (AEBF), where industry experts highlighted exploration risks, transmission constraints, financing challenges and complex approval processes as major barriers to development. Read more here
ASEAN recently held a series of energy ministerial meetings and business forums to build consensus on the region’s energy development. (Photo: AEBF)
From offtakers to infrastructure: Six priorities for Vietnam’s hydrogen development
Hydrogen can be used as a chemical feedstock, reducing agent, fuel, or energy-storage medium. However, its development requires careful consideration of the energy and economic costs of converting electricity into hydrogen and subsequently transporting, storing, or converting it again.
The strategic question is therefore not whether hydrogen can replace conventional energy across the economy, but where hydrogen can create the highest value within an integrated future energy system. This question is particularly important for Vietnam, where electricity demand is expected to continue increasing while the country develops renewable energy and pursues net-zero emissions by 2050. Read more here
ETS Asia: As renewables, AI data centers expand, can Asia’s grids keep pace?
With its large population, growing economies and strong industrial base, Asia was the summit’s first destination outside Europe. Energy Tech Summit founder Skaiste Knyzaite said on Sept. 29 that the region’s energy transition is not only about cutting emissions, but also about supporting economic growth and maintaining energy security. Read more here
Energy Tech Summit Asia brought together energy and data center players to discuss rising power demand from AI. (Photo: Hsu Tsu-lin)
ETS Asia: What investors look for as climate tech moves from FOAK to scale
For climate technologies moving from the laboratory to the market, proving that the technology works is only the first hurdle. Building the first commercial-scale facility can require substantial capital, yet companies often lack the track record needed to secure bank financing.
On the second day of Energy Tech Summit Asia, discussions turned to this financing challenge. From first-of-a-kind (FOAK) projects to blended finance, investors and industry experts explored how emerging technologies can bridge the funding gap and move toward commercial scale. Read more here
Between ambition and trust: Tracking Southeast Asia’s climate transition
The latest United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report released in early September 2026 delivered a sobering notice. The world is set to cross the 1.5 degree Celsius global warming limit that 194 Parties to the Paris Agreement (minus the US) agreed to avoid hitting at all costs. This is the irreversible tipping point that scientists have been warning about for years. In other words, without concentrated and collective efforts to cut emissions, climate crises and the magnitude of disasters — from typhoons, cyclones, floods, to wildfires and the recent devastating Nepal landslide — will intensify. Read more here
Indonesia’s geothermal push runs into local fears at Mount Ungaran
Communities living near Mount Ungaran in Indonesia’s Central Java province have slammed plans to revive a geothermal power project there, saying it could threaten water supplies and farming livelihoods.
Indonesia sits in one of the most seismically active zones in the world, which gives it massive potential to generate electricity from geothermal energy: an estimated 23.2 gigawatts, according to the latest data from the Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources. The ministry describes Indonesia as having the world’s largest geothermal resource potential, ahead of countries including the United States and the Philippines. Read more here
Track ASEAN energy and carbon markets with clarity. Subscribe to RECCESSARY for policy intelligence and business-ready insights across Asia-Pacific.

articles.title: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027 - BBC
articles.summary: UK growth upgraded but energy prices and rates to bite in 2027  BBCUK economy to grow more than expected - but households face sharper rise in inflation, IMF says  Sky NewsIMF upgrades outlook for UK as AI drives growth spurt  Financial TimesUK inflation pressures hit three-year high; Nobel prize for economics awarded today – business live  The GuardianEconomic outlook: headwinds on the horizon  IFS | Institute for Fiscal Studies
articles.full_text:
The UK economy is forecast to grow by more than previously expected this year before higher energy prices and interest rates hit growth in 2027, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has said.
The organisation's latest report, which is closely watched by the government, said the UK economy would expand by 1.3% in 2026, up from the 1% it predicted in July, before slowing in 2027.
Economies across the world have proved more resilient to the energy price shock caused by the US-Iran war, the IMF said, but it warned the economic fallout from the conflict remained "highly uncertain".
Chancellor John Healey said the government would look to "provide some breathing space" for households in the Budget.
Healey is making the final preparations to Andy Burnham's new-look government's tax and spending plans, which will be announced on 28 October.
Government borrowing costs have surged, placing pressure on the chancellor to ensure his plans are credible in the eyes of financial markets, which the UK relies on to borrow money.
But IMF chief economist Silvana Tenreyro told BBC News on Tuesday that the UK's process of managing its debts is now leading the major G7 economies.
"As you know, the UK has already started the consolidation process and it is the country that basically stands out, along with India", she said.
The organisation said the UK is one of the only major economies on course to stabilise levels of national debt. It projects the UK will reduce its annual borrowing by nearly four percentage points of GDP from 2025 to 2031, significantly more than the rest of the G7, many of which are increasing their deficit over this time period.
The UK is also projected to have the lowest annual borrowing in the G7 in 2031, and the longest maturity of debt, locking in lower rates for longer.
Asked if the UK was one of the countries the IMF was telling to reduce borrowing, Tenreyro said that the country had begun the process already and should "stay the course".
The head of the IMF has previously called on the world's advanced economies to cut borrowing and reduce debt levels.
The reversal of downgrades to economic forecasts made at the start of the US-Iran war, mean the UK is expected to have the second-fasted growing economy in the G7 along with Germany.
But growth is estimated to slow in 2027 to 1.2% due to higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weighing on household spending and business investment.
Healey acknowledged that wars in the Middle East and Europe were "hitting people in the UK and around the world", but added that "Britain's economy is showing strong international resilience".
When the economy is growing, businesses tend to invest more, more jobs are created and people, on average, tend to feel better off. The opposite can occur if the economy stagnates or shrinks.
Maike Currie, head of personal finance for Pension Bee, told the BBC the IMF's report "does give the chancellor a little bit of breathing space" but that "it doesn't mean that families are feeling better off just yet and I don't think it is a gamechanger".
Economists have suggested Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget.
On Tuesday, the Resolution Foundation called on the chancellor to make "make repairs" to the public finances, but said well-targeted support was needed for those "struggling to heat their homes".
"The challenge of continuing to bring down borrowing must be paired with the pressing need for fresh cost of living support to help families facing a difficult winter ahead," the think tank said.
Andrew Griffith, Conservative shadow chancellor, said if Healey "reaches for more tax rises" in his Budget, "he is choosing slower growth and working people will pay for it".
Burnham has pledged to create "good growth in every postcode" as part of his plans to giving nations and regions more control, but his strategy has faced criticism inside his own party.
The IMF said households are likely to continue feeling the pinch of rising prices, with inflation expected to average 3.3% this year and remain above the Bank of England's 2% target in 2027 at 2.8%.
The Bank itself has predicted inflation could rise above 4% at the beginning of next year - making it more likely that interest rates will rise.
Healey is expected to meet with other finance ministers at the IMF's annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, on Tuesday to discuss how the economic impact of the Middle East and European conflicts could be limited.
The IMF said the global economy had shown a "remarkable capacity to absorb shocks" not just from the current Middle East conflict, but also from the Covid pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

articles.full_text:
And that concludes our live blog coverage for today.
We’ll be back at 7am tomorrow. Have a good evening.
Welcome back to City AM‘s FTSE 100 live blog.
The UK’s blue-chip index is set to make gains on Monday morning, picking up where Friday’s rally left off. Oil prices fell in early trading, as Brent crude – the international benchmark for oil – dipped below $104 per barrel following President Trump’s plans to import Russian diesel.
Stick with us throughout the day for the latest news from the London Stock Exchange and the wider business world, as soon as we get it.
Here’s a few of our top headlines this morning:
By Felix Armstrong
Here’s a look at your closing London Stock Exchange market moves, with 20 minutes left until the closing bell.
The biggest riser on the FTSE 100 is ConvaTec Group Plc which has jumped 4.3 per cent, followed by Lion Finance Group Plc which is up 3.2 per cent. The biggest faller is Vodafone Group plc which has dropped 1.8 per cent.
Over on the mid-cap FTSE 250, the biggest riser is GlobalData plc which is up 6.3 per cent, while the biggest faller is Hays plc which is down 12.1 per cent.
Meanwhile on the small-cap AIM 100, Cohort plc is the biggest gainer, rising 5.6 per cent, while ActiveOps plc is the biggest faller, sinking 47.5 per cent.
By Samuel Norman
Wall Street was little changed on Monday after a booming week for New York’s indices.
The S&P 500 traded around the flatline, while the Dow Jones edged up slightly by 0.2 per cent.
But the tech-heavy Nasdaq struggled into the red, down 0.2 per cent.
The group behind the hack of fast-fashion retailer Asos have claimed responsibility for a data breach of airline group Air France-KLM.
The individuals who hacked into the e-commerce firm, who call themselves Xuanye Group, last week circulated data which they claimed was obtained from the airline group.
Air France-KLM confirmed that it recently detected a data breach and the Asos hackers told City AM they are behind it.
Read the full story here.
Top Bank of England aficionados are speaking at the IMF this week and one influential rate-setter has called for more optimism around AI.
Sarah Breeden, deputy governor for financial stability at the central bank, said the UK needs to “think ahead” on the future use cases of AI for “how we might need to act now to be resilient about them”.
“What we’re focused on is how an increasingly autonomous financial system that’s operating at speed and scale might do things that we’re not expecting it to… that might be because AI is in the hands of bad actors or it might be that AI agents have gone rogue.”
But the central bank official, who is also tasked with overseeing payments innovation and fintech, added that “AI as a general purpose technology and then innovation has got to be our best pathway at getting growth”.
“We should be optimists about AI.. we’ve been talking a long time about how our economies need growth,” Breeden said.
Oil prices are ticking back upwards in the early afternoon.
Brent crude had been showing modest losses this morning but has now gained more than one per cent and is nearing the $106 per barrel mark.
Neil Wilson, a strategist at Saxo, said Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh airport are spooking traders.
President Trump’s claims of an energy ceasefire betweeen Russia and Ukraine were “muddy” and the deal to purchase some Russian diesel is a “drop in the ocean,” he said.
The Bank of England has been targeted in an inflation installation stunt in the centre of the City of London.
A black canon printer, sitting atop a decorative silver-beaded pedestal surrounded by a stream of banknotes, was locked inside a tall transparent display case. The case, held up by a bright red frame, read: “In case of emergency inflation. Break Glass.”
A pair of black handcuffs were also resting on the base of the pedestal.
The installation appears to satirise a Bank of England strategy known as “quantitative easing,” that involves the creation of new money to purchase government bonds from private institutions.
The method aims to inject liquidity into the financial system in a bid to lower interest rates, encourage borrowing and stimulate spending.

articles.title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year - The Guardian
articles.summary: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year  The GuardianEU hybrid curbs to offer only ‘temporary’ respite against Chinese carmakers  Financial TimesChina's $7.5 billion EU hybrid boom faces new curbs under China-EU deal  ReutersEU’s China trade breakthrough risks taking pressure off Beijing  Euronews.comThe EU-China trade and investment understanding: a welcome buying of time  Bruegel
articles.full_text:
The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.
Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.

The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.
The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.
Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.
Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.
China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.
As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.
Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.
“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.
Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.
On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.
The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.
Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.
Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.
“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.
Andrew Small, the director of the Asia programme at the European Council for Foreign Relations, said China was likely to “suck the EU into drawn-out negotiations” on other sectors but the mood had changed in the EU.
“I think if China had offered a deal like this earlier in the year, say in spring, it would have been much easier to take the heat out. My sense is that things have now moved somewhat too far politically,” he said.

articles.title: Malaysia wants Europe to bring tech, high-paying jobs — not just investment - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Malaysia wants Europe to bring tech, high-paying jobs — not just investment  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia wants European investments to deliver technology transfer, develop highly skilled talent and create better-paying jobs as the country seeks to move up the global value chain amid intensifying economic competition between the US and China.
Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said Malaysia would place greater emphasis on the quality and long-term value of inbound investments as it moves into its next phase of economic development.
"We want investments that facilitate technology transfer, develop highly skilled talent, generate more opportunities for local businesses and create better-paying, high-skilled jobs for Malaysians.
"Ultimately, our objective is to move beyond simply participating in global value chains to capturing and creating greater value within them," he said in his keynote address at European Union (EU)-Malaysia Business Day 2026: Selangor in Focus here today.
Johari said the global political and economic landscape was undergoing a profound transformation, with countries increasingly prioritising the protection of domestic industries and strategic economic interests, often at the expense of global economic integration and the multilateral trading system.
He said heightened strategic competition between the US and China had become a defining feature of the new economic nationalism, particularly in the race for leadership in artificial intelligence (AI), critical minerals, advanced manufacturing and defence technologies.
The US has a gross domestic product (GDP) of approximately US$32 trillion, while China's economy is valued at about US$19 trillion, compared with Malaysia's roughly US$470 billion economy.
"These developments are compelling countries around the world, including Malaysia, to reassess their economic strategies," he said.
Johari said the US had pursued an increasingly aggressive and unilateral tariff regime affecting many of its major trading partners.
Meanwhile, the growing international presence of Chinese companies, backed by China's substantial manufacturing capacity and technological capabilities, was reshaping competitive dynamics across industries and markets.
"As a highly open economy deeply integrated into global supply chains, Malaysia would continue to engage constructively with all its economic partners.
"We strongly believe that dialogue and cooperation must always take precedence over unilateral action," he said.
Johari said there was considerable scope for Malaysia and the EU to deepen cooperation in diversifying trading relationships, strengthening supply chain resilience and unlocking opportunities in areas of mutual interest.
These include semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, renewable energy, and green and digital technologies.
He said Malaysia did not believe its economic future should be defined by a choice between East and West, as the country intended to maintain and strengthen relationships with partners prepared to innovate and grow on the basis of mutual respect and benefit.
The EU remained one of Malaysia's most important economic partners, with total bilateral trade amounting to RM228.1 billion in 2025.
Malaysia exported RM129.3 billion worth of goods to the bloc and imported RM98.9 billion, resulting in a trade surplus of approximately RM30.3 billion.
Johari said European companies had established a significant and longstanding presence in Malaysia, contributing to the development of its industrial base, introducing advanced technologies and creating employment opportunities for Malaysians.
In return, Malaysia offered European investors an established manufacturing ecosystem, a skilled workforce and a strategic base from which to access the broader Asean market.
As Malaysia sought to strengthen its technological capabilities and develop industries of greater economic complexity, he said the government was ready to work with European companies to identify new projects, facilitate investments and bring the right partners together.
Malaysia also wanted to help local companies expand into Europe and establish stronger commercial links.
"We must turn the goodwill and longstanding relationships we have built into concrete commercial opportunities, new investments and partnerships that deliver lasting economic value to both sides," he said.
Johari said the proposed Malaysia-EU Free Trade Agreement (MEUFTA), which both sides are negotiating, would be an important catalyst for the next phase of their economic relationship.
He said a comprehensive, balanced and mutually beneficial agreement would strengthen market access, facilitate trade and investment, and provide a stronger foundation for future economic cooperation.
He added that such an agreement would reinforce Malaysia's position as an attractive investment destination and an important gateway for European businesses seeking to expand their participation in the growing Asean economy.

articles.title: IMF Warns Europe’s Growth Will Slow as Russia’s War, Middle East Crisis Drive Up Energy Costs - Kyiv Post
articles.summary: IMF Warns Europe’s Growth Will Slow as Russia’s War, Middle East Crisis Drive Up Energy Costs  Kyiv Post
articles.full_text:
Economic growth in the eurozone is expected to slow to just 1.1% in 2026 as Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine and escalating conflict in the Middle East push energy prices higher, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned in its latest World Economic Outlook.
The forecast, released Tuesday, Oct. 13, represents a modest 0.2-percentage-point upgrade from July but remains below the 1.2% growth recorded in 2025.
The IMF expects the eurozone economy to expand by only 1.2% in 2027, with persistently high energy costs, weak consumer confidence and inflation continuing to constrain economic activity.
The Fund forecasts eurozone inflation at 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year – both significantly above the European Central Bank’s 2% target.
The figures underscore Europe’s vulnerability to energy disruptions as Russia continues its invasion of Ukraine and instability across the Middle East threatens global oil and natural gas supplies.
Russia’s war and Middle East crisis expose Europe’s energy vulnerability
The IMF warned that elevated energy costs could continue weighing on European households and businesses through next year.
Europe remains particularly vulnerable because many of its economies depend heavily on imported oil and natural gas.
The Fund warned that gas storage levels in parts of Europe remain below normal seasonal levels, potentially exposing consumers to further price increases during the winter heating season.
The combination of higher energy costs and persistent inflation could force the European Central Bank to maintain restrictive interest rates, limiting household spending and business investment.
The IMF expects underlying inflation to return to the ECB’s 2% target only around mid-2028, suggesting that price pressures could persist even if economic growth remains weak.
The latest projections also follow a volatile period for the eurozone economy, which recorded no growth in the first quarter of 2026 before rebounding by 2.6% in the second quarter.
Germany outperforms France as UK faces slower growth
The IMF projects significant differences among Europe’s largest economies.
Germany, the EU’s biggest economy, is expected to grow by 1.3% in 2026, while Spain is forecast to maintain stronger expansion of 2.5%.
France faces a much weaker outlook, with growth projected at just 0.4%, compared with 0.9% in 2025.
French unemployment is expected to rise to 8.4%, up from 7.7% last year.
For Britain, the IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast to 1.3%, an increase of 0.3 percentage points from July.
However, UK growth is expected to slow to 1.2% in 2027 as higher energy prices and borrowing costs weigh on consumption and investment.
The diverging forecasts reflect the uneven economic consequences of energy shocks and financial pressures across Europe.
IMF warns Middle East oil exporters face sharp contraction
During the World Economic Outlook press briefing, IMF officials said the economic consequences of the Middle East conflict differ sharply between oil-producing and oil-importing countries.
An IMF official said the Fund had revised its forecasts shortly before publication to account for higher oil prices, while warning that further escalation could worsen the outlook.
“We actually revised in the last minute almost our forecast to incorporate the higher oil prices,” the official said.
For Gulf oil exporters, the IMF forecasts a sharp contraction in production and exports, followed by a strong rebound in 2027, assuming conditions develop as projected.
Some of these economies are also experiencing slower growth in non-oil sectors.
Oil-importing countries, however, received modest forecast upgrades in several cases, supported by domestic demand, remittances and tourism.
Egypt was among the countries benefiting from upward revisions for both 2026 and 2027, partly because of a recovery in Suez Canal activity and petroleum-related industries.
But officials warned that renewed Houthi attacks and disruptions around the Bab al-Mandab Strait could jeopardize regional trade, shipping and economic activity.
AI boom shields global trade – but raises new economic risks
The IMF also highlighted the growing importance of artificial intelligence in sustaining international trade despite geopolitical instability.
Responding to questions from Bloomberg and Reuters about whether the global economy could face a recession if the AI investment boom collapsed, an IMF official said demand for AI-related products had made a substantial contribution to trade growth.
Global trade expanded by a cumulative 8.3% between 2023 and 2025, while trade in AI-related goods increased by 29%.
Without AI-related products, overall trade growth would have reached just 4.6%, according to the Fund’s calculations.
The IMF outlined several possible scenarios for the technology boom.
In the most favorable case, continued investment in AI would generate genuine productivity improvements, strengthening economic activity without adding to inflation.
A less favorable scenario would see investment and demand remain strong without corresponding productivity gains, producing weaker growth benefits and greater inflationary pressure.
The Fund is also examining the consequences of investors reassessing expected profits from AI, potentially triggering a correction in asset prices.
The IMF’s latest assessment suggests that the technology sector has become an increasingly important source of global economic resilience, even as its future contribution remains uncertain.

Kyiv • UNN
China and the EU have reached a preliminary agreement to limit supplies of Chinese hybrids. The new measures could take effect on December 1.
China and the European Union have reached a preliminary agreement to limit the export of Chinese hybrid vehicles to the European market. Beijing hopes this will help it avoid tougher trade restrictions from the EU. Bloomberg reports, according to UNN.
Details
The negotiations concluded with an agreement on 16 points covering trade, investment, export controls, and intellectual property protection. One of the key outcomes was China’s agreement to reduce supplies of hybrid vehicles to Europe.
According to Bloomberg, the European Union is preparing safeguard measures against excessive imports. In particular, it is considering tariff quotas that would impose additional duties on vehicles once the established supply volume is exceeded.
Why the EU wants to limit Chinese cars
Chinese manufacturers are actively expanding their presence in Europe, in part because hybrid vehicles were not subject to the duties imposed by the EU on Chinese electric vehicles in 2024. In August, Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales.
At the same time, the EU’s trade deficit in relations with China exceeds €1 billion a day. Germany and France have already called for tougher measures to protect European manufacturers.
According to Bloomberg sources, the new restrictions could take effect on December 1. At the same time, the parties plan to continue negotiations in January and March, as the agreement reached so far does not resolve the fundamental trade disputes between the EU and China.

articles.title: Russia Launches Manhunt for Europe’s Top Defense Executives, FT Reports - UNITED24 Media
articles.summary: Russia Launches Manhunt for Europe’s Top Defense Executives, FT Reports  UNITED24 MediaRussia steps up bid to kill European defence chiefs, spy agencies warn  Financial TimesRussia is targeting heads of defence companies. Europe has already had warning signals  Defence24.comEuropean security agencies warned about Russian sabotage plans  The Brussels TimesRussia steps up assassination attempts targeting defence company executives in Europe, FT says &nb...
articles.full_text:
Russia is reportedly targeting senior executives and key employees of European defense companies for assassination, as Moscow expands covert operations aimed at intimidating arms manufacturers and disrupting military support for Ukraine.
According to the Financial Times on October 11, intelligence officials from five European countries warned that Russian intelligence agencies are increasingly targeting personnel at both major defense manufacturers and smaller companies, particularly those producing drones and military equipment for Ukraine.
European intelligence services have already identified and disrupted several suspected Russian operations, including cases involving surveillance of potential targets near their homes and workplaces.
Officials believe Russia’s military intelligence agency, commonly known as the GRU, is coordinating much of the activity. Russian operatives are reportedly working with organized criminal networks, recruiting local intermediaries, and distributing assignments among individuals operating across different countries.
The use of criminal organizations allows Russian intelligence services to conduct operations through intermediaries while making it more difficult for investigators to establish direct connections to Moscow.
Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), has increased its engagement with defense companies in response to the threat. Executives and employees have been advised to strengthen security arrangements, including hiring private protection.
BfV President Sinan Selen has warned German lawmakers that Russia is deliberately planning violent attacks against individuals, with organized criminal groups playing an increasingly prominent role in such operations.
Several defense industry executives told the Financial Times that they had increased personal security over the past six months following warnings from intelligence services. Others have introduced additional protective measures when traveling internationally.
The growing security requirements are also creating financial challenges for defense manufacturers. Smaller companies and startups face potentially significant expenses associated with protecting employees, facilities, and sensitive operations.
According to the FT, one defense company relocated its production operations to another part of Western Europe because of threats attributed to Russia.
European intelligence officials believe the reported assassination plots are intended not only to eliminate specific individuals but also to intimidate the wider defense industry.
By making executives and employees fear becoming targets, Moscow reportedly hopes to discourage European manufacturers from supplying weapons, drones, and military technologies to Ukraine.
The Financial Times also reported that some suspected Russian operatives have demonstrated limited operational capabilities, allowing European security services to detect surveillance activities and prevent planned attacks.
The reported threats follow an earlier Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, CEO of German defense manufacturer Rheinmetall. In January 2025, NATO confirmed that US and German intelligence agencies had thwarted the assassination plan, which was reportedly part of a broader campaign targeting European defense industry leaders supplying Ukraine.

articles.title: EU-China trade talks grapple with tariffs, rare earths, and export controls - The Brussels Times
articles.summary: EU-China trade talks grapple with tariffs, rare earths, and export controls  The Brussels Times
articles.full_text:
EU and Chinese trade chiefs agreed to hold further talks on tariffs, export controls and market access after meeting in Beijing on 8 – 9 October 2026.
China’s Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met Maroš Šefčovič, the European Commission’s Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security, Interinstitutional Relations and Transparency, for the second meeting of the EU-China Trade and Investment Consultations, the European Commission announced on Friday.
Both sides reaffirmed they would handle differences within World Trade Organization rules and continue work intended to stabilise and make the bilateral relationship “more balanced”, according to a joint statement published by the Commission.
A third ministerial meeting was scheduled for March 2027, with a ministerial video conference planned for January before that.
Hybrid vehicles, rare earths and market access
The EU and China said they would explore the possibility of reducing or eliminating tariffs on certain goods within WTO rules, according to the statement.
The two sides stated they had reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles “in a WTO compliant manner”, while also recalling a guidance document on “price undertakings” in the EU’s battery electric vehicles anti-subsidy case — a process in which companies can agree minimum prices to address subsidy concerns — and said they would continue related procedures.
They also agreed to continue dialogue on access to each other’s markets for medical devices, with the EU welcoming China’s stated effort to increase imports of EU medical devices, including through a matchmaking event during the 9th China International Import Expo.
China said it would accelerate recognition of the “regionalisation principle” for eligible EU member states — a risk-based approach that can limit trade restrictions to affected areas — and both sides agreed to exchange methods and technologies for disease control as they explore lifting restrictions on animal products affected by bluetongue disease.
On export controls, the EU and China said they would strengthen their export control dialogue and increase exchanges on their respective policies.
China said it was willing to continue facilitating export licences for rare earths and permanent magnets to the EU through a fast-track mechanism, while the EU said it would continue working with member state authorities to facilitate specific priority licences to China in “dual-use” sectors — goods that can have both civilian and military applications.
The two sides also said they had reached an understanding to provide advance warning and improve transparency around the listing and delisting of entities under export control procedures.
The statement added that the EU and China would continue work on intellectual property issues through an EU-China Intellectual Property Working Group and strengthen communication on WTO reform.

articles.title: ECB's Patsalides says monetary policy has limits against inflation shocks - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: ECB's Patsalides says monetary policy has limits against inflation shocks  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
What he told lawmakers and reporters
Speaking in Nicosia on Monday, Patsalides cautioned that there is only so much central bankers can do when inflation is driven by forces outside their control. "A central bank's monetary policy cannot solve wars, fiscal problems, or supply chain issues," he said. He also urged people to be realistic about what officials can achieve if gas or oil prices climb again.
Why this inflation fight is hard
Right now, where consumer prices go next is closely linked to how long the conflict in the Middle East drags on. That puts the ECB up against forces it cannot directly influence. As Patsalides put it, if price pressures come from other causes, interest rates will not control them.
Central bankers admitting the limits of policy is itself informative. Market Briefs covers the ECB free every morning.
Policy into year end
Patsalides noted, "The ECB has raised interest rates." He added that decisions are based on the data, and the outlook is shaky: "the landscape has become highly unpredictable; everything could change by December." Against that backdrop, borrowing costs have already gone up and another increase is probable by year's end.
What it means for your money
The takeaway is simple: the ECB will follow the data, but if oil or gas spike again, rate moves have limited sway over that kind of inflation, and the situation could shift by December. That mix makes near term outcomes uncertain, so keep your expectations flexible and your time horizon in mind.
