articles.summary: Britain won't tolerate threats on our soil, Miliband says as he summons Iran ambassador  BBCIran’s Revolutionary Guards ‘almost certainly’ behind RAF Fairford threats, says Burnham  The GuardianJoint Statement on the United Kingdom’s Attribution of Iran’s Involvement in Attempted Terrorist Attack at RAF Fairford  U.S. Department of State (.gov)UK blames Iran for airbase plot, sanctions two Iranian nationals  Al JazeeraUK PM Burnham says Iran's IRGC likely ...
articles.full_text:
The foreign secretary has summoned the Iranian ambassador to make clear that "Britain will not tolerate threats on our soil" following last month's incident at RAF Fairford.
Ed Miliband said attempts by Iran to undermine the UK's security "through its criminal networks, proxy groups and state-backed malign activity is unacceptable".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham told MPs the incident in Gloucestershire was "almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard", while the home secretary said the likely coordinator was a "known individual based in Iran".
Iran's ambassador to the UK, Seyed Ali Mousavi, said Tehran was not involved and was willing to cooperate with British authorities.
The Foreign Office has also sanctioned two Iranians, including the head of the regime's counterespionage operations - with both men subjected to travel bans and asset freezes.
Burnham also indicated Iran could be hit with further sanctions over its suspected role.
It comes as the UK and 28 other countries - including the US, Canada, Australia, France and Germany - issued a joint statement condemning "in the strongest terms" violent attacks by Iran.
The statement accuses Tehran of carrying out "lethal plotting, arson, sabotage, cyber-attacks, and other hybrid activities" and also recognises the UK's attribution of Iranian involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.
A huge police operation began after officers were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base in the early hours of 27 September.
Dozens of homes were evacuated in the nearby village of Whelford and a large cordon was put in place around the site.
So far, a total of seven men - all in their 20s - have been arrested and later bailed in connection with the incident. No one has been charged.
Last week, Downing Street insisted the airbase was safe after the US withdrew all of its bombers – about a dozen B-1s from the base – back to their home stations on American soil.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the US air force for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved an American request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
A US state department spokesman confirmed that US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had a call with Miliband on Monday where they discussed "holding Iran to account for its actions and of continued collaboration to secure US assets in the United Kingdom".

articles.title: Trump’s Russian Diesel Debacle Risks Backfiring - The Moscow Times
articles.summary: Trump’s Russian Diesel Debacle Risks Backfiring  The Moscow TimesTrump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia  BBCUkraine war briefing: Russian diesel exports could return to past levels after Trump deal, Moscow claims  The GuardianTrump turns on Europe after Putin deal  The TelegraphRussia deal, execution plans and deportations tell a defining tale about Trump and power  CNN
articles.full_text:
President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 9 that the United States would begin importing Russian diesel has roiled transatlantic relations. Such abrupt and dizzying shifts have been a consistent feature of Trump’s war diplomacy.
To assess its significance, we must distinguish the genuinely new from the wearily familiar. Since there is less to this policy than meets the eye, it is unlikely to have any real impact on the course of the war. Its few novel aspects will merely compound failure with ignominy.
This latest initiative resembles earlier Trumpian forays in three ways.
First, it restores Trump’s natural preference for Russia. Despite taking occasional steps that displeased Moscow, such as sanctioning its two biggest oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, Trump always returns to his default setting of rewarding Russia and pressuring Ukraine. Since the fighting can only stop if Moscow is decisively constrained from achieving its war aims, such a policy pursues the opposite of what is needed to end the war. It thus cannot succeed in its strategic goal.
Second, Trump’s main goal is to restore economic ties with Russia and, above all, to make new energy deals. Moscow has repeatedly dangled the carrots of huge investment proposals to American negotiators. While Trump’s latest move concerns energy trade, not investment, even this is not new. From March to June this year, the U.S. granted a temporary license allowing Russia to ship crude and oil products to mitigate the supply shock caused by the war with Iran.
Third, in importing Russian fuel without a quid pro quo, the White House is not striking a deal but making a unilateral concession to Moscow that weakens its negotiating position. Again, this is not new. In 2025, America abandoned earlier positions, notably by dropping the demand on Russia for an immediate ceasefire and the threat of new sanctions. In doing so, it surrendered its leverage and put its own objectives further out of reach. Now, it is repeating this error.
So what is new and consequential about the diesel deal? First, it is driven not by the prospect of lucrative deals for those around the White House, but by the urgent political need to reduce domestic fuel prices before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3.
Unlike the temporary waiver in March, which allowed more Russian oil onto the world market, the new volumes will be shipped specifically to the U.S. For this reason, it may be found illegal. A bipartisan group of senators has already declared that the trade would violate the 2022 ban on Russian energy imports and has called for the administration to “immediately reverse course.” The trade also cuts directly across the Lindsey Graham Act, passed with overwhelming congressional support last month, which included provisions to punish major importers of Russian oil.
Second, even in its own terms, the deal may fail. The modest volumes are too small to have any significant effect on prices at the pump and will likely arrive too late for the midterms.
Moreover, Russia may not even be able to deliver them. While it could make use of the temporary waiver Washington granted earlier this year to sell more oil products, Ukrainian attacks on its refineries caused exports to collapse in June. Russia imposed an export ban in July to stem and secure its own supply, but has now lifted it to export to the U.S. But its ability to do so will depend on the perilous security of its energy infrastructure.
All this lays bare the central contradiction in Trump’s position. On the one hand, he attributes the global fuel shortage to Ukraine’s attacks on Russian facilities when his own war against Iran is primarily responsible for the worldwide fuel deficit. On the other hand, he claims that supplies from Russia can meet the shortages that its absence from the market has created.
Third, America has reportedly threatened to cut off Ukraine’s access to intelligence and the PURL program if it continues to target Russian refineries. We have been here before, too. Washington suspended such support for brief periods several times in 2025, most severely in March, and issued similar threats last November to try to compel Zelensky to accept the administration’s 28-point peace plan. These cut-offs lasted only a few days, but hindered Ukraine’s operations.
What is new is the prospect of a longer, perhaps permanent, cut-off from all assistance that would be harmful to Kyiv, but not fatal. Ukraine has developed its own long-range strike weapons and Europe can provide some intelligence. The most serious consequence would be the loss of critically needed Patriot interceptors, 95% of which are obtained for Ukraine through PURL.
But America’s defense industry would suffer too. It would lose not only billions of dollars in weapons sales paid by Europe and delivered to Ukraine, but potentially also Kyiv’s cooperation as a unique and valuable source of technology and data. These losses would far outweigh any impact of a small, brief fall in domestic fuel prices.
In short, much about the diesel deal is a repeat of past efforts. Since it shares their flaws, it will share their failure.
But it adds contradictions of its own: trivial volumes of fuel that may not even arrive and are likely illegal if they do; threats that, if carried out, would hurt America’s national security.
Fresh absurdities appear every day. In its dealings with Russia, the administration has reportedly tried to offer assets, frozen in Europe, that it does not control; has proposed reviving the Nord Stream gas pipeline, a move that would require Europe’s consent; and has announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that neither country was aware of. This is a policy approaching total incoherence.
It was said of the Bourbon dynasty that it learned nothing and forgot nothing. History may record of this White House that, on its Russia policy at least, it learned nothing and understood nothing. Other countries have learned, to their cost, the lessons that await. When policy is driven by venal ineptitude rather than a judicious understanding of the national interest, the result is a masterclass in strategic failure.

articles.title: UK Growth Figures, US Inflation and French Protests: Sterling Update - FrenchEntrée
articles.summary: UK Growth Figures, US Inflation and French Protests: Sterling Update  FrenchEntrée
articles.full_text:
Here’s the latest currency news from our partner Moneycorp, to help you find out what your money is worth.
Sterling faces a busy week, with UK monthly activity figures and a series of Bank of England speeches likely to shape expectations for interest rates. Meanwhile, the euro remains under pressure from political uncertainty and protests in France and Spain, while markets await the latest US inflation data for clues on the Federal Reserve’s next move.
The International Monetary Fund’s latest global economic forecasts will also be in focus, with concerns over weak growth, rising borrowing costs and geopolitical tensions weighing on the outlook. Across North America, comments from the Bank of Canada and continued pressure on the Mexican peso add to a packed week for currency markets.
UK monthly activity figures in focus, alongside Bank of England speeches
This week sees the release of UK monthly activity figures for August on Thursday, alongside a series of Bank of England speakers throughout the week.
The case for a further increase in official interest rates continues to centre on inflationary pressures, although there remain limited signs that these pressures are being driven by the domestic economy.
Sterling remains under pressure against the US dollar but continues to hold up well against the euro. This divergence appears to be driven more by developments in those economies than by domestic UK factors.
One additional area of interest is today’s parliamentary debate on rejoining the European Union. However, this is unlikely to alter the UK’s position on EU membership in the near term, in my view.
IMF forecasts to offer few crumbs of comfort
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) will release its full global economic report this week, following earlier warnings about rising debt servicing costs.
The report, due on Tuesday, is unlikely to offer much relief to financial markets, given weak global growth, geopolitical tensions and further increases in government borrowing costs.
There could be downward revisions to growth expectations across the UK, the euro area and North America.
US CPI figures for September in focus this week
This week is likely to see considerable attention focused on the US consumer price index (CPI) inflation figures for September, due on Wednesday.
Markets will be watching to see whether core inflationary pressures have picked up or whether inflation remains largely concentrated in more volatile headline components such as energy, fuel and food.
Producer price index (PPI) figures, industrial production data and Federal Reserve staff projections are also due this week. However, alongside the CPI figures, comments from Fed officials are likely to attract the greatest attention.
Will the Fed argue for a further immediate increase in interest rates, or are concerns about parts of the US economy sufficient to keep policymakers on hold at their meeting at the end of October?
In my view, US dollar strength may prove another factor arguing against an additional rate increase at this month’s meeting.
Energy markets could also remain in focus, as renewed tensions in the Middle East and recent comments from President Trump regarding a possible energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine add another layer of uncertainty to the inflation outlook.
ECB speeches and political uncertainty to determine euro direction
The European Central Bank (ECB) appears to be preparing markets for another interest rate increase, potentially as early as the Governing Council meeting at the end of October.
Speeches last week indicated that several ECB officials believe acting sooner could provide a credibility boost to their efforts to tackle inflation, although I would question that assessment.
This week brings further appearances from policymakers, including Lane and Schnabel. Schnabel is also in focus as the candidate list for her Executive Board position closes the day before the ECB Governing Council decision.
There is also likely to be significant interest in developments in Spain and France, where protests showed little sign of easing over the course of last week.
Unless these political disruptions begin to ease, pressure on the euro could increase as downside risks to growth continue to build, in my view.
Bank of Canada speeches dominate as Mexican peso remains under pressure
Monetary policy signals from the Bank of Canada (BoC) will come primarily through three speeches this week.
Governor Tiff Macklem is scheduled to speak on Wednesday, 14 October, and Friday, 16 October, while Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers is due to speak on Thursday, 15 October.
Ahead of the Bank’s late October rate decision, markets will focus on how policymakers interpret the latest economic data, particularly employment and activity figures. The Canadian dollar could weaken further if it appears unlikely that the BoC will sanction a rate increase.
In Mexico, last week’s inflation and vehicle production figures have added to pressure on the peso.
The Bank of Mexico has left interest rates unchanged for several months, and recent data suggests it may need to consider reducing rates, despite several other central banks continuing to debate further tightening.
Peso weakness could therefore continue this week, with little on the economic calendar, or in diplomatic developments around trade and border tensions, likely to alter the prevailing direction of travel.

articles.title: Monetary, fiscal coordination needed to address climate change in EU - Green Central Banking
articles.summary: Monetary, fiscal coordination needed to address climate change in EU  Green Central Banking
articles.full_text:
Key points
- Economists say central banks cannot tackle climate-driven inflation and supply shocks alone, urging closer coordination with fiscal policy.
- Higher interest rates can squeeze public spending and make green investment more expensive, prompting calls for a lower green rate and expanded ECB green collateral rules.
- The European Commission warned that extreme weather is already hitting revenues, spending, growth and public budgets.
- ECB research found heatwave-hit regions see activity fall by 1.5% after two years and 3% after four years, strengthening the case for both adaptation and decarbonisation.
Europe cannot rely on central banks alone to manage the economic fallout from climate change, economists warned at a European Parliament panel, calling for closer coordination between monetary and fiscal policy.
“Coordination between central banks and government is not something new. It’s something that’s happening already, but in much more of a kind of reactive sense,” said Jaya Sood, a senior economist at the New Economics Foundation in London, during a panel organised by the New Economics Foundation and cross-party group of MEPs..
Sood highlighted the ability for governments to use targeted fiscal measures to address price pressures, rather than leaving it entirely to central banks to solve.
“This is just about coordination on being on the front foot versus coordination that sort of comes from crises.”
While the European Central Bank (ECB) has taken steps to green its collateral, monetary policy alone can’t address the supply shocks from climate change. Adding to the complication is that increased interest rates could constrain fiscal spending, according to Romain Svartzman, a professor at Bocconi University and former economist at the Banque de France.
“When there are increasing interest rates, you usually have a decrease of fiscal spending, government expenditure on key sectors, be it health, climate and population age in general,” he said during the panel.
Increased rates can also make borrowing more expensive for green projects. Campaigners have been pushing for the ECB to consider a green interest rate, or a rate that is lower than the threshold if applied to transition projects, to increase investments in renewables.
Another potential way to address the impact of interest rates is for the ECB to expand its green collateral framework to include sovereign bonds, Svartzman said. The ECB could also to reconsider how forward-looking it views inflation targets, as central banks tend to only consider inflation targets over the medium term of one to three years.
But if inflation is generated by a dynamic that will increase climate resilience in 5, 10, or 15 years, “do you still want to increase interest rates?” he asked.
Nicola Gagliardi, senior economist at the Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs at the European Commission, said the commission is aware of the economic and fiscal impact of climate change and that the “impacts on the public budget… is really clear-cut” as disruptions from extreme weather events could mean lower incomes and more uncertainty.
“All this turns into impacts on expenditure, clearly on revenues and on growth… whether we look at physical or transition risks,” he said.
The panel was held just a few weeks after European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen announced a new framework for climate resilience would be released in late October.
Irene Heemskerk, head of the climate change centre at the European Central Bank, welcomed current efforts in Brussels to look at climate adaptation but warned that “we cannot live in a 3 Celsius world so we should not lose sight of still making the transition happen”.
While the EU economy has so far been resilient to increasing energy prices and the stresses from the summer’s extreme weather, ECB research shows that economic activity in regions hit by heatwaves is, on average, 1.5% lower two years later and 3% lower four years later.
Economists have estimated that the 2026 barrage of heatwaves could decrease the EU economy by at least 1%, with larger losses in areas hit harder by the summer’s unbearable heat such as France and Italy.
While the heatwaves caused a decline in renewables in some countries, those in the EU bloc that have a mix of renewables have been hit less by energy prices, Heemskerk said, which “makes the case for making the transition happen”.
The ECB is going “step-by-step” with what it already has in place, even as there is a lot of uncertainty about climate change and the transition, Heemskerk said. It has still “stayed the course” on climate issues as its efforts have been “anchored within our mandate”.
She added: “When we published our climate and nature update or strategy in January, this was the message, and we stayed the course because we see there’s an increasing impact.”
This page was last updated October 9, 2026

articles.title: Can Europe Curb China’s $7.5 Billion Hybrid Car Boom Without Triggering a Trade War? - Modern Diplomacy
articles.summary: Can Europe Curb China’s $7.5 Billion Hybrid Car Boom Without Triggering a Trade War?  Modern Diplomacy
articles.full_text:
China’s fast-growing hybrid vehicle exports to Europe face fresh uncertainty after Beijing agreed to curb shipments to the European Union, threatening a key growth channel for Chinese automakers as domestic demand slows and competition intensifies.
Chinese exports of hybrid vehicles to the EU’s 27 member states tripled to $7.5 billion in the first half of 2026 from $2.5 billion a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data. The figure was nearly nine times the $845 million recorded for the whole of 2021.
The surge followed the EU’s introduction of additional tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles in 2024. Plug-in hybrids were exempt from the extra duties, prompting manufacturers to expand shipments of models that combine electric driving with conventional engines.
Demand has also benefited from limited charging infrastructure in parts of Europe, where consumers value the longer driving range and fuel efficiency offered by plug-in hybrids.
Chinese manufacturers SAIC, BYD and Chery accounted for more than 90% of Chinese hybrid sales volume in the EU, while hybrids represented more than half of their European sales, according to Jefferies.
The emerging agreement could restrict this expansion, although its practical impact will depend on how Beijing and Brussels implement the arrangements.
China’s Automakers Face a New Trade Barrier
The EU agreement marks a potential shift in the trade dispute over Chinese electric vehicles, with restrictions on hybrid exports now threatening another important route into the European market.
Chinese brands captured a record 15% share of Europe’s electric vehicle market in the second quarter, up from 9.5% in the first quarter of 2024. Chinese plug-in hybrids have expanded even more rapidly, accounting for more than a quarter of the segment after holding just 1.7% at the beginning of 2024, according to Schmidt Automotive Research.
The growth has intensified competition for European manufacturers, including Volkswagen, which has traditionally held a strong position in the plug-in hybrid market.
Felipe Munoz of Car Industry Analysis said the agreement would make conditions more difficult for Chinese manufacturers but was unlikely to stop their expansion into Europe entirely.
He argued that European policymakers would eventually have to decide how far they wanted to protect domestic manufacturers against growing Chinese competition.
Quotas Could Replace Tariffs as the Main Risk
The agreement’s implementation remains uncertain. European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said on Friday that it would reduce imports by several million cars over four years, but Brussels and Beijing have yet to disclose the detailed arrangements.
China’s Commerce Ministry said on Monday that the agreement would allow exports to continue growing and guarantee China a quota no smaller than that granted to any other source of imports.
The arrangement has been viewed by some investors as a step towards easing trade tensions, potentially reducing the immediate risk of additional tariffs on Chinese hybrids. However, questions remain over possible import quotas, minimum prices and exemptions.
Shares in BYD fell 1.8%, while Chery and SAIC gained 1.4% and 0.5%, respectively. Citi analysts said the agreement offered relief from trade risks, although its ultimate effects would depend on technical negotiations over implementation.
Renault Chief Executive Francois Provost described the surge in Chinese hybrid imports as unsustainable for Europe but said the agreement was preferable to a trade war. He called for a more measured approach to managing trade relations.
The uncertainty means Chinese automakers could face restrictions on the number of vehicles they export even if additional tariffs are avoided.
Volkswagen Faces Intensifying Competition
The rapid expansion of Chinese hybrids has increased pressure on European manufacturers competing for market share in one of the region’s most important automotive segments.
Li Yanwei, an analyst at the China Automobile Dealers Association, said the growth of Chinese brands had increasingly challenged European producers, including Volkswagen, which has long been a leading seller of plug-in hybrids.
BYD, China’s largest hybrid vehicle exporter to Europe, sold more plug-in hybrids than fully electric vehicles during the first eight months of the year, according to data compiled by Li. Its Seal U sport utility vehicle was its best-selling model.
Together with Chery, SAIC and Geely, BYD has narrowed the competitive gap with Volkswagen, which still held a 31.8% share of the EU plug-in hybrid market.
The outcome of the agreement could therefore influence not only Chinese export volumes but also pricing, product strategies and competition across Europe’s automotive industry.
Michael Dunne, a consultant who follows China’s automotive sector, said it remained to be seen whether Beijing would comply with the agreement or seek alternative arrangements, including temporary tariff exemptions.
Could Chinese Automakers Move Production to Europe?
The prospect of tighter restrictions on imports could encourage Chinese manufacturers to accelerate plans to produce vehicles within Europe rather than rely on exports from China.
Building factories closer to European customers could provide a way to maintain market access if quotas constrain imported vehicles. However, establishing local production requires substantial investment and may be more difficult for smaller manufacturers.
Bill Russo, founder of Shanghai-based consultancy Automobility, said restrictions on imports would strengthen the incentive for Chinese automakers to manufacture in Europe. He cautioned that the capital requirements could force smaller players to reconsider their expansion plans.
Jefferies analysts said the agreement could shift the main concern from tariffs to quotas, potentially encouraging Chinese manufacturers to focus on higher-priced vehicles while increasing pressure on German premium brands.
The deal could also accelerate investment in European production facilities, reshaping how Chinese automakers serve the region’s market.
Europe’s Automotive Trade Dispute Enters a New Phase
The agreement highlights the EU’s challenge in balancing access to competitively priced vehicles with concerns about the competitiveness of its domestic automotive industry.
For Chinese manufacturers, Europe remains a major growth market as they expand internationally and face pressure to find new sources of demand. For European producers, the rapid rise of Chinese brands has increased the urgency of improving competitiveness while navigating changing trade rules.
Much will depend on the agreement’s final implementation, particularly the size of any quotas, pricing requirements and exemptions. Until those details are settled, automakers and investors will face uncertainty over the future of Chinese hybrid imports.
If restrictions become binding, the next phase of competition may be fought less through exports and more through local manufacturing, investment and control over access to the European market.
With information from Reuters.

articles.full_text:
Diesel drivers are being hammered
Diesel drivers face 16p per mile charges, Octopus Energy has warned. Diesel drivers are being hammered at the pumps as prices hit £2 per litre.
With diesel at around £2 a litre, filling a typical 55-litre family car now costs about £110. That's roughly 16.5 per mile. A long-range EV with a 109kWh battery, by comparison, can cost as little as £8 to charge on a smart EV tariff – or around 2p a mile, or roughly 9x less.
Octopus has revealed its five best-selling electric cars for Q3. Four of the five cars that made the Q2 top five remain in the top five. But every single one has changed position.
Alvin Castillo, Procurement Director at Octopus Electric Vehicles, said: “Diesel is getting more expensive while electric cars are becoming more competitive.
"Chinese brands are shaking up the market, but Europe is fighting back with exciting new models like the Renault 5. That's great news for drivers, with more choice, better value and innovation coming from every direction.
“Drivers are shopping across a much wider range of manufacturers than they were even a couple of years ago. Established household names are competing with brands that are relatively new to the UK, and that competition is pushing everyone to deliver better technology, more equipment and better value.
“That’s ultimately brilliant news for drivers. While the cost of sticking with diesel keeps climbing, the choice available to people considering an EV keeps getting better.”
Castillo commented: “The pace isn’t slowing down. We’re seeing more models, more technology and more competition coming into the market, and that gives drivers more reasons to take another look at electric.
“The big change is that choosing an EV is becoming less about whether there’s a car that works for you and increasingly about which one you want.
"With fuel costs putting more pressure on household budgets, that breadth of choice is only going to become more important.”

articles.title: India-EU Free Trade Agreement: Implications of Source Code Rules - Institute Of South Asian Studies (ISAS-NUS)
articles.summary: India-EU Free Trade Agreement: Implications of Source Code Rules  Institute Of South Asian Studies (ISAS-NUS)
articles.full_text:
Amitendu Palit, Atyantika Kothuri Mookherjee
12 October 2026
Summary
Provisions restricting government access to software source code have become a standard feature of digital trade agreements. Because artificial intelligence (AI) systems are software, these provisions now sit at the boundary between trade law and AI governance. This working paper examines draft source code rules in the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement (FTA) from a comparative perspective for understanding their potential implications on Indian digital exports. While the source code rules are largely identical in the FTA with those in the EU’s other major recent Asian FTAs, like those with Korea and Indonesia, the perceived disadvantages for Indian exporters arise from a lack of domestic regulations for AI. The absence of these regulations subjects Indian source codes to the possibility of pre-market reviews in the EU, while no such provisions exist for checking EU source codes in India, except for sensitive sectors like critical infrastructure.
This working paper, however, argues that this imbalance does not constitute the ground for revisiting the source code rules for making them more specific to safeguard against the downsides of high-risk AI systems. On the contrary, it argues for India speeding up the growth of sectoral regulations impacting the use of externally developed frontier AI systems in the country and working closely with the EU in this regard.
Introduction
India and the European Union (EU) concluded negotiations on a bilateral free trade agreement (FTA) on 27 January 2026, with the provisional text of the FTA becoming available soon after. Both sides aim to sign the FTA following the finalisation of the legal text by the end of 2026 and operationalise it by early 2027.[1] The FTA has been widely proclaimed as the ‘mother of all deals’ for creating one of the world’s largest common markets; and the faith of two of the world’s largest economic actors – with historically divergent views on trade – in a comprehensive rules-based framework for advancing mutual trade.[2]
The FTA includes digital trade rules agreed upon by India and the EU. Among India’s new-generation FTAs signed in the current decade, the EU FTA will join those signed by India with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and the United Kingdom (UK) as agreements containing digital trade rules. Salience of these rules in India’s FTAs is significant, given the global growth in digital trade and its growing prominence in India’s external trade.
A critical enabler of bilateral digital trade is the rules regarding disclosure of source code. These provisions in the draft India-EU FTA have generated interest in their potential impact on digital trade. The impact extends to cross-border usage of artificial intelligence (AI) in bilateral trade between India and the EU, along with their capacities to regulate such use.[3] Given the rapid adoption of AI by Indian enterprises in cross-border digital service deliveries, India’s ability to frame effective domestic regulations for AI, and their alignment with similar regulations in major global markets such as the EU, have significant implications for its long-term digital trade prospects.
This paper explores the wider implications of source code rules in the India-EU FTA through a comparative lens. These implications are significant for an economy like India, as it figures among those economies where externally developed AI systems operate at scale across various regulated sectors, with domestic firms often lacking ownership of proprietary software. The comparative lens employed in the paper entails studying a few more major trade agreements with source code provisions. Apart from the India-EU FTA, these include the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), signed in July 2025, which, till now, is India’s only other FTA with source-code commitment. Two other major EU trade agreements are also studied. These are the EU-Korea Digital Trade Agreement (DTA)[4] signed on 10 June 2026, and the EU-Indonesia Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), signed and concluded in September 2025.[5] The paper also studies the source code rules in the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which set the precedent for 21st-century digital trade rules.[6]
The paper is divided into five sections. Section 1 examines source code rules in the draft EU-India FTA text and the need for domestic regulatory catch-up for India. Section 2 studies similar rules across the five mentioned trade agreements. Section 3 discusses India’s disadvantages arising from lesser protection for software exports. Section 4 discusses asymmetry between the EU’s domestic laws and FTA provisions. Section 5 summarises and concludes.
Section 1: Source Code Rules in EU-India FTA
Source code rules in FTAs commit signatory states to not demand transfer of, or access to, the source codes of other members’ software products as a condition of market entry. Source code is among the most valuable assets of firms providing software services. It’s compelled disclosure, whether demanded directly or extracted through certification and testing requirements, amounts to forced technology transfer, and surrender of proprietary knowledge of the source code owning firm. These rules began featuring in global trade agreements after their formalisation by the CPTPP, with the EU gradually adopting these rules in its own FTAs.[7]
Disclosure conditions for source codes have implications for firms using AI applications in cross-border delivery of services. AI systems are considered software. Trade rules drafted in the past for pre-AI packaged software programmes now apply to algorithms that price credit, screen job applications, and manage power grids. Countries agreeing to source-code provisions in FTAs accept these as conditions governing their AI-embedded cross-border digital trade with other members of the FTAs.
Source code rules are critically important for India, given the importance of the EU as a market for its technology exports. According to the National Association of Software and Service Companies, India’s information technology (IT) exports were at around US$250 billion (S$319 billion) in FY2026.[8] Europe, including the UK, was the second largest global market for Indian software exports, after the US, accounting for 33 per cent of these exports.[9] Indian IT service exporters, especially software exporters, would be eyeing enhanced export prospects following the FTA with the EU. Source code rules will be key determinants of these prospects. EU technology businesses are also looking closely at these rules, given that European software and AI systems are expected to extend deeper in various sectors of the Indian economy.
Article 9.9 of the EU-India FTA sets out the source code rules. It prohibits “the transfer of, or access to, the source code of software owned by a natural or legal person of the other Party as a condition for the import, export, distribution, sale or use of such software, or of products containing such software, in or from its territory”.[10] The rule will enable software exporters from India and the EU to access each other’s markets without disclosing the proprietary source codes. However, regulatory, law-enforcement, judicial and conformity-assessment bodies might ask for disclosure of codes. Courts, administrative tribunals and competition authorities might also demand access to codes ostensibly for addressing violations in competition laws and other domestic laws. Such access might be asked for operations in critical infrastructure sectors also.
Do these rules impact prospects of digital trade using AI applications? Rules prohibiting transfer of, or access to, source code are broad and sweeping without specifically identifying AI features like algorithms. Indeed, rules addressing cross-border algorithmic interoperability are yet to feature in most global FTAs. By accepting non-disclosure of source codes, neither India nor the EU can insist on pre-market testing of AI algorithms. Given that risks associated with products and services comprising AI algorithms can only be judged post-facto, it might be considered rather short-sighted, especially for India, since Indian-origin algorithms will have to undergo prior testing in the EU market following the EU’s domestic AI regulations.[11] The imbalance in this regard arises from India not having any domestic regulations like the EU mandating prior scrutiny of AI algorithms.
However, notwithstanding the absence of specific rules on algorithmic audit authority, the India-EU FTA text does emphasise ensuring safe and trustworthy use of AI as a legitimate objective justifying exceptions for access to source codes.
Whether absence of domestic regulations in India for checking foreign AI algorithms prior to their market entry, vis-à-vis those that may require Indian algorithms to be checked in the EU, amount to a comparative disadvantage for India’s digital exports to EU, will depend on the sincerity of both India and EU in ensuring safe and trustworthy use of AI by employing appropriate contextual exceptions in the FTA, for source code disclosure. Moving forward, however, the FTA’s rules must be complemented and aligned with respective domestic regulations. The EU has been far ahead of India in this regard, leaving the latter to work on regulatory ‘catch-up’. Domestic regulations mostly develop independently of FTAs. To that extent, how those of the EU, and the upcoming ones for India, might influence the working of the FTA on AI governance, is very much a hypothetical issue at this stage.

articles.title: Oil prices edge lower as Russia-Ukraine energy truce eases supply concerns - Anadolu Ajansı
articles.summary: Oil prices edge lower as Russia-Ukraine energy truce eases supply concerns  Anadolu Ajansı
articles.full_text:
Oil prices fell on Monday as the possibility of Russia and Ukraine agreeing to halt attacks on energy infrastructure eased concerns over supply disruptions, while investors took profits following recent price gains.
International benchmark Brent crude futures for December delivery decreased 0.14% to $104.57 per barrel at 9.40 a.m. local time (0640 GMT), down from $104.72 at the previous close.
US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures for November delivery dropped 0.44% to $91.44 per barrel from $91.85.
US President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate ceasefire covering energy infrastructure, urging both sides to uphold the agreement.
The announcement is raising expectations that attacks on Russian oil refineries and export facilities could ease, reducing the risk of global supply disruptions and putting downward pressure on oil prices.
Trump had criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy over attacks on Russian refineries and his approach to peace talks, saying Ukraine should elect a new leader.
Zelenskyy responded by proposing a full 60-day ceasefire to allow elections in Ukraine, adding that Kyiv could stop targeting Russian refineries and diesel facilities if Moscow halted attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
He said Russian attacks had targeted Ukraine's energy sector 196 times and its oil and natural gas infrastructure 20 times over the past week, describing an end to mutual attacks on energy facilities as a potential first step toward ending the war.
The prospect of reduced attacks eased concerns over disruptions to Russian oil and petroleum product supplies, and lowered the geopolitical risk premium in oil prices.
- Production outages in Gulf of Mexico support oil prices
Meanwhile, continued supply disruptions in the Gulf of Mexico are preventing a sharper decline in oil prices, despite the gradual resumption of oil and natural gas production halted by Hurricane Isaias.
According to the latest data released by the US Minerals Management Administration (MMA), approximately 1.17 million barrels per day of oil production, equivalent to 57.54% of the region's daily output, remains offline.
Natural gas production outages stand at approximately 1.05 billion cubic feet per day, representing 49.11% of the region's output.
Energy companies bp and Shell, which suspended production due to the hurricane, have also begun efforts to return personnel to facilities and resume operations as weather conditions improve.

articles.title: Heathrow needs Burnham green light for runway by end of year, warns boss - Financial Times
articles.summary: Heathrow needs Burnham green light for runway by end of year, warns boss  Financial TimesUK's Heathrow rallies support for third runway as Parliament weighs expansion plans  ReutersHeathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins  The GuardianLondon Heathrow chief urges UK government to clear third runway  FlightGlobalBritish Airways urges Burnham to take stake in Heathrow  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Heathrow’s investors will reassess plans to build a third runway if Andy Burnham does not give explicit backing to the ambitious £33bn project by the end of this year, the airport’s boss has warned.
Thomas Woldbye told the FT that the backers of Britain’s only hub airport “cannot wait forever” for commitment from the prime minister, who has so far declined to support the new runway, in contrast with Sir Keir Starmer’s administration.
Heathrow’s owners — which include Ardian, Qatar’s investment authority, Saudi Arabia’s PIF and Singapore’s GIC — must decide in the new year whether to submit a formal planning application for a third runway.
“Our shareholders would like to do this,” Woldbye said in an interview. “They do think that things are taking a long time, and so far they have decided to be OK with that . . . But of course we cannot wait forever.”
He added: “At some point in time we need a level of certainty. I think by the end of the year we’ll be looking and saying, ‘Let’s assess this, let’s take stock and see where we are’.”
New chancellor John Healey has said an expanded airport would boost growth, but Burnham has avoided questions so far on whether he supports the plan, which is opposed by environmental campaigners and Labour Mayor of London Lord Sadiq Khan.
The FT previously reported that Burnham told several Labour MPs that he had always opposed the idea.
Speaking before the Holborn and St Pancras by-election in which Labour defeated the Green Party, Burnham said the runway was a “matter for London” despite Starmer being a firm supporter of the scheme.
Without the premier’s explicit backing, it will be very hard to push the project through the planning and legal processes required to get approval to start construction work.
Heathrow has stressed the economic benefits to ministers, including 100,000 new jobs and a fillip to GDP, while it forecasts that 60 per cent of the economic benefit will be felt outside of London.
Woldbye said supportive figures within the government were “clear” about the benefits of the scheme, for which political support has ebbed and flowed over the past two decades.
He added: “I’m not a politician; there may be other reasons why [Burnham] is not committed to that right now. But of course there is a point where we would probably look and say, ‘We need to commit’. It may not be the highest on his agenda, but I think we can get it up there because that is where it belongs.”
Several key processes need to be completed before Heathrow and its investors push the button on a planning application.
MPs on the House of Commons transport committee are scrutinising a new policy framework that would allow the airport to build a new runway, while the Civil Aviation Authority, the sector regulator, is exploring changes to Heathrow’s model for clawing back investment costs.
Heathrow is also holding its own consultation on the project, which closes in December.
Former chancellor Rachel Reeves, who resurrected the idea of a third runway in 2025 to help boost the economy, set out a timeline for building work to start by 2029, with a new runway partly operational by 2035.
Delays to the process mean Heathrow has already pushed the earliest opening date for the runway to 2039.
Woldbye said hitting the 2029 deadline for planning permission would be “challenging” but “we are working to 2029 and can see a path to 2029 now”. Meeting the deadline would “require the government to be clear,” he stressed.
The independent Climate Change Committee warned last month that Heathrow expansion was incompatible with the government’s climate targets, and that it would produce as much CO₂ as Birmingham, the UK’s second city.
The Department for Transport said it supported “airport expansion across the country where this can contribute to growth and opportunity, while meeting tests on the environment”. 
“We are moving swiftly to review the responses received to the recent consultation on the policy framework underpinning expansion, and considering the appropriate next steps,” it added.

Kuwait has bought an air defence system built in Britain under a £370 million contract that will create a hundred jobs in the United Kingdom, according to the Ministry of Defence.
The contract with MARSS Systems Limited, an EOS company, covers skilled engineering and manufacturing roles, and the work will expand the company’s British offices with production based in Bristol.
MARSS will provide and integrate the system for Kuwait, bringing together jammers, radars and interceptors with its NiDAR platform, an AI-enabled command and control centre, to improve the country’s ability to detect, deter and defeat airborne threats.
The deal forms part of Taskforce Sabre, the British effort that brings government and industry together to help Gulf states secure systems and weapons quickly, and it follows Iranian missile and drone attacks in the region.
Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard said: “This deal is a clear demonstration of the UK delivering on its promise to support our regional partners.
“By backing Kuwait with world-leading British technology, we’re not just strengthening a vital ally’s defences against real and growing threats. We’re creating skilled jobs here at home and proving that UK industry can deliver when it matters most.”
Johannes Pinl, chief executive of MARSS, said: “Countering drones and aerial threats is not about any single system, it is about an intelligent, layered architecture that detects, decides and defeats within seconds, and MARSS has built exactly that.
“Through 2027, MARSS will integrate the sensors and effectors that protect Kuwait’s people, critical infrastructure and national assets, backed by British engineering and new skilled jobs here in the UK.”
Britain has already supported Kuwait with Rapid Sentry, a ground-based air defence missile system, and the Royal Air Force’s ORCUS counter-drone system is operating in the country, helping personnel detect drones early and act on what they find.
The Ministry of Defence describes the latest contract as building on that existing support and cementing Britain’s role as a defence partner to Kuwait and the wider Gulf region.

The new BYD Atto 8 is a large seven-seat electric SUV that will serve as the Chinese firm's flagship and rival the Kia EV9 and Skoda Peaq.
Unveiled at the Paris motor show, the new model will top the brand’s SUV range, which also includes the Atto 2 and 3, the Sealion 5 and the Seal U. It will become the largest EV offered in the UK by BYD, and its first to feature more than five seats.
The Atto 8 also becomes the firm’s first European model to benefit from its second-generation 115kWh Blade battery, which allows for BYD’s ultra-rapid Flash charging. This means the Atto 8 can go from 10-70% capacity in five minutes when using one of the firm’s proprietary chargers. Brimming it from 10-97% takes an additional four minutes.
The Atto 8 will be available with two different powertrains, both using the same battery pack. The Design RWD model has a single rear-mounted electric motor producing 455bhp and 270lb ft, can do 0-62mph in eight seconds and has a WLTP range of 405 miles.
The other option, the Excellence AWD, has an electric motor on each axle to produce 764bhp and 571lb ft. The 0-62mph sprint takes 4.6sec, while the WLTP range falls to 374 miles.
At 5040mm long, 1996mm wide and 1760mm tall, the Atto 8 has very similar dimensions to the EV9, but is larger than the Peaq.
Inside, the new model gets a panoramic glass roof, a 10.25in digital instrument panel, a 26in windscreen head-up display and a 15.6in central infotainment touchscreen with built-in Google functions.
With all three rows of seats in use, the Atto 8 has 270 litres of luggage capacity in the rear, along with a 136-litre front boot. For comparison, the EV9 has 333 litres of boot space with the third row of seats up, and either 90 litres (RWD) or 52 litres (AWD) in the front, while the Peaq has 299 litres in the rear and 37 litres in the front.
The Atto 8 is due to go on sale across Europe in the first quarter of 2027. No pricing has yet been announced.

articles.title: Should Britain have joined the Euro? - The Spectator
articles.summary: Should Britain have joined the Euro?  The Spectator
articles.full_text:
Critics of the Labour government looking for a stick to beat it with have hit on a novel line of attack. Britain, they point out, now pays more to borrow than Greece, which a decade and a half ago had to be rescued from national bankruptcy with three bailouts worth more than €250 billion (£211 billion), the largest in history. Greece pays around 4.5 per cent on its ten-year debt; Britain pays 5.4 per cent. Some have called the difference a “moron premium” – though it is not clear that any such premium is baked into British borrowing costs today, unlike during Liz Truss’s 49-day reign of financial terror.
The real irony lies in the choice of Greece to embarrass Labour. This is a country that Brexiteers used to predict would crash out of the eurozone. They saw in Greece’s debt crisis the possibility of their own deepest wish fulfilment: the collapse of the single currency and, perhaps, God willing, the EU too. Yet Greece, along with other victims of the eurozone crisis such as Spain and Portugal, is now held up as a model of fiscal virtue: a country that took its neoliberal lumps and is now reaping the benefits.
The obvious retort is to ask whether Britain would be better off in the euro too. But the question lies so far outside the Overton window that it is never asked. Yet there were moments in Britain’s not-so-distant history when membership of a currency union was a subject for legitimate debate.
In the late Eighties, there was broad cross-party support for joining the Exchange Rate Mechanism, the precursor to the single currency, widely seen as necessary both to anchor Britain’s inflation-fighting credibility and to demonstrate its commitment to Europe. Margaret Thatcher reluctantly took Britain in, in October 1990. A second moment came after Labour took office in 1997, when government policy was that Britain should adopt the euro once the economic case was “clear and unambiguous”.
This proved a high bar. It turned what was essentially a political decision into a pseudo-technical one. And it pitted Tony Blair, who hoped to make euro entry a defining part of his legacy, against Gordon Brown, who, as custodian of the five economic tests (reportedly conjured up with his adviser Ed Balls in the back of a car in New York), would decide if and when Britain joined. Would British and eurozone business cycles converge? Was there enough flexibility to absorb shocks? Would membership boost investment, help the City, and promote growth and jobs? Having ruled out entry in 1997, Brown declared the tests again not met in 2003.
What is striking, looking back at Brown’s arguments, is the extent to which they reflected his obsession with “stability”. This was a chancellor who really did believe he had abolished boom and bust.
All of this looks like hubris now. Even as he delivered his verdict on the tests, Brown was presiding over the greatest boom and bust in modern British history. Barely four years later, shortly after he had taken over as prime minister, he was confronted with queues forming outside Northern Rock, the first of several British lenders to fail. The government had to spend more than £40 billion recapitalising the banks, while the budget deficit blew out to around 10 per cent of GDP. Though the boom had its origins far beyond Britain’s shores, the bust which his system was supposed to have made impossible proved fatal to his own career.
Still, Brown had reason to fear that euro entry could produce an even bigger boom-and-bust nightmare than the ERM debacle of 1992. That crisis was triggered when Britain had to keep interest rates high to defend the pound as the Bundesbank tightened to cool a post-reunification boom. Because British mortgages were almost entirely variable-rate, rate rises passed quickly through to borrowers, and house prices collapsed. George Soros – thanks to research by a junior member of his team, a certain Scott Bessent – bet that the government could not keep raising rates under sustained speculative attack. He was right.
Brown feared the same feature of the mortgage market would leave Britain vulnerable inside the euro. A study published alongside the 2003 assessment of what might have happened had Britain joined in 1999 backed him up: eurozone interest rates would have been inappropriately low for Britain, fuelling the housing boom and overheating the economy. He judged the same held true in 2003 – even though the gap between UK and eurozone rates had narrowed to around 1.75 percentage points – and that the fallout would have been far more painful in the euro, with much of the adjustment falling on the labour market.
Alternative Histories
Brown would later claim that the eurozone crisis vindicated him, given that Spain and Ireland suffered precisely the kind of boom and bust he feared. Britain had its own boom and bust, but it was much shorter, thanks to a sharp depreciation, a central bank quicker to embark on quantitative easing, and a government that could rely on that central bank as it spent billions bailing out the banks. It is hard to argue with that assessment. Indeed, the protracted trauma of the eurozone crisis, and its drag on growth across the continent, helped turn British sentiment against the European project as a whole by the time of the 2016 referendum.
Yet with the passage of time, it becomes harder to say who emerged best. With the exception of Greece, the former bailout countries have long since recovered their lost ground and are now growing faster than Britain, with falling debt ratios and lower borrowing costs. There is little evidence that the euro has held the former crisis countries back.
A stronger objection is that had Britain been in the euro when the crisis hit, it would have been too big to save and could have blown the single currency apart. More likely, surely, is that the eurozone would have been forced to innovate faster, creating facilities that would have let Britain borrow to recapitalise its banks had it been at risk of losing market access. In that respect, Britain inside the euro might have brought a quicker resolution to the crisis – and perhaps a more stable and prosperous currency area today.
Any counterfactual must also take account of the benefits forgone by staying out. Brown himself acknowledged in 2003 that these were real, and the Treasury estimated that membership could boost trade with the euro area by up to 50 per cent and raise national income by between 5 and 9 per cent over 30 years. Certainly, the pattern of British growth would have been very different inside the euro. The price of exchange-rate flexibility has been a higher cost of capital to compensate for greater volatility. That has surely shaped the kind of foreign investment Britain attracts, which has skewed towards financial flows routed through the City rather than greenfield investment.
The Tests Today
So what would a chancellor conclude if they ran the same five tests today, judged purely on the economics and leaving politics aside? Here is my verdict, taking each in turn:
- Convergence: Brown considered this test close to passed in 2003, and it would be hard to argue that it isn’t passed comfortably now. The gap between Bank Rate and the ECB’s main refinancing rate is down to 1.1 percentage points, and UK inflation is now at or below the euro area’s for the first time in years. More than 90 per cent of mortgage balances are now on fixed rates, removing the vulnerability that was exposed in 1992 and that most worried Brown.
- Flexibility: Brown judged this test a fail on the grounds that inside the eurozone, the UK would lose the exchange rate as a shock absorber, along with national control of interest rates and fiscal policy. But in the intervening decades, the eurozone’s fiscal rules have been honoured more in the breach than the observance, and during both the eurozone crisis and the Covid pandemic, the EU created instruments to help member states cope with shocks. Meanwhile, Britain’s labour market is more flexible than most, and would become more flexible still with the restoration of free movement. The biggest concern is that the single market itself still has too many internal barriers to trade and the movement of labour. With that proviso, I would judge this test a pass.
- Financial services: Brown judged this test passed in both 1997 and 2003. Since then, Brexit has cost Britain significant European business, while the higher cost of capital Britain now faces has been ruinous for the London stock market. Inside the euro, the ECB’s concerns over the clearing of euro-denominated transactions would fall away, since a London-based clearing house would come under ECB supervision and have a direct line to ECB liquidity; outside, London’s equivalence expires in 2028. Against these gains would need to be weighed the costs of EU regulation – though the UK would once again have an influential say in shaping it. What once seemed a slam-dunk pass may today be a qualified pass, subject to negotiation.
- Investment: Brown declared this test not met in 2003, primarily because he had concluded that the convergence and flexibility tests were not met. But I think he underestimated the long-term consequences of Britain’s higher cost of capital and exchange-rate volatility for UK investment. British governments like to congratulate themselves on attracting foreign direct investment, but much of this has taken the form of purchases of UK financial assets that have weakened the national balance sheet, while business investment has been among the lowest of any major economy. I would rate this test a clear pass today.
- Growth: Brown acknowledged in 2003 that his assessment of this test was largely a function of the first two. On the same basis, if those are met today, this one must surely be considered passed too. The caveat concerns the stability of the eurozone itself: banking union remains incomplete, capital markets are fragmented, and it is unclear whether the bloc could cop

articles.title: Europe is divided in the race to develop the next-generation fighter jet between GCAP and FCAS. - Vietnam.vn
articles.summary: Europe is divided in the race to develop the next-generation fighter jet between GCAP and FCAS.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
The European military aviation industry landscape is witnessing a clear divergence between two future fighter programs. While the GCAP alliance, led by the UK, Italy, and Japan, continues to achieve key financial and design milestones, the joint Franco-German effort to develop a fighter aircraft under the FCAS project has officially stalled due to disagreements over operational requirements and industrial interests.
The Global Combat Air Force Programme (GCAP) was launched in December 2022 with the goal of developing a sixth-generation fighter aircraft, expected to enter service by 2035. On July 3, 2026, the UK Ministry of Defence announced the awarding of a £4.6 billion contract to the Edgewing consortium to implement the next design and development phase. Prior to this, participating nations had signed an initial agreement worth £686 million, with London alone committing £8.6 billion over four years.
Technically, the sixth-generation fighter jets under GCAP are designed to focus on advanced stealth capabilities, integrating multispectral sensor arrays, modern electronic warfare, broadband communication systems for sharing tactical data, and coordinated command and control capabilities with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Notably, Canada joined GCAP as an observer nation on July 21st, thereby exploring the technological cooperation framework before deciding whether to participate more fully.
In contrast to the progress of GCAP, the project to build a next-generation manned fighter aircraft under the Future Air Combat System (FCAS) has been temporarily halted. Launched in 2017 with the participation of France, Germany, and later Spain (2019), FCAS aimed for a synchronized integration of stealth fighters, support UAVs, and a combat network. However, intense disagreements between France's Dassault Aviation and Airbus (representing Germany and Spain) over design lead rights, intellectual property rights, and job allocation have caused a prolonged deadlock.
Differences in combat doctrine were also a decisive obstacle: France demanded that the new fighter jet be capable of operating from aircraft carriers and performing strategic nuclear deterrence missions, while Germany prioritized air superiority and compatibility with NATO air defense systems. By June 2026, Berlin confirmed that the two sides had agreed not to continue joint research on the common fighter jet airframe, although cooperation on networked components and supporting UAV systems would remain.
Modernizing existing equipment serves as a technological stepping stone.
To compensate for operational gaps while next-generation projects remain incomplete, European military powers are simultaneously strengthening transitional solutions through upgrading their existing fleets:
- Germany orders Eurofighter Typhoon: In October 2025, Germany signed a contract to purchase an additional 20 Typhoon fighter jets, with delivery expected between 2031 and 2034. This move helps maintain air defense capabilities and keep defense factories running.
- France upgrades Rafale to F5 standard: On September 10, 2026, the French Directorate General of Defence Equipment signed preparatory agreements with Dassault Aviation, MBDA, Safran, and Thales to upgrade the Rafale to the F5 standard by the end of 2026. The F5 variant optimizes electronic warfare capabilities, combat network data connectivity, UAV coordination, and nuclear deterrence capabilities, and is expected to complete certification assessment by 2033.
- Sweden maintains independent research: Saab Group received a contract worth approximately 2.9 billion kronor from the Swedish Defence Materials Agency on September 9, 2026, to research manned and unmanned combat technology for the period 2026-2028.
These upgrade programs share a common focus on modernizing phased-array radars, electronic warfare equipment, and air-to-air coordination algorithms with UAVs. However, military experts believe this is purely a temporary solution, as the limitations of the airframe and heat dissipation and infrared emission architecture of 4th and 4.5th generation fighter jets cannot completely replace next-generation aircraft.
Challenges in defense resources and economic calculations.
A report published on July 16th by the European Defence Agency (EDA) indicates that the total defense budget of the 27 EU countries is expected to reach €454 billion in 2026 (approximately 2.4% of the bloc's GDP). Within this structure, spending on equipment procurement accounts for 36%, while funding for military research and development (R&D) is projected to increase to around €20 billion.
Despite abundant financial resources, the collapse of the Franco-German fighter jet project clearly reflects the challenge of reconciling industrial interests. Europe's divergence into multiple independent development paths, on the one hand, helps countries maintain technological autonomy and preserve domestic industrial capacity. On the other hand, this dispersion of resources directly threatens supply chains, driving up production costs and creating the risk of widespread duplication of investment.

articles.title: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist - The Guardian
articles.summary: ‘Super app’ aimed at UK students uses servers owned by Chinese firm on US blacklist  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
A new messaging and payment “super app” marketed at British students uses servers owned by a Chinese company that has been put on a US military blacklist for its alleged affiliation to the People’s Liberation Army.
ZyMix, which is being pushed on university campuses as the UK’s first super app designed “for gen Z”, combining chat, payments and community features, has a contract with a German-based subsidiary of Tencent Holdings, a Chinese conglomerate in Shenzhen.
Tencent Holdings was added in January 2026 to the US Department of Defense’s (DoD) list of Chinese military companies, which is formally known as the section 1260H list.
The citation on the DoD list says that the company, which is a gaming and social media conglomerate, is indirectly affiliated to the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.
The blacklist is part of a US attempt to counteract what it regards as Beijing’s efforts to increase its military power by using technology from Chinese firms, universities and research programmes.
The DoD is prohibited from entering into, renewing or extending contracts for goods, services or technology with any entity on the list although wider sanctions are not automatic.
A Tencent spokesperson said: “Tencent’s inclusion on this list is clearly a mistake. We are not a military company or supplier. Unlike sanctions or export controls, this listing has no impact on our business. We will nonetheless work with the Department of Defense to address any misunderstanding.”
China’s footprint in higher education in the UK has become a controversial issue. MI5 recently warned British universities to cut ties with the China General Technology Research Institute.
The domestic intelligence service claimed it was secretly channelling funding from Beijing’s intelligence apparatus to UK-linked academics to improve the technical espionage capabilities of China’s ministry of state security.
The link between the Chinese-owned infrastructure and ZyMix was initially disclosed in the company’s privacy policy at the time of its launch last week.
The document, which is legally required, said that Tencent (Frankfurt) stored user-generated content and messages. After the Guardian approached the company, the privacy policy was rewritten and mention of Tencent was removed.
The policy now states that users’ personal data is stored and processed primarily in the United Kingdom and the EU, adding that “some of our service providers are located in other countries, including the United States”.
It goes on to say that “auxiliary infrastructure providers, hosted in the EU, receive only encrypted user messages and limited technical data, such as technical statistics, licence validation when the app starts”.
A spokesperson said: “As a newly launched startup, we are updating our privacy notice as we develop our services, including clarifying that Tencent, Twilio and the other providers concerned are used solely for performance testing.”
The spokesperson added: “Our agreement is with Tencent Cloud Europe BV, which we use for auxiliary services, rather than as the provider that stores ZyMix user data. We take our obligations under UK data protection law seriously.”
The new privacy policy invites those who wish to know the identity of their suppliers to request the information from the company.
In response to a request from the Guardian, Tarique Ghaffur, a former assistant commissioner at the Metropolitan police, who described himself as a security consultant for ZyMix, responded.
He said: “We have reviewed your request as against our private privacy [sic] you mentioned. Unfortunately, at the present time for reasons of commercial confidentiality, contractual obligations and legal privileges, we are not able to provide you with the requested information.”
Fraser Sampson, a professor of security and national governance and formerly the UK’s biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, said he was “sceptical when ‘commercial confidentiality’ arguments are used to duck basic policy questions and amending policy on the fly is never reassuring”.
He added: “When companies ask us for our personal data, they should expect us to ask them where it’s being kept, for what purpose(s) and who they’re going to share it with – and be prepared to answer fully.”
Sam Dunning, the director of the UK-China Transparency NGO, said: “There are serious questions about whether ZyMix have taken due care before launching this product.”
A spokesperson for ZyMix said: “Whilst still in its beta stage, the ZyMix app has been developed to fully comply with all UK data, privacy and financial regulations.”
ZyMix is heavily targeting the university market and is offering £200 to £400 a month to people who agree to be brand ambassadors on campuses. Staff roles have also been advertised in the UK by ZyMix for Mandarin-speaking applicants.
One advert on LinkedIn for the job of operations manager (Mandarin speaking) required “excellent written and verbal communication skills in both English and Mandarin (required for daily communication with the China team)”.
Separately, a distinct company appeared to be recruiting on behalf of ZyMix on WeChat, the Chinese instant messaging service, saying: “The product, R&D, design and testing team is in Greater China, with branch-company bases covering: Taipei / Shenzhen / Guangzhou / Hangzhou / Chengdu / Zhengzhou.”
Ghaffur said that Flicknmix, the UK company that publishes the ZyMix app, “does not have any subsidiaries or branch offices in China. Our aim is to create opportunities within the UK”. A spokesperson for ZyMix described it as “British born”.

articles.title: This French AI stock is up 570% in 2026: Analysts see a further 90% upside - AOL.co.uk
articles.summary: This French AI stock is up 570% in 2026: Analysts see a further 90% upside  AOL.co.uk
articles.full_text:
A little-known French semiconductor company has become one of Europe's biggest artificial intelligence stock market winners in 2026, thanks to a technology few competitors can produce.
Shares in Soitec SA have risen almost sevenfold this year, from about €23 at the start of January to roughly €154 on Monday afternoon in Paris.
Yet the company reported a 34% decline in annual revenue last year.
Now, Bank of America believes the stock could nearly double again.
On Friday, the US bank upgraded Soitec from Neutral to Buy and raised its price target from €152 to €300, implying more than 90% upside.
So what is driving this rally, and how much of it rests on a single product?
Soitec shares have risen almost sevenfold in 2026
The French company behind a critical AI technology
Soitec does not make the processors that train artificial intelligence models. It makes the engineered silicon wafers on which other semiconductor companies build their chips.
Based in Bernin, near Grenoble, the company was spun out of French research institute CEA-Leti in 1992.
It employs more than 2,000 people and holds more than 4,700 patents.
Earlier this month, Euronews journalist Valérie Gauriat visited Soitec's production facilities for the Made in Europe series.
Inside its clean rooms, silicon wafers undergo dozens of manufacturing stages, allowing the company to manipulate incredibly thin layers of material.
"Our job is to run faster than the competition," Chief Technology Officer Christophe Maleville told Euronews.
That expertise is becoming increasingly valuable as AI data centres need to transfer enormous amounts of information between processors.
Silicon photonics offers a faster, more energy-efficient alternative to traditional copper connections by using light instead of electrical signals.
Soitec supplies the specialised silicon wafers used to manufacture these optical chips, giving it a critical role in the expanding AI infrastructure market.
Why Bank of America sees a near monopoly in AI photonics
"We estimate that Soitec currently holds ~95% market share in supplying Photonics-SOI wafers," Bank of America analyst Oliver Wong and his colleagues said.
Rivals, including Taiwan's GlobalWafers, are attempting to enter the market.
However, the bank expects Soitec's technological expertise and decades of manufacturing experience to protect its dominant position.
That advantage could become increasingly valuable as AI data centres grow larger and require more optical connections between processors.
Bank of America estimates that the total wafer area required for photonic chips will expand by approximately 60% annually between 2026 and 2030.
In other words, demand for Soitec's materials could grow considerably faster than the number of AI processors themselves.
The company's latest forecasts already suggest a major acceleration.
In September, Soitec projected that photonics revenue would reach between 2.5 and three times the previous year's level in the financial year ending March 2027.
It also forecast approximately 50% growth in total revenue for the September quarter.
Meanwhile, Soitec expects to secure multi-year capacity agreements with eight of its roughly ten largest photonics customers.
These agreements could make future demand more predictable, supporting investment in additional production capacity.
Related
How AI could reshape Soitec profitability
Until recently, Soitec depended heavily on the smartphone industry, which accounted for roughly half of its revenue last fiscal year.
But in the June quarter, its broader Edge & Cloud AI division generated 57% of sales.
Bank of America expects that transformation to accelerate.
It projects photonics revenue will climb from €92 million in fiscal 2026 to approximately €680 million in fiscal 2029.
That would represent almost half of projected group revenue of €1.43 billion, compared with just 16% last fiscal year.
More importantly, profitability could grow even faster than sales.
The bank estimates that photonics wafers retain about 80 cents from every euro of sales after raw material costs, compared with 56 cents for Soitec's other products.
As photonics becomes a larger part of the business, Bank of America expects the company's gross profit margin to rise from 16% to 44% by fiscal 2029.
"We believe FY26 gross margin of 16% marked the trough for Soitec," Wong and his colleagues said.
That expected recovery underpins their forecast of €10.62 in earnings per share for fiscal 2029, approximately 71% above the Visible Alpha analyst consensus.
Related
Why a nearly 600% rally still carries substantial risks
Soitec's transformation is far from complete.
Annual revenue declined 34% to €592 million in fiscal 2026, while mobile communications sales plunged 43%.
The smartphone division contracted another 10% in the June quarter as customers continued reducing inventories.
Bank of America expects the mobile business to reach its lowest point this fiscal year, but a recovery is not guaranteed.
Meeting growing demand for photonics will also require substantial investment.
The bank expects Soitec to announce an extension of its Singapore manufacturing plant in the coming months, potentially costing around €700 million.
Valuation presents another challenge.
At approximately €154 per share, Soitec trades at nearly 96 times Bank of America's projected earnings for the financial year ending March 2027.
Such an elevated valuation leaves investors vulnerable if AI infrastructure spending slows or competing technologies gain ground.
Soitec will publish its first-half results on 18 November, offering a fresh test of its ambitious growth outlook.
At the beginning of 2026, investors were focused on shrinking smartphone sales and deteriorating profits.
Today, Soitec is increasingly being valued as a critical supplier to the global AI industry.
The question is whether its photonics business can grow fast enough to justify a share price that may have already anticipated an extraordinary transformation.

Readers should conduct their own research and consult a qualified financial adviser before making any investment decisions. Investing involves risk, including the potential loss of capital. Past performance is not indicative of future results.
