articles.title: IMF forecasts 3.1% global growth in 2026, with eurozone at 1.1% - Euronews.com
articles.summary: IMF forecasts 3.1% global growth in 2026, with eurozone at 1.1%  Euronews.com
articles.full_text:
The IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1%, citing resilient economies and AI investment. However, high energy prices linked to conflicts will weigh on growth, with eurozone expansion forecast at 1.1%.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) on Tuesday has raised its 2026 global growth forecast to 3.1%, citing resilience in advanced economies and increased AI investment.
However, growth will still slow from 3.5% in 2025, while high energy prices linked to the US–Iran war pose significant risks, particularly for low-income countries excluded from the AI-driven investment boom.
Meanwhile, economic growth in the eurozone will slow to 1.1% this year before a slight acceleration in 2027, the IMF said, due to persistently high energy costs and weak consumer confidence.
The 2026 forecast in the latest World Economic Outlook by the International Monetary Fund was a slight upgrade of 0.2 percentage points from its July report and follows 1.2% growth last year.
Although eurozone GDP growth rebounded to 2.6% in the second quarter of this year after zero growth in the first three months, the fund expects inflation risks to persist well into next year.
The Middle East conflict and Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine have sent oil and natural gas costs surging around the globe, a major threat to the eurozone and other economies that import most of their energy needs.
The IMF noted in particular that "gas inventories remain below seasonal norms in parts of Europe, leaving gas market conditions vulnerable to adverse weather ahead of the winter heating season".
Inflation is forecast at 3.1% this year and 2.8% next year, well above the European Central Bank's target of 2%.
That could require ECB interest rates that curb household spending and investment, with eurozone GDP expected to edge up to just 1.2% in 2027.
"Core inflation is expected to return to 2% only gradually," the fund said, in the eurozone by mid-2028 and in Britain by the end of 2027.
Growth in Germany, Europe's biggest economy, is expected to reach 1.3% this year, and Spain's GDP growth will remain strong at 2.5%.
But France's economy is seen expanding by just 0.4% this year, sharply below the 0.9% growth in 2025, with unemployment rising to 8.4% from last year's 7.7%.
For Britain, the IMF raised its growth forecast for this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from July.
But UK growth is expected to slow to 1.2% next year "as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment."
Prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressure
The United States' war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and driven global energy prices higher as a result of Tehran's retaliatory actions.
Prices of refined petroleum products remain 70% to 95% above pre-war levels, pressuring countries that depend on energy imports for economic activity.
The war is in its eighth month, and Tenreyro warned that "a prolonged conflict in the Middle East could put additional pressure on inflation and slow down growth."
Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF called a "bifurcated outlook" in its WEO report.
The report said the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a "fragmented" world economy.
"Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest," it said.
"At the same time, the current technology tailwind could stop abruptly if expectations about AI-related profits and productivity gains are reassessed, weakening investment and tightening financial conditions."
China's growth expected to slow
The world's advanced economies were forecast to grow by 2.1% in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain, such as Taiwan and South Korea, posting significantly higher figures.
Growth in China, the world's second-largest economy, was expected to slow by 0.5 percentage points to 4.5% this year, the IMF said, mainly due to weak domestic demand.
Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7% in 2026, fuelled by the war in Iran and the AI boom, with effects spreading across both advanced and developing economies.
Call for urgent action
IMF Chief Economist Tenreyro warned that "urgent action" was required by all countries in the face of downside risks.
On the fiscal side, she called on governments to use only temporary and targeted measures to ease the burden on the public from high energy and other costs.
In lockstep, "monetary policy should remain firmly focused on price stability," she added, indicating that interest rate hikes to curb high inflation were appropriate.
"The economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits," she said. "The task ahead is to move from coping to rebuilding, restoring fiscal space, and rebuilding supply-side resilience."

articles.title: Air passengers panic after power bank explodes in overhead locker at 35,000ft - Metro.co.uk
articles.summary: Air passengers panic after power bank explodes in overhead locker at 35,000ft  Metro.co.ukPassengers panic in mid-air as power bank catches fire during flight  The IndependentPlane Carrying 180 Passengers Makes Emergency Landing After Power Bank Catches Fire Mid-Flight  People.comIncident: Indigo A21N near Hyderabad on Oct 11th 2026, powerbank in overhead locker caught fire  The Aviation HeraldPower Bank Risk On Planes: Why Lithium Batteries Can Be Dangero...
articles.full_text:
A plane was forced to make an emergency landing after a passenger’s power bank caught fire 35,000ft in the air over India.
The Delhi to Chennai flight operated by India’s top carrier, IndiGo, was abruptly diverted to Hyderabad this afternoon.
Passengers noticed smoke spewing from the overhead bins around halfway into the two-and-a-half-hour flight.
Footage shared on social media shows the compartment interior ablaze as passengers move their bags away.
The cabin crew put out the fire with fire extinguishers, IndiGo said.
The airline said a ‘customer’s personal electronic device’ burst into flames, with Indian news channel NDTV reporting it was a power bank.
Sign up for all of the latest stories
Flight 6E 6115 took off from New Delhi at 1.30pm local time, set to land in the southern city of Chennai at 4pm.
But at around 2.50pm, the plane began to descend from 35,000ft to 3,700ft, according to aviation tracker FlightAware.
The plane turned 90° and landed at Hyderabad Rajiv Gandhi International Airport at 3.30pm.
IndiGo said: ‘The cabin crew responded promptly, and the situation was brought under control.
‘In line with established protocols, the pilots diverted the flight and landed safely at Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad.’
An alternate plane was arranged for passengers to fly to Chennai.
‘We regret the inconvenience caused to our customers due to this unforeseen situation and are making all efforts to minimise it, including offering refreshments and sharing timely updates,’ IndiGo added.
‘At IndiGo, the safety of our customers and crew remains our top priority.’
Are power banks a flight risk?
Power banks are only allowed in hand luggage, according to IndiGo’s ‘dangerous items’ policy.
The policy states that they ‘must remain within the passenger’s personal reach at all times’, such as under the seat.
‘Power must be visible on the battery; more than 160 Wh not allowed,’ the airline adds.
The portable charger cannot be stowed in the overhead compartment or cabin luggage.
Lithium batteries, which power banks use, have been used in smartphones and laptops for decades and are heavily regulated.
But portable chargers aren’t as regulated, meaning the danger lies in off-market, damaged or improperly charged power banks, Giuseppe Capanna, product safety engineer at Electrical Safety First, told Metro.
‘Power banks are popular travel items that keep you powered up on the go,’ Capanna says.
‘But they contain lithium-ion batteries which can hold a sizable amount of energy in a very small space, so can pose a serious fire risk if they become damaged or are manufactured to a substandard level.’
Electrical Safety First, a charity, says that power banks can even explode if the battery is damaged, overcharged, overheated or exposed to water.
These can cause a chemical reaction inside the self-fueling battery, called a ‘thermal runaway’, that makes the battery cells volatile and hot.
A sign this could happen is if the power bank begins to swell and appear misshapen.
People should dispose of damaged or deformed power banks by dropping them off at their local recycling centre.
The fire risk posed by lithium batteries is now the number one safety risk to planes, according to the Civil Aviation Authority.
The regulator said that in 2024, 316 incidents of devices with lithium batteries detected in hold bags were reported. In 2025, that rose to 643.
Reports of devices overheating or malfunctioning nearly doubled the same year, from 123 to 206, or about two a week.
Capanna adds: ‘Always follow airline rules and never put power banks in your checked luggage.
‘Only take them in the cabin and if you spot any signs of damage or deformation while flying, alert airline staff straight away.’

articles.title: John Healey rules out cutting ‘mansion tax’ threshold to £1.5mn in UK Budget - Financial Times
articles.summary: John Healey rules out cutting ‘mansion tax’ threshold to £1.5mn in UK Budget  Financial TimesBritain’s Mansion Tax Shows the Difficulty of Targeting Wealth  Bloomberg.comThe triple threat facing Britain’s most valuable homes  The TelegraphProperty, tax and the budget  BuyAssociation GroupMansion Tax U-turn spares almost one in 10 London homes  The Negotiator
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Chancellor John Healey will not cut a planned “mansion tax” threshold from £2mn to £1.5mn in this month’s Budget, after Labour MPs warned that the move would hit the governing party in its central London strongholds. 
The Treasury last month declined to comment on “speculation” that ministers were considering doubling the number of property owners forced to pay the new levy in England by reducing the threshold on October 28. 
But the chancellor has concluded that changing the rules around the levy — which is due to come into effect in 2028 — would undermine public support for the policy, according to people familiar with the discussions.
The idea of cutting the threshold to £1.5mn, reported by The Times, led to a backlash from many Labour MPs. Some warned that the measure would be “electoral suicide” for the party in parts of central London where property prices have soared in recent years.
A reduction from £2mn would have increased the number of properties affected by the measure from about 127,000 to roughly 243,000, according to research group Tax Policy Associates.
Last year Rachel Reeves, then chancellor, announced that homes in England valued above £2mn would have to pay the new annual levy from April 2028.
It will start at £2,500 on properties just over £2mn and rise to £7,500 for homes valued at more than £5mn.
Reeves had considered setting the threshold at £1.5mn but decided it was politically risky after representations from Labour MPs in London and the South East.
The Office for Budget Responsibility, the fiscal watchdog, estimates that the tax will hit less than 1 per cent of UK properties, raising a relatively modest £400mn a year by 2029-30.
The new regime requires a revaluation of properties in the top three council tax bands — F, G and H — in the first such revaluation since 1991.
The surcharge will be levied on top of the existing council tax charge, but unlike council tax it will end up in the coffers of the Treasury, not with local authorities. Homeowners will be able to roll up the annual payments and defer them until they move house or die.
Healey’s preparations for his first Budget have been hit by higher government borrowing costs and the economic fallout of the Iran war.
He also needs to find money to fund higher defence spending, address household energy costs, hold down fuel prices and tackle long-term youth unemployment.
But the chancellor is expected to limit fresh tax rises by allowing the existing “fiscal headroom” in the Treasury’s forecasts to be reduced significantly.
The Treasury said in a statement: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events, rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

The Euro extends its losses against the US Dollar on Monday, even falling below the psychological 1.1200 level as sellers step in following hawkish comments from a Fed policymaker and growing geopolitical concerns on two fronts: the US-Iran war and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The EUR/USD trades at 1.1155, down 0.40%.
EUR/USD tumbles towards 1.1150 as geopolitical tensions reinforce US inflation concerns
The Columbus Day holiday kept the markets quiet, with the cash markets closed. But over-the-weekend news, with US President Trump announcing a ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war on energy facilities, was cheered by investors, who later scrambled to buy Oil as Ukraine’s President Zelenskyy warned that hostilities will remain if Russia attacks infrastructure.
Tensions in the Hormuz remain high, even though Iran revealed that the US agreed, in some form, to the seven conditions Tehran required to reopen the Strait. This pushed West Texas Intermediate (WTI) higher, with WTI ending Monday’s session up over 1.60% at $93.17.
The US economic docket was absent, yet eyes were on Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, who commented that higher rates are needed as inflation broadens and that, within the FOMC, she has one of the highest projections for the neutral rate.
Ahead this week, traders' focus will be on Fed speakers, led by Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, and on the release of US inflation figures, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) expected on October 14, followed by the Producer Price Index (PPI) on October 15.
In the European Union, investors would target the release of Germany’s Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) and speeches by European Central Bank (ECB) members Elderson and Escriva.
EUR/USD Price Forecast: Technical outlook
In the daily chart, EUR/USD trades at 1.1157, extending a bearish phase as spot holds well below the clustered simple moving averages (SMA) group around 1.1496. The pair also remains under the long-running downward resistance trend line, whose break reference near 1.1295 now acts as an additional cap, while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at about 22 stays deep in oversold territory, hinting that sellers remain in control even if short-lived corrective rebounds become more likely.
On the topside, initial resistance emerges near the former break area of the descending trend line around 1.1295, ahead of the dense 50-, 100- and 200-day SMA band at roughly 1.1496, which reinforces the broader bearish structure. Further up, the horizontal barrier at 1.1849 represents a more distant obstacle whose recovery would be required to alleviate the medium-term downside pressure.
(The technical analysis of this story was written with the help of an AI tool. Know more.)
Euro FAQs
The Euro is the currency for the 20 European Union countries that belong to the Eurozone. It is the second most heavily traded currency in the world behind the US Dollar. In 2022, it accounted for 31% of all foreign exchange transactions, with an average daily turnover of over $2.2 trillion a day. EUR/USD is the most heavily traded currency pair in the world, accounting for an estimated 30% off all transactions, followed by EUR/JPY (4%), EUR/GBP (3%) and EUR/AUD (2%).
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy. The ECB’s primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means either controlling inflation or stimulating growth. Its primary tool is the raising or lowering of interest rates. Relatively high interest rates – or the expectation of higher rates – will usually benefit the Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
Eurozone inflation data, measured by the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), is an important econometric for the Euro. If inflation rises more than expected, especially if above the ECB’s 2% target, it obliges the ECB to raise interest rates to bring it back under control. Relatively high interest rates compared to its counterparts will usually benefit the Euro, as it makes the region more attractive as a place for global investors to park their money.
Data releases gauge the health of the economy and can impact on the Euro. Indicators such as GDP, Manufacturing and Services PMIs, employment, and consumer sentiment surveys can all influence the direction of the single currency. A strong economy is good for the Euro. Not only does it attract more foreign investment but it may encourage the ECB to put up interest rates, which will directly strengthen the Euro. Otherwise, if economic data is weak, the Euro is likely to fall. Economic data for the four largest economies in the euro area (Germany, France, Italy and Spain) are especially significant, as they account for 75% of the Eurozone’s economy.
Another significant data release for the Euro is the Trade Balance. This indicator measures the difference between what a country earns from its exports and what it spends on imports over a given period. If a country produces highly sought after exports then its currency will gain in value purely from the extra demand created from foreign buyers seeking to purchase these goods. Therefore, a positive net Trade Balance strengthens a currency and vice versa for a negative balance.

Ukrainian defense firm FirePoint has carried out the first strike using a domestically produced tactical ballistic missile against targets inside Russian territory.
Company General Director Iryna Terekh confirmed the operational deployment, according to TSN on October 12.
“We are working on an extended-range version, which will also appear this year,” Terekh noted.

Fire Point made significant progress on its domestic missile program during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, aiming to complete its 850-kilometer FP-9 ballistic missile by late 2026.

articles.title: Citroën's iconic 2CV returns as an all-electric model - Euronews.com
articles.summary: Citroën's iconic 2CV returns as an all-electric model  Euronews.comCitroen revives the 2CV for an electric age  BBCCitroen confirms new electric 2 CV for 2028  PistonHeadsStellantis Unveils Six Concept Cars “The Night Before” the Paris Motor Show  Stellantis.com2028 Citroën 2CV revealed – iconic value car goes electric for second coming  What Car?
articles.full_text:
Almost 40 years after disappearing, the iconic 2CV returns at the Paris Motor Show as a fully electric city car, keeping things simple and affordable in an increasingly competitive market.
It is one of the most eagerly awaited stars of the Paris Motor Show, which will open its doors in the French capital from 13 to 18 October: Citroën’s legendary 2CV is making a major comeback almost forty years after disappearing from the market, in a fully electric version.
With its V-shaped bonnet, upright windscreen and distinctive round headlights, the new city car keeps the lines of its ancestor, as well as its down-to-earth, popular DNA.
Launched in 1948 and produced until 1990, the 2CV left its mark on several generations of drivers, becoming one of the symbols of France’s post-war boom years and the first holiday getaways, with more than five million units built in all versions combined.
Simplicity, versatility and an affordable price
Just like the original model, this new 2CV is built around simplicity, versatility and an affordable price tag, at around €15,000.
"The 2CV became an icon not because of what it had, but because of what it allowed people to do. And today that spirit is back," said Citroën’s chief executive Xavier Chardon during the 2CV’s unveiling at the motor show.
To keep costs down, Stellantis is betting on a car weighing under one tonne, fitted with a small battery tailored to everyday journeys. Still at the concept-car stage, the new 2CV is expected to go on sale at the end of 2028, to coincide with the 80th anniversary of the original model, and could even be offered as a small van.
The switch to electric is being helped along by purchase incentives in France, where battery-powered vehicles reached the record level of 42% of new registrations in September. The trend is driven in particular by small electric models and by the state-backed social leasing scheme, with around 9,500 registrations over the past month.
Faced with mounting competition from Chinese brands, which are set to have a strong presence at the show, other European manufacturers are also turning to affordable electric cars, such as the new Dacia Spring or Volkswagen’s ID. Polo.

articles.title: EU Kids Act: What digital platforms & AI providers must know - Browne Jacobson
articles.summary: EU Kids Act: What digital platforms & AI providers must know  Browne Jacobson
articles.full_text:
On 17 September 2026, the European Commission published a proposal for a new EU Regulation titled the 'EU KIDS ACT – EU Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy'.
The proposal represents one of the most significant and wide-ranging EU legislative interventions targeting the online safety of children to date, introducing harmonised obligations across the EU on a broad set of digital services.
At a glance
- The EU KIDS Act introduces EU-wide child safety obligations for social media platforms, video-sharing services, online games, AI companions and more.
- Four core pillars: social media age restrictions, safety-by-design, age assurance and enforcement.
- Non-EU platforms and AI providers may be caught in the proposed new rules.
- The EU KIDS Act builds on and complements existing digital regulatory frameworks including the Digital Services Act (DSA) and EU AI Act.
Background
The Commission frames the initiative as a response to substantial online risks to minors' health, development and wellbeing, including: cyberbullying, child sexual abuse, grooming, and the mental and physical health impacts of excessive or harmful digital engagement. The Commission President, Ursula von der Leyen, emphasised that technology was not created with children’s wellbeing in mind.
The proposal follows recommendations from a Special Panel on Child Safety Online and is intended to establish EU-wide access restrictions, safety-by-design rules, and proportionate privacy-preserving age assurance, with coverage extending beyond just social media platforms to a range of other services (as further detailed below).
A key driver is also the growing patchwork of Member State initiatives on age restrictions, with varying scope and age limits, the proposal seeks to harmonise diverging national rules to ensure uniform protection of children across the EU.
Who will be impacted?
| In-scope | Providers of the following services or systems which are accessible to minors (i.e., an individual under the age of 18) in the EU will fall within scope: | 
| Territorial reach | The Act applies regardless of where the provider is located, provided the service is offered to recipients located or established in the EU. For AI companions and general conversational chatbots, providers placing those systems on the market or putting them into service in the EU, irrespective of the provider's location will be caught. This means that non-EU platforms and AI developers may also be impacted. | 
| Out-of-scope | Not all digital services are captured. The Act expressly excludes not-for-profit online encyclopaedias; not-for-profit educational or scientific repositories; primarily educational services operated by or for educational establishments; open-source software platforms (unless the platform itself is an in-scope AI system); services developed solely for research and development purposes; and systems made available exclusively to public authorities. | 
The 4 Pillars of the EU KIDS Act
The Act has four key pillars:
1. Social media delay
Pillar one introduces a gradual uptake of social media and video-sharing platforms, with an EU-wide minimum age of 15 for minors to create autonomous accounts.
| Age group | Status | Key rules | 
| Under 3 | Banned. | No access permitted. | 
| 3 – 13 years | Restricted. | No autonomous account permitted. Limited access via a parent / guardian’s own account only, subject to limitations and conditions. | 
| 13 – 15 years | Partially permitted. | Minors cannot set up their own account but may have mini social media and video-sharing accounts set up and supervised by their parents / guardians. These accounts must have access to limited features and reduced screen time. | 
| 15 – 18 years | Permitted. | Autonomous accounts allowed without parental consent. Safety-by-design protections apply by default. | 
2. Safety-by-design requirements
Pillar two introduces wide-ranging safety-by-design requirements. Providers must apply these protections by default and may only derogate once they have established the user is an adult using compliant age assurance.
Key obligations include:
- Addictive design and time management: Providers must not design their services in a way that encourages compulsive or excessive use and should ensure time-limited access and interruption of usage in ways that protect school time and core sleep hours for minors.
- Recommender systems: Providers must prioritise explicit preferences, disable by default recommendations based on implicit engagement signals for minors, and offer tools to control or reset preferences and choose at least one non-profiling option.
- Default safe settings: Geolocation/tracking, microphone/camera access, account recommendations, contact sync and push notifications must be switched off by default for minors, and certain harmful features must be made unavailable to them.
- Contact and interaction safeguards: Providers must limit the ability to initiate direct contact with minors, apply default limits on visibility of minors' information and content, and disable livestreaming by default for minors.
- Economic transactions: Providers must clearly disclose that a transaction is taking place, display the real-money value, and prohibit design patterns that lead to excessive, impulsive or unwanted spending and exposure to variable reward systems for minors.
3. Age assurance framework
Age assurance is a core focus of the new proposal. Pillar three establishes a dedicated age assurance framework, requiring the implementation of age assurance solutions to be accurate, reliable, robust, non-intrusive, privacy-preserving and non-discriminatory, with specific data-protection constraints. Self-declaration is explicitly stated to be insufficient for compliance purposes.
The data protection constraints are significant. Providers must not enable identification of the recipient or locate, track, target, advertise to, or profile users. Providers must also not process more personal data than strictly necessary to determine whether an age threshold has been met, and must not further process, share, or combine that data.
Where the delayed access rules apply (i.e., the rules that apply to under 15s) providers must rely exclusively on a certified EU age verification solution using an EU proof of age attestation supplied by a certified third party and listed on Commission-maintained EU lists. For safety-by-design and app-store obligations, providers may use alternative age assurance solutions, provided they can demonstrate compliance with the same substantive quality and data protection requirements.
Providers must verify the age of users opening an account, as well as the age of users who already have an account once the rules enter into force.
4. Enforcement and interaction with existing EU Digital Regulatory Architecture
Pillar four, does not create an entirely new enforcement regime. Instead, it builds on and complements the existing frameworks under the DSA and the EU AI Act, while introducing targeted additions.
| Service | Enforcement | 
| For online social networking services, video-sharing platform services, software application stores, and online games that are video gaming platforms. | Chapter IV enforcement provisions of the DSA apply. | 
| For AI companions and general conversational chatbots. | Chapter IX enforcement provisions of the EU AI Act apply. | 
| Very large online platforms (as designated under Article 33 DSA) and providers of AI systems (as designated under EU AI Act). | An expedited enforcement procedure applies to Commission-initiated proceedings involving VLOPs and AI systems under the Commission's exclusive supervision. The Commission must endeavour to communicate preliminary findings to the provider within 30 working days of opening proceedings, and to adopt a final decision within 90 working days. | 
| For processing personal data, data protection obligations under the EU GDPR apply in the usual manner. | Competent data protection supervisory authority enforcement powers apply. | 
Member States must ensure that authorities already designated under DSA, Article 49 and EU AI Act, Articles 70 and 74 are competent to supervise and enforce the Act for providers within their remit, and Member State authorities may not adopt decisions that contradict a decision of the EU Commission.
Whilst the Act is intended to sit alongside and supplement various other EU digital regulatory instruments, none of those instruments were designed with children’s online safety specifically in mind, despite containing provisions targeted at children’s safety and experiences online. The DSA imposes certain child safety obligations, most notably Article 28, which requires online platforms accessible to minors to put in place appropriate and proportionate measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors on their service.
The Audiovisual Media Services Directive (AVMSD), similarly requires video-sharing platform providers to take appropriate measures to protect minors from harmful content. In Ireland, Coimisiún na Meán has further operationalised these obligations under the AVMSD through its Online Safety Code, which came into effect in 2024 and imposes binding rules on designated online services regarding the protection of children from harmful online content. However, the European Commission has concluded that these existing measures, while important, are insufficient to adequately protect children in the digital environment. The EU KIDS Act seeks to bridge that gap.
Why is this important to businesses now?
Whilst the proposal remains subject to negotiation, the direction of travel is clear. The EU KIDS Act reflects a growing international consensus that stronger protections for children online are needed. Similar initiatives have already been introduced in the United Kingdom, Australia and France, signalling that regulatory action in this space is accelerating globally.
I

articles.title: British destroyer sails with five Ukrainian warships - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: British destroyer sails with five Ukrainian warships  UK Defence Journal'It’s like a computer game or fireworks, but more difficult' – meet the Ukrainians learning to hunt mines in the English Channel  LBCRoyal Navy destroyer HMS Dauntless joins Ukrainian warships as they complete South Coast workout  Royal NavyUkraine's Navy trains in British waters for the dangerous task of clearing Black Sea mines  Forces News'Intensive training' prepares warship to joi...
articles.full_text:
Five Ukrainian minehunters have completed seven days of intensive training off the south coast of England, closing with a run in close formation around the Type 45 destroyer HMS Dauntless in the eastern Solent, according to the Royal Navy.
The ships are based in Portsmouth as part of British support to Ukraine, and the training ranged across the Dorset, Hampshire and Isle of Wight coastlines, taking in gunnery, the destruction of dummy mines and formation sailing with a major warship.
UNS Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv and Cherkasy made up the quintet. Under the supervision of British military personnel they first demonstrated their ability to defend themselves with gunnery shoots off Portland, then moved on to locating, identifying and where necessary destroying underwater explosive devices.
That work used Seafox, the remotely operated submersible that has been a mainstay of Royal Navy mine countermeasures for a couple of decades. Chernihiv and Cherkasy both carried out live firings of the system, which ended in controlled explosions neutralising the mine threats they had been set.
The seven days formed the final chapter of Exercise Lion Protector, a Joint Expeditionary Force exercise running from August until the weekend and intended to refine how member nations respond militarily to protect Europe’s northern flank. Its fifth and last phase shifted the emphasis onto the ability of JEF navies to protect maritime infrastructure and guarantee the security of sea lanes.
Earlier phases took the UK Commando Force to the Faroe Islands to work on safeguarding the Greenland, Iceland and United Kingdom gap, the first time Royal Marines have operated in the Atlantic chain since the Second World War. The Royal Navy rates Lion Protector second only to Sea Breeze, the Ukrainian Navy’s premier annual exercise, in scope and complexity. Sea Breeze itself was held off the south coast of England over the summer.
Dauntless played the part of the major warship in the closing serial, with the Ukrainian ships manoeuvring around her as a small task group. The destroyer is preparing to escort the fleet flagship HMS Prince of Wales when she resumes her Firecrest 2026 deployment to the High North. Mine countermeasures have become one of the more practical forms of British help to Ukraine, since the Black Sea remains heavily mined and the Ukrainian Navy has had to rebuild capability.
I wonder what would happen if the Russian frigate that seems to be permanently based in the North sea/channel area attacked these Ukrainian mine hunters, would the RN come to their aid ?
Only if it took place in uk territorial waters. However the Ukrainians are not daft, if they were anywhere near a Russian warship it would be to sink it.
I was just wondering what (if anything) the UK government would do if it kicked off between the Ukrainian naval vessels and the Russian Frigate. The ex RN mine hunters would be no good in a fight against a Frigate (even one as old as the one currently in the Channel) but would make excellent launch platforms for drone’s.
Perhaps we will find out … but I doubt it. Russia will I suspect want to avoid any contact.
Let us hope so.

articles.title: Niall Ferguson: Why Europe Is Burning - The Free Press
articles.summary: Niall Ferguson: Why Europe Is Burning  The Free Press
articles.full_text:
“The most French thing I’ve ever seen” was a couple sipping wine in a sidewalk café, probably discussing Jean-Paul Sartre, while a fire started by protesters raged on the other side of the boulevard. Disappointingly, the video posted on X was from three years ago, but it suited the moment last week.
As their national anthem contains the phrase, “Aux armes, citoyens!,” don’t be surprised if, quite regularly, young French people decide to reenact revolutionary scenes. As I write, French schools are burning—set ablaze by high schoolers who say they want more investment in education but for some reason think they can achieve this by filling the streets with garbage, setting it on fire, waving Palestinian flags, and clashing with the police. The latest reincarnations of the sans-culottes are out in force—though, as in 1968, their attire is quite chic. As a cynical friend observed, what the first Communion is for a young Roman Catholic, so the first manifestation is for a young Parisian: a rite of passage.
And yet it’s not just France. The kids are out in the streets of Madrid, too, incensed (they claim) about a growing housing crisis. In Brussels the burning issue is government budget cuts.
So what’s going on in Europe?
No, I don’t think it’s the beginning of Eurozone Crisis 2.0. Those with good memories will recall that the first Eurozone crisis began in 2009 with a Greek debt crisis that spread to other countries. As we shall see, the recent wave of protests has indeed coincided with a French debt crisis that also threatens to spread to other members of the Eurozone. However, if the European Central Bank (ECB) learned anything from the events of 2011–2012 it was that it must stand ready “to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro”—the immortal words of ECB president Mario Draghi in July 2012. If French bond yields go up much higher—say by another 100 basis points (1 percent)—then the ECB has the tools to intervene and stabilize the market.

articles.title: EUR/USD Price Forecast — EUR/USD Near 17-Month Low as French Spread and 102.4 Dollar Bite - TradingNEWS
articles.summary: EUR/USD Price Forecast — EUR/USD Near 17-Month Low as French Spread and 102.4 Dollar Bite  TradingNEWS
articles.full_text:
Key Points
- EUR/USD slips 0.17% to 1.1180 after failing at 1.1218, holding just above the 1.1163 October low.
- The U.S.-German 10-year yield gap stands at 175bp, with Treasuries at 5.24% against Bunds at 3.49%.
- France’s OAT-Bund spread peaked at 152bp, its widest since 2011, after the October 1 budget.
The euro gave up an early bounce on Monday, October 12, 2026, and slid back toward the bottom of its October range. EUR/USD traded at 1.1180 near midday in New York, down 0.17% from Friday’s 1.1201 close, after reaching an intraday high of 1.1218 during the European morning. The pair opened the Asian session at 1.1189, rallied 29 pips into London, and then reversed through the U.S. morning as the dollar firmed across the board.
That path is the story of the past month in miniature. Each attempt by the euro to build a recovery has been sold by mid-session, and each low has been only marginally above the last. Monday’s trading kept the pair 17 pips above the October 7 intraday low of 1.1165 and 17 pips above the month’s lowest print of 1.1163. EUR/USD now trades near its weakest level in 17 months.
The broader numbers are unforgiving. The euro is down 3.18% against the dollar over the past month and 3.36% over 12 months. It fell 2.5% in September alone and has lost more than 1% in October through the first eight sessions. Over the last 20 trading days the pair has dropped 2.28%, while its five-day return is only -0.08%, meaning the selling has slowed but has not stopped. The latest close sits only 8.8% of the way from the period low to the period high, about as close to the floor of its range as a currency pair can sit without breaking it.
The six-month view shows how far the euro has fallen. EUR/USD peaked at 1.1808 on April 16, 2026, and the six-month average stands at 1.1543. At 1.1180 the pair is 628 pips, or 5.3%, below its April high and 363 pips below its six-month mean. Every leg of that decline has come from the same two forces: a U.S. dollar supported by the highest Treasury yields since 2002, and a euro weighed down by a French sovereign debt scare that has pushed the spread between French and German bonds to its widest since the 2011 eurozone crisis.
The euro is being squeezed from both ends of the pair at once. The dollar side benefits from higher yields, Fed hike expectations and safe-haven demand tied to the Middle East. The euro side suffers from fiscal stress in its second-largest economy and a European Central Bank that cannot raise rates as aggressively as the Fed without risking a bond-market accident. Until one of those pressures eases, rallies toward 1.1250 remain selling opportunities.
A 17-Month Low: Mapping the Euro’s Slide From 1.1808
The euro’s decline since April has unfolded in clear stages, and the September and October legs have been the most violent.
In late September, EUR/USD was still trading in the 1.13s and 1.14s. The pair opened at 1.1448 on September 23 and fell 0.59% that session to close at 1.1382. It held near 1.1391 on September 25 before a run of four straight losing days took it to 1.1330 by September 30. Through that stretch the euro was retreating steadily but in an orderly way.
October 1 broke the pattern. The French government presented its 2027 budget that day, and the euro fell 0.78% in a single session, from 1.1330 to 1.1242, with an intraday low of 1.1215. That was the largest one-day drop of the selloff, and it lined up exactly with the French 10-year yield climbing to 4.96%, its highest since July 2002. The currency market treated the French budget as a eurozone event, not a national one.
The first week of October was a series of failed recoveries. The euro bounced 0.11% to 1.1254 on October 2, then fell 0.28% to 1.1223 on October 5 after testing 1.1161 intraday. It rallied 0.33% to 1.1260 on October 6, touching 1.1277, the highest level of the past week. That rally was erased the next day, when the pair fell 0.56% to 1.1197 with a low of 1.1165 as the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.28%. The euro added 0.13% to 1.1211 on October 8, then slipped 0.08% to 1.1202 on October 9, with Friday’s session ranging from 1.1188 to 1.1244.
The pattern is clear in the highs. EUR/USD topped at 1.1338 on October 1, 1.1286 on October 2, 1.1277 on October 6, 1.1244 on October 9 and 1.1218 on Monday. Five consecutive lower highs in eight sessions describe a market where sellers are lowering their offers each time the euro bounces. The lows, by contrast, have held between 1.1161 and 1.1165 for a week, which makes 1.1160 the line that matters most.
The last time EUR/USD traded at these levels was in the spring of 2025. The pair has given back the entire rally that carried it to 1.1808 in April 2026, and with the dollar index at its strongest since April 2025, the euro has no cushion left.
The Dollar Index at 102.35: Broad Strength, Not Just Euro Weakness
The euro’s weakness on Monday was part of a wider dollar move. The U.S. dollar index, which tracks the greenback against six major currencies, traded around 102.35, near levels last seen in April 2025. It closed Friday at 102.23, and on September 24 it was near 101.05, a 1.3% gain in less than three weeks. The euro makes up about 58% of the index, so a weaker euro mechanically lifts the DXY, but Monday’s moves show the dollar gaining across the board.
The cross-section confirms it. The dollar was up 0.21% against the euro on Monday, 0.19% against the yen, 0.24% against the Australian dollar, 0.30% against the New Zealand dollar and 0.37% against the Swiss franc. It was roughly flat against sterling, up 0.03%, and the Canadian dollar, also 0.03%. GBP/USD held near 1.3233 with no change on the day. A dollar that gains against the franc and the yen, the two classic safe havens, is not simply a safe-haven trade. It is a yield trade.
The dollar’s support comes from three directions. The first is yields: the 10-year Treasury sits at 5.24%, frozen for Monday’s Columbus Day bond-market closure but near its 24-year high. The second is the Federal Reserve, which raised rates in September to a range of 3.75% to 4.00% and is still priced for an 85% chance of another hike by December. The third is geopolitics. Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia’s main airport killed 12 people over the weekend, and talk of U.S. participation in retaliation has added a safe-haven layer to the dollar bid.
The thin holiday session magnified the moves. With U.S. Treasury trading shut, currency traders had no fresh yield data, and the dollar advanced modestly on bets that the Fed will hike at least once more before year-end. Those same bets are what make Wednesday’s U.S. consumer price index so important for EUR/USD.
For the euro, the dollar’s broad strength means relief cannot come from Europe alone. Even a full resolution of the French budget standoff would leave EUR/USD facing a dollar index above 102 and a U.S. yield advantage near its widest of the cycle. The pair needs both pressures to ease to sustain a recovery above 1.1250, and only one of them is under European control.
The Rate Gap: 175 Basis Points on the 10-Year, 150 on Policy
The single biggest structural driver of EUR/USD is the interest-rate differential, and it is running wide against the euro.
On policy rates, the Fed’s September hike lifted the federal funds target to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. The ECB has raised rates twice this year, taking its deposit facility rate to 2.50%. That leaves a gap of 150 basis points between the top of the Fed’s range and the ECB’s deposit rate. Cash parked in dollars earns 1.5 percentage points more a year than cash parked in euros, and that carry advantage rewards holding the dollar while the gap persists.
On the long end, the spread is wider. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yields 5.24%. The German 10-year Bund yielded 3.49% on October 7, the latest recorded reading, which puts the U.S.-German 10-year gap at 175 basis points. Even the French 10-year, which has blown out on fiscal fears, yielded 4.83% on October 7, still 41 basis points below Treasuries. A global investor choosing between U.S. and European government bonds is paid substantially more to own American paper, and that capital flow supports the dollar.
The direction of the gap matters as much as its size. In September both central banks hiked, but the Fed is still priced for more tightening by December while the market has scaled back ECB expectations. Before the French bond turmoil, markets priced an 80% chance of another ECB hike by year-end. That expectation has since faded, and another ECB increase is now not fully priced until February. Futures put the probability of a Fed hike at the October 28 meeting near 19%, with further tightening in December partially priced in.
Put those together and the differential is set to widen, not narrow. If the Fed hikes in December and the ECB waits until February, the policy gap would expand to 175 basis points by year-end. A widening rate gap is the textbook setup for a currency to keep falling, and EUR/USD has followed the textbook since April.
The opening for the euro would come from a U.S. inflation surprise to the downside. A soft CPI print on Wednesday would push December Fed hike odds down, pull Treasury yields lower and narrow the gap from the U.S. side. That is the most likely source of a meaningful EUR/USD rally this month, because the European side of the gap is boxed in by France.
France’s Debt Crisis: A 5% OAT and a 152-Basis-Point Spread
The euro’s second problem is homegrown. France, the eurozone’s second-largest economy, is in the middle of a sovereign bond selloff that has pushed its borrowing costs to the highest levels in more than two decades.
The trigger was the 2027 budget, presented on October 1. On that day the French 10-year OAT yield rose to 4.96%, its highest level since July 2002. articles.title: IFS finds £1bn annual funding gap in UK defence spending plans - ADS Advance
articles.summary: IFS finds £1bn annual funding gap in UK defence spending plans  ADS Advance
articles.full_text:
New analysis highlights outstanding funding decisions for the UK’s Defence Investment Plan ahead of the Autumn Budget.
The UK government has yet to identify funding for around £1 billion a year of its planned increase in defence spending, according to new analysis from the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS).
In its Green Budget 2026, published on 12 October, the IFS found that the government’s Defence Investment Plan increased planned expenditure by an average of £3 billion annually compared with previous commitments.
However, around £1 billion a year of that increase remains unfunded.
The IFS said this represents “money that the new Chancellor will have to find at the next Budget, whether from tax, borrowing or other spending, if he sticks to existing plans”.
The institute also highlighted “domestic and international political pressure to move further and faster on defence spending”.
How much of the Defence Investment Plan is funded?
The government’s Defence Investment Plan, published in June, sets out almost £298 billion in Ministry of Defence expenditure between 2026–27 and 2029–30.
The plan includes £15 billion in additional investment over four years to support priorities identified in the 2025 Strategic Defence Review.
According to the government’s funding breakdown, £10.3 billion of the additional spending has an identified funding source, leaving £4.7 billion to be addressed at the Autumn Budget.
The government intends to fund much of the increase by reallocating capital spending from other departments, including reductions to transport and energy budgets.
UK defence spending commitments
Under existing plans, NATO-qualifying UK defence spending is due to reach 2.7% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2027–28 and remain at that level until 2029–30.
The government has also committed to increasing core defence spending to 3% of GDP in the next Parliament, subject to future funding decisions.
The UK is among NATO allies that have agreed to spend 3.5% of GDP on core defence by 2035.
The IFS estimates that meeting the 2035 commitment would require approximately £25 billion in additional annual spending, in today’s prices, compared with current plans.
In its June assessment, IFS Senior Research Economist Max Warner said: “Defence spending will likely remain one of the biggest fiscal pressures facing the UK in the medium term.”
Warner also questioned how the government would meet its longer-term commitments, given the difficulty of identifying funding for the more modest increases announced in June.
The IFS’s latest analysis notes that reaching 3.5% by 2035 would require defence spending to increase substantially faster in the next Parliament if the government maintains its existing plans through 2029–30.
The institute also noted that other NATO members have increased defence spending as a share of national income more rapidly than the UK.
Autumn Budget funding decision
The outstanding defence funding requirement comes as the Treasury faces wider pressures on public spending.
In a parliamentary response on 15 September, the government confirmed that the remaining £4.7 billion for the Defence Investment Plan would be addressed at the Autumn Budget.
The Chancellor must now determine how to meet that commitment through taxation, borrowing or changes to other spending plans if the government maintains its existing defence investment programme.

EUR/GBP remains on the defensive on Monday, sliding to a fresh year-to-date low of 0.8445 as French political and fiscal concerns keep the Euro (EUR) under sustained pressure. At the time of writing, the cross trades around 0.8450, down 0.17% on the day.
France aims to bring its budget deficit down to 5% of GDP in 2027, with parliamentary debate on the plans expected to begin this week. However, securing support for large spending cuts could prove difficult in a divided parliament. With public debt approaching 119% of GDP, markets fear that failure to pass the measures could deepen concerns about France’s finances.
French fiscal concerns and the broader global bond sell-off have pushed French government bond yields higher, widening the yield spread over Germany to multi-year highs. Higher borrowing costs could weigh on Eurozone growth. Against this backdrop, the European Central Bank (ECB) faces a difficult balance between bringing inflation under control and protecting growth, as higher energy costs linked to the Middle East war keep price pressures elevated.
A Reuters poll published on Thursday shows that 70 of 73 economists expect the ECB to hold its deposit rate at 2.50% on October 29, while 64 of 73 anticipate a 25-basis-point hike in December.
Analysts at MUFG note that “negative developments in the euro zone have boosted the relative appeal of the pound,” reinforcing recent gains in EUR/GBP. They add that media reports suggest the Labour government is “well aware of challenging global bond market conditions ahead of this month’s budget scheduled for 28th October,” which is “encouraging them to play it safe as they seek to limit the risk of negative market reaction.” MUFG argues that such fiscal caution would be “a development that would help to ease downside risks for the pound.”
The British Pound (GBP) also benefits from growing bets on a Bank of England (BoE) rate hike before year-end after six consecutive holds, as higher energy costs keep inflation sticky above the central bank’s 2% target.
On the data front, Germany releases its final September inflation figures on Tuesday, followed by the UK’s August Gross Domestic Product (GDP) report on Thursday. The final Eurozone inflation reading for September is due on Friday. These releases, alongside comments from ECB and BoE officials throughout the week, could offer further clues on the outlook for interest rates on both sides.

articles.title: The EU invites Canada to become an “Associate Member,” but what does that really mean? - IR Insider
articles.summary: The EU invites Canada to become an “Associate Member,” but what does that really mean?  IR Insider
articles.full_text:
On September 16, Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, announced Canada would be “opening the door” to Canada becoming an "Associate Member” of the European Union (EU). The proposed “associate membership,” which does not exist in any current EU treaties, would sit somewhere above free-trade partners but below full EU membership.
The decision to strengthen their alliance and create this new “associate member” category is a direct response to the breakdown of trade negotiations between the US and Canada in August of this year. After weeks of negotiations, the US imposed a 50% tariff on a series of Canadian goods and Canada responded with reciprocal tariffs. This made it clear that Canada needed to look outside of the US for support. Von der Leyen echoed this in her State of the Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, saying “...[I]n this new world we must urgently reimagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies.”
This association will allow EU-Canadian cooperation to enter new domains like defense, cybersecurity, and AI. There has also been a significant focus on energy since the 2022 Europe Energy crisis which was the result of sanctioning Russian oil. Canada, importantly, has resources that are attractive to the EU including oil and rare earth minerals like lithium, nickel, cobalt, and rare earths which are important for battery making and a transition to a greener future.
Canada and the EU have long been trade partners. In 2016 they removed 98% of tariffs with the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA). However, the agreement has yet to be ratified in 10 of the 27 EU member states. Additionally, there is the Strategic Partnership Agreement (SPA), which encourages diplomatic dialogue on climate change, human rights, research, and more. This association membership takes a history of cooperation one step further. It is likely that a lot of the specifics about the deal and the extent of the cooperation will be hashed out at the EU-Canada conference in Montreal at the end of October.
Joining the EU as a member state is a lengthy process. Countries must first meet the Copenhagen Criteria by having strong democratic institutions, a free market, and the ability to enact existing EU legislation into their national framework. Then the European Commission, composed of one commissioner per member state, agrees to begin accession negotiations between the country and the EU. These negotiations can last years or even decades and there are currently nine countries in the accession process. As part of the accession process, an Association Agreement, usually a bilateral trade and security agreement, is signed between the EU and the candidate State.
There has been some suggestion of Canada joining the EU as a full member state by several European leaders, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot. Canada, despite meeting most of the EU’s requirements, is not interested in joining as a full member state, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney saying “Canada is not in a position, nor seeking, to become a full member of the European Union." It seems geography is the main reason preventing Canada from joining the EU as a member state.
US president Donald Trump responded poorly to the news saying that it would likely trigger hostile “heavy tariffs.” The Canadian response is fairly positive although it has provoked the anger of certain Canadian MPs like Jamil Jivani who said on X “Conservatives will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU.”

articles.summary: Rostov Oil Terminal Burns for Third Day After Reported Ukrainian Drone Attack  The Moscow TimesTrump’s deal with Putin will not deter Zelensky from playing his strongest card  The TelegraphHow Ukraine uses precision drone strikes to hobble Russian oil refineries  The Washington PostTrump’s Ex-Envoy Says Ukraine Should Be Free to Strike Russia  Bloomberg.comSamara Oil Pumping Station Attacked for Fourth Time Since Start of Month  Мілітарний
articles.full_text:
A fire at an oil terminal in the southern Russian city of Rostov-on-Don continued to burn for a third day Monday after a reported Ukrainian drone attack over the weekend, according to independent media and Ukrainian monitoring channels.
Footage published by Astra and Exilenova+ showed flames and thick smoke rising from the terminal’s fuel storage tanks. The facility, owned by the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, has a total storage capacity of 60,000 cubic meters and can handle 3.5 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, according to publicly available data.
Authorities had not announced that the fire had been extinguished as of midday Monday.
The Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova said preliminary information indicated that seven of the terminal’s 12 tanks had burned and another showed signs of fire damage. Footage it published showed blackened tanks alongside others still engulfed in flames. The reported extent of the damage could not be independently confirmed.
The local Telegram channel Rostov Glavny also published footage of the blaze, saying the city had been shrouded in smoke for a second day. Its post suggested that reeds might be burning, citing rumors, but Astra’s analysis placed the fire at the oil terminal.
The facility, formerly known as Yug Rusi, was reportedly struck overnight into Saturday in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at the site.
The terminal transfers petroleum products onto sea and river tankers for export and has reportedly been used to supply fuel to the Russian military.
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said air defenses had shot down more than 100 drones over the region that night. He reported several fires following strikes and said six people had been injured, but did not mention damage to the terminal.
Ukraine had not publicly claimed responsibility for an attack on the facility.
The overnight attacks also damaged a railway drawbridge on the line between Rostov-on-Don and nearby Bataysk, causing lengthy delays to dozens of trains, according to Russian Railways.
Slyusar said two vessels were also damaged in the nearby city of Azov.

articles.title: Frankreichs wahres Energiedilemma: Atomare Zukunft – Risiko oder Chance? - Xpert.Digital - Konrad Wolfenstein
articles.summary: Frankreichs wahres Energiedilemma: Atomare Zukunft – Risiko oder Chance?  Xpert.Digital - Konrad Wolfenstein
articles.full_text:
Published on: October 12, 2026 / Updated on: October 12, 2026 – Author: Konrad Wolfenstein
The challenges facing France's nuclear power plant fleet: A balancing act between safety and cost
Energy policy in France: The tightrope walk between nuclear power and renewable energies
Flamanville and the illusion of cheap nuclear power: Lessons for the future
For decades, France's nuclear power plants have played a central role in national energy policy, making the country one of the largest net exporters of low-carbon electricity. However, while the existing reactor fleet represents both a valuable industrial asset and a growing financial risk, those in charge face the challenge of transitioning nuclear energy to a new market and technological landscape. Discussions surrounding the aging reactor fleet often give the impression that France is on the brink of a supply crisis, but current figures paint a different picture: electricity production remains stable and surplus. Nevertheless, the challenges are significant: maintenance and modernization measures, the construction of new reactors, and the parallel development of renewable energies must be carefully coordinated. The recent failure of the Flamanville EPR reactor has definitively shattered the illusion of cheap nuclear power and underscored that France's energy future cannot depend solely on nuclear energy. Developing a viable strategy for 2040 requires making the right investments while simultaneously keeping a close eye on public finances. The path to the future is therefore anything but easy and requires smart management of available resources and technologies.
France's nuclear gamble: Between industrial wealth and fiscal risk
The reactor fleet is not France's millstone – but the belief in cheap nuclear power could become one
France's nuclear power plant fleet is both an exceptionally valuable industrial asset and a growing financial risk. Those who describe it merely as a millstone underestimate its current economic benefits. Conversely, those who continue to view it as a virtually inexhaustible source of cheap electricity ignore aging, maintenance requirements, construction costs, financing risks, and the long time it takes to commission new reactors. The economic truth, therefore, lies not in a simple judgment for or against nuclear energy, but in the question of how France transitions a historically developed system into a new market and technological landscape.
France's power plant fleet comprises 57 reactors at 18 sites with an installed capacity of approximately 63 gigawatts. A large proportion of these plants were built in the 1970s and 1980s. This standardized expansion program was remarkably successful from an industrial policy perspective: for decades, France was able to generate large quantities of domestically produced, comparatively low-CO₂ electricity, limit its dependence on fossil fuel imports, and establish a complete value chain from research and development through plant construction and operation to fuel management.
The plants are now largely fully depreciated on their balance sheets. This reduces their ongoing capital costs and explains why existing reactors can generate electricity at significantly lower costs than newly built plants. However, this does not mean that the electricity is free or that the entire historical expansion would have been possible without government support. From the outset, France's nuclear industry was part of a centrally controlled industrial and infrastructure policy. The state bore technological, regulatory, and financial risks, and it continues to bear them today through the fully nationalized energy company EDF.
The crucial challenge now lies in financing three waves of investment simultaneously: the extension and modernization of existing reactors, the construction of new nuclear power plants, and the expansion of renewable energies, grids, storage facilities, and controllable flexibility. France cannot completely avoid any of these tasks. It can only decide to what extent, in what order, and with what distribution of risk they are implemented.
An old park with high residual value
The age of reactors is often treated as if there were a technically defined limit after 40 years. In reality, France does not have an American licensing model where an operating license, once granted, automatically applies for a specific total duration. The reactors are assessed in regular safety reviews. Therefore, continued operation beyond 40, 50, or 60 years is neither automatically permitted nor categorically ruled out. The decisive factor is whether each individual plant meets the current safety requirements and what upgrades are necessary to achieve this.
Economically, the situation is only partially similar to that of an old car. With increasing age, maintenance and repair costs rise, while unexpected breakdowns become more likely. However, in the case of a power plant, these costs are offset by a very large remaining production value. A fully depreciated reactor can generate billions of kilowatt-hours over another year of operation without requiring the financing of a completely new replacement power plant. As long as the safety upgrades remain manageable and availability is sufficiently high, extending the operating life of an existing plant can therefore be significantly cheaper than building a new one.
The modernization of the existing wind farm fleet under the Grand Carénage program is now expected to cost at least €100.8 billion between 2014 and 2035. Including additional operating expenses, the total economic burden is even higher. This sum is enormous, but it needs to be put into perspective. It is spread over more than two decades and applies to a fleet that generates several hundred terawatt-hours of electricity in a typical production year. This translates to a cost of approximately €51 per megawatt-hour for extending the operating life from 40 to 60 years, assuming the projected production levels are actually achieved.
This means that continuing to operate existing reactors is likely to be not the most expensive, but rather the most economically attractive pillar of France's electricity supply. However, this is only true under certain conditions. Major serial technical failures, prolonged shutdowns, additional regulatory requirements, or significantly lower electricity revenues could worsen the equation. The corrosion problem on safety-critical pipelines in 2022 demonstrated how severely a common technical issue in a standardized fleet can impact many plants simultaneously. Standardization reduces costs during normal operation, but increases the risk of cluster failures in the event of systematic deficiencies.
Extending the operating lives of existing reactors is therefore more than just a stopgap measure. It is an economic bridge that gives France time to build new capacity. Without this bridge, nuclear power production would decline sharply within two decades, before a sufficient number of new reactors were available. The price of this strategy is a growing dependence on the technical reliability of older plants and on EDF's ability to implement complex retrofit programs on schedule.
Flamanville shatters the old cost illusion
The Flamanville EPR is the strongest argument against uncritically believing in cheap new nuclear power. The reactor was originally planned with construction costs of approximately €3.3 billion. After years of technical problems, rework, and delays, the total costs, including financing, amount to around €23.7 billion at 2023 prices. The plant was connected to the grid at the end of 2024, reached full power output for the first time at the end of 2025, and was shut down again for an extended period in 2026 for a comprehensive inspection and the replacement of the reactor pressure vessel lid. Compared to the original plan, the delay was approximately twelve years.
Flamanville is therefore not a typical infrastructure project with a moderate cost overrun, but rather an example of the loss of industrial routine. France had built very few new reactors for a long time. Supply chains, skilled workers, quality control, project management, and cooperation between clients, manufacturers, and regulators had to be partially rebuilt. At the same time, the EPR, a complex reactor type, was being constructed, the design of which was not yet sufficiently mature during the project. The combination of this initial project, new safety requirements, weak construction organization, and interrupted serial production led to a spiral of delays and financing costs.
Flamanville's profitability is correspondingly weak. At 85 percent capacity, electricity revenue of more than €122 per megawatt-hour would be required to achieve a real return of approximately four percent. Below €90 per megawatt-hour, even a real return of two percent seems difficult to attain. For a private operator without government backing, such a project would hardly have been viable. EDF was only able to complete it because the company holds a special strategic position and is ultimately supported by the French state.
Nevertheless, it would be analytically flawed to simply multiply the costs of Flamanville by 57 and conclude that replacing the entire fleet is unaffordable. Firstly, the existing reactors are not to be replaced simultaneously. Secondly, a series production program is economically different from a single problematic prototype. Thirdly, the simplified EPR2 is intended to learn from the mistakes of previous projects, be more standardized, and be built in pairs at existing sites. The crucial question is not whether every new reactor will necessarily be as expensive as Flamanville, but whether France can credibly demonstrate that the next series can be built significantly cheaper, faster, and more reproducibly.
The EPR2 program remains a gamble
France initially plans to build six EPR2 reactors at the Penly, Gravelines, and Bugey site

articles.summary: Martin Lewis MSE guide to staying warm for 'less than 1p' at home as energy bills rise  Wales OnlineRooms will stay warmer on cold nights using 1 bathroom item  Daily ExpressUK households urged to follow ‘6pm rule' in October  AOL.co.ukOctopus Energy's '6.30pm rule' keeps your home warm while reducing bills  The MirrorNine expert tips for staying warm at home without turning up the heating  The Independent
articles.full_text:
There are plenty of ways to beat the chill as colder temperatures settle in
Martin Lewis has shared a list of some of the most affordable ways to keep warm this winter, with some costing less than 1p to power up. His MoneySavingExpert (MSE) website team found some options that are some of "the cheapest to run" on a tight budget.
This comes as temperatures are expected to drop further, with homes across the UK set to become considerably colder in the coming weeks. Despite October getting off to a milder-than-average start, chillier conditions are on their way.
The latest forecasts from the Met Office point to "a smorgasbord of weather types", with shifts from "relatively balmy conditions to relatively cool". With the price cap having risen at the beginning of the month, keeping expenses to a minimum could be a key concern for many households, reports the Mirror.
Martin Lewis said: "This is a guide I really wish we didn't need to publish. The reason I asked the team to put this together is due to my overflowing email bag of desperation from people who can't afford their energy bills.
"Don't see this as an 'MSE or Martin says you should do this'. It's more that we're trying to help provide some options and information for those that may need to drastically cut down on energy usage due to financial desperation and some help for others who may want to do it out of a commitment to green issues."
How can I stay warm without using the central heating?
As winter drives up both heating and electricity consumption, typical bills during the colder months tend to be considerably higher than the annual average. The headline advice from personal finance specialists is to focus on keeping yourself warm rather than heating the entire home if monthly bills are a pressing concern.
The MSE report said: "There are lots of options out there – we can't vouch for which will keep you warmest, but we've tried to work out which is cheapest to run. Generally, we found it was those which could be charged via USB, but these items tend to be smaller, and may only warm part of your body (such as hands or feet)."
Personal heating methods (ranked by cheapest to run per hour)
- USB gloves: Cost initially - £13 | Cost per hour: Less than 1p
- Heated insoles: Cost initially - £11 | Cost per hour: Less than 1p
- USB hand warmers: Cost initially - £15 | Cost per hour: Less than 1p
- Electric gilet: Cost initially - £41 + battery pack | Cost per hour: Less than 1p
- Microwaveable wheat bag: Cost initially - £4 | Cost per hour: Less than 1p
- Electric heat pad: Cost initially - £20 | Cost per hour: 2.6p
- Electric footwarmer: Cost initially - £25 | Cost per hour: 2.6p
- Electric blanket, single: Cost initially - £35 | Cost per hour: 2.6p
- Reusable hand warmers: Cost initially - £10 for 5-pack | Cost per hour: Less than 1p (gas hob), 4p (electric hob)
- Hot Water Bottle, 1.5L: Cost initially - £5.50 | Cost per hour: 5.3p
Beyond direct heating devices, Martin's MSE team recommends a range of methods to help maintain warmth that likely use items households already have and require no additional cost.
Layering your clothing to trap body heat can prove beneficial. People may wish to purchase thermal tops and leggings, or simply add extra layers using garments they already own.
When layering, don't overlook your feet with a pair of socks or slippers. The MSE team said: "It's said that if your feet are cold, the rest of you will feel cold too. So wearing slippers can be essential to staying warm inside, particularly if you have hard floors."
When thinking about your floors, consider putting some covers on cold materials like wood. laminate or tiles. Invest in some small rugs or bathmats to stop your feet from getting cold when entering these rooms.
