articles.title: Why AI reuse makes privacy risk a business decision - SC Media
articles.summary: Why AI reuse makes privacy risk a business decision  SC Media
articles.full_text:
When organizations deploy AI before completing a purpose review, they face business accountability risk that legal compliance alone cannot resolve. The gap between AI deployment speed and governance review creates exposure that appears in customer trust, regulatory inquiry, breach investigation scope, and vendor accountability — all business consequences that arrive faster than legal defense.
AI reuse as a governance gap
AI systems consume existing data faster than governance decisions authorize that consumption. Customer support transcripts become AI training inputs. Purchase histories power behavioral scoring algorithms. Employee communications feed vendor AI platforms. Each use case can deliver legitimate business value, but the speed of AI deployment often outpaces the purpose review required to defend that data use.
The governance gap is not about AI systems behaving badly — it is about AI systems being deployed before the organization confirms it was authorized to use existing data in these new ways. When an AI system processes customer data for model training, automated scoring, or vendor enhancement, the question becomes: does the original data collection purpose cover this AI application? Organizations that cannot answer this question with documented purpose review face accountability exposure that grows with every model update and capability expansion.
Purpose review establishes whether existing data can support new AI uses without violating the relationship contract with customers, employees, or users. When that review happens after deployment, the organization may be defending a use it cannot adequately justify — a position that weakens customer trust, complicates regulatory response, and expands breach investigation scope. Retroactive review is possible, but conducting it after deployment rather than before increases the risk that a violation has already occurred and reduces the defensibility of any remediation.
Consequence 1: customer trust and relationship accountability
Customer data reused for AI creates a relationship accountability question that legal compliance cannot fully resolve. When customers discover their service interactions were used to train AI models, their support tickets powered automated systems, or their behavioral data fed targeting algorithms, they evaluate whether this use matched their reasonable expectations at data collection.
When the customer discovers this use, the organization must defend whether the original service purpose covered AI model development — a question that cannot be answered without purpose review. A customer who provided data for order processing reasonably questions whether that purpose included training a recommendation engine that influences pricing or product availability. The trust breach can occur regardless of legal justification when the customer feels the data use exceeded the relationship boundary they understood.
The accountability consequence extends beyond individual customer relationships to public trust and competitive position. Organizations that cannot explain their AI data use face customer objections, media scrutiny, and competitor advantage when AI reuse becomes visible. Trust recovery requires demonstrating that AI uses were considered and authorized — not defended after discovery.
AI reuse: business value vs. governance accountability
| Reuse decision | Business value sought | Privacy/control question | Executive risk if unanswered | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Training on customer interaction data (support transcripts, session logs, communication history) | Model trained on real customer language and issues improves support quality and automation | Does the original service delivery purpose cover AI model development that embeds customer communications into model weights? | Regulatory inquiry at model deployment; customer trust breach if use becomes public; retention obligations become unenforceable for data inside model parameters | 
| Behavioral scoring for product or commercial decisions (purchase history, engagement signals, content consumption used to score users for access, pricing, or priority) | Personalized experiences and optimized commercial outcomes | Does the original data collection purpose cover automated scoring that produces material effects on users? | Automated decision-making obligations triggered without safeguards; users denied rights they are entitled to; regulatory enforcement for undisclosed automated processing | 
| First-party data into third-party AI platforms (customer or employee data processed by AI-powered vendor tools, copilots, or enrichment services) | AI productivity and capability without internal model development cost | Does the vendor AI constitute a new processor, and is personal data contributing to vendor model training outside the organization's retention controls? | Data entered into vendor AI may be retained in vendor model infrastructure; controller accountability extends to how vendor processes and uses the data; cross-border transfer obligations may apply | 
| Audience data for AI-powered advertising or targeting (first-party editorial or commercial audience data used in AI-powered targeting, lookalike modeling, or audience extension) | Improved targeting efficiency and audience reach | Does the audience relationship purpose cover AI-powered modeling and third-party activation? | Audience members file access requests and objections to profiling; regulator inquires into AI-powered targeting without documented purpose coverage; customer trust impact if targeting scope becomes visible | 
| Internal analytics becoming automated decisions (analytics outputs — segment assignments, priority rankings, risk scores — fed into automated product or operational workflows without a governance transition) | Analytics insight scaled into operational efficiency through automation | When analytics outputs affect individuals automatically, does the original analytics purpose cover automated decision-making? | Automated decisions affecting individuals operate without legal basis review; no accountability chain from decision back to governance approval | 
Consequence 2: breach scope and investigation burden
Data breaches involving AI systems create investigation complexity that standard forensic response cannot resolve without purpose review records. When an AI system or its supporting data infrastructure is compromised, investigators must account for how personal data was processed, stored, and potentially exposed within the AI context. Data absorbed into model weights, used as training inputs, or processed by vendor AI platforms creates scope questions that require governance documentation to answer.
Investigation scope becomes more bounded when governance records exist — organizations that can trace AI training datasets back to purpose review decisions, including dates, owners, and determinations, are better positioned to contain and characterize breach scope. Without purpose review, breach investigators face greater difficulty determining which data uses were authorized, making it harder to distinguish between intended AI processing and potential misuse during the incident.
The investigation burden extends to notification obligations and regulatory reporting. Breach notification requirements depend on the type of personal data involved and the processing purposes that were affected. AI reuse without purpose review means investigators cannot categorize the data exposure accurately, potentially triggering broader notification requirements than the actual breach scope justified. This uncertainty expands legal costs, extends investigation timelines, and complicates regulatory reporting when precise scope cannot be established.
Consequence 3: regulatory exposure at deployment
Regulatory exposure from AI reuse is created at deployment, not at breach discovery. When organizations deploy AI systems that process personal data outside documented collection purposes, exposure exists from the moment the system processes its first data input. GDPR obligations for automated decision-making, sensitive category processing, and high-risk processing all activate at deployment — requiring safeguards, impact assessments, and user rights that are significantly more difficult and costly to implement after regulatory inquiry begins than before deployment.
Automated decision-making creates immediate obligations when AI outputs affect individuals. Customer scoring algorithms that influence pricing, access, or service levels trigger GDPR Article 22 protections that require documented legal basis, algorithmic transparency, and user objection rights. Organizations that deploy these systems without purpose review may be unable to provide the legal basis documentation that regulators expect during investigation.
Data protection impact assessments become required when AI processing creates high risks to individual privacy. Model training on large customer datasets, behavioral profiling for commercial decisions, and vendor AI processing often meet GDPR Article 35 thresholds for mandatory impact assessment. The assessment requirement exists whether or not the organization performed it before deployment — and conducting it after the fact, while possible, is more expensive, less defensible, and may confirm that a violation has already occurred.
Consequence 4: vendor AI dependency and accountability
Third-party AI platforms create controller accountability that extends beyond the organization's direct data processing to how vendors use that data. Customer service platforms with AI transcription, marketing tools with AI targeting, and productivity applications with AI enhancement all process personal data under vendor agreements that may permit broader use than the organization's original collection purpose authorized.
Vendor AI contracts require data processing terms that align with the organization's purpose limitations. Standard softwa

articles.title: 🌐🤝🏻 Growing commitment: How 12th EU-ASEAN Business Summit builds stronger regional economic partnership - The Southeast Asia Desk
articles.summary: 🌐🤝🏻 Growing commitment: How 12th EU-ASEAN Business Summit builds stronger regional economic partnership  The Southeast Asia Desk
articles.full_text:
🎯 The Main Takeaway
Southeast Asian and European government and enterprise executives have gathered to discuss strengthening the trade agreement between both regions at the 12th ASEAN-EU Business Summit as part of ASEAN’s 58th Economic Ministers’ Meeting in Manila on 22 September 2026.
The meeting focused on five critical long-term growth areas: energy transition, financial inclusion, digital connectivity, AI transformation, and health-nutrition.
The Summit was led by Ditte Juul Jørgensen, European Commission’s Director-General for Trade and Economic Security, and Satvinder Singh, ASEAN Deputy Secretary-General. It was also attended by executives from HSBC, Prudential, SWIFT, FrieslandCampina and Coca-Cola Europacific Partners.
📡 Why It’s on Our Radar
This summit signals a strong commitment to partnership development between the two blocs, particularly in trade and investment.
The European Union has considerably prioritised strengthening its economic partnership with ASEAN in recent years. It has also shown that the EU is trying to diversify markets to reduce excessive dependence on the United States and China.
Southeast Asian countries see the EU as a strategic partner able to hedge against uncertainties from US-China rivalry. ASEAN member states also recognise the EU as a reliable partner associated with a rules-based international order and multilateralism.
📊 By the Numbers
- ✨ Southeast Asian countries’ trust in the EU has reached 55.9%, the second highest amongst ASEAN Strategic Partners.
- 🛡️ The EU (37.7%) remains ASEAN’s most preferred and trusted “third-party” strategic partner to hedge against US-China rivalry.
- 💶 EU total foreign direct investment (FDI) is the largest in ASEAN, valued at US$31.3 billion in 2025, nearly double the previous year.
- 📈 In 2024, EU FDI stocks into ASEAN accounted for €363.4 billion, while ASEAN’s investment in the EU totalled €294.1 billion. The EU remains ASEAN’s third-largest investor, after the US and China.
- 🌐 ASEAN is the EU’s third-largest trading partner outside Europe, with US$313.1 billion in goods trade in 2025. Bilateral services trade amounted to €139.2 billion in 2024.
🔮 What’s the Next Target
Leaders welcomed the EU-Philippines Free Trade Agreement (FTA), expected to be ratified in 2027. Similar deals with Thailand and Malaysia are also expected to conclude next year, adding to existing FTAs with Indonesia, Vietnam, and Singapore.
The two blocs also pursue a broader region-to-region economic framework to mark the 50th anniversary of ASEAN-EU partnership next year. The EU-ASEAN Business Council urged adoption of an ASEAN-EU Economic Framework Agreement allowing advanced economic integration.
According to a release, Jens Ruebbert, Chairman of the EU-ASEAN Business Council, stated that these bilateral deals should not be the endpoint but the foundation for a more ambitious, longer-term goal to establish a region-to-region FTA.
He added that the council strongly believed a regional deal would provide a competitive edge for European and Southeast Asian companies alike, bringing trade and investment to a level that reflects the scale and strategic importance of the ASEAN-EU relationship.
⚖️ EU-ASEAN B2B Opportunity & Challenge
According to the EU-ABC 12th Sentiment Survey, 74% of European businesspeople believe an ASEAN-EU FTA would deliver more benefits than bilateral agreements, and 49% want negotiations for a regional FTA next year.
There is a set of opportunities and challenges for those looking to expand in ASEAN.
🚀 Opportunities
- 📊 ASEAN ranks as the region offering the strongest economic opportunities for the EU for the fourth consecutive year, with 61% choosing it over China and South Asia — up from 56% in 2025.
- 📈 Nearly four in five (78%) EU business representatives expect to increase trade and investment in ASEAN over the next five years.
⚠️ Challenges
- 💰 US tariff policy uncertainty remains a key concern, with 81% saying it has weakened business confidence in ASEAN.
- 🚧 Nearly three-quarters (73%) of European businesses see too many barriers for efficient supply-chain usage, while 67% identified the lack of harmonised regulations as a key challenge.
🌍EU Largest Trade Partners in Southeast Asia
According to United Nations Comtrade data, the largest Southeast Asian-European trade commodity is primarily agricultural and livestock products. Southeast Asia’s strongest export to the EU is coffee, valued at US$3.8 billion**. The most widely accepted European commodity is **milk and cream**, valued at **US$620.9 million in 2025.
- 🇻🇳 Vietnam: US$85.7 billion
☕ Largest export to EU: **Coffee** (US$3.3 billion)
🥛 Largest import from EU: Milk & Cream (US$116 million)
- 🇲🇾 Malaysia: US$54.7 billion
🌴 Largest export to EU: **Palm Oil** (US$1.28 billion)
🥩 Largest import from EU: Meat of Swine (US$206.3 million)
- 🇸🇬 Singapore: US$53.5 billion
⛏️ Largest export to EU: **Copper Ore** (US$256.3 million)
🥩 Largest import from EU: Meat of Swine (US$83.3 million)
- 🇹🇭 Thailand: US$49.6 billion
🍖 Largest export to EU: **Prepared/Preserved Meat** (US$416.8 million)
🌾 Largest import from EU: Wheat & Meslin (US$63.9 million)
- 🇮🇩 Indonesia: US$31.2 billion
🌴 Largest export to EU: **Palm Oil** (US$1.12 billion)
Largest import from EU: Milk & Cream (US$141 million)
🏁 The Bottom Line
The numbers are no longer the question. The EU is ASEAN’s largest foreign investor, its third-largest trading partner outside Europe, and the strategic partner Southeast Asians trust second-most after decades of hedging between Washington and Beijing.
What remains unresolved is architecture. Europe and Southeast Asia are building their relationship one bilateral FTA at a time—the Philippines in 2027, Thailand and Malaysia close behind—while the larger prize, a region-to-region agreement, stays on the drawing board.
Three-quarters of European businesses say they want it. The question is whether governments will move at the same speed as the capital already flowing between them.
If they do, the 50th anniversary next year could mark more than a milestone. It could mark the moment ASEAN and the EU stopped treating each other as alternatives to somewhere else—and started treating each other as the destination.

articles.title: EU’s carbon rules enter implementation phase, putting Indian MSMEs under pressure - Down To Earth
articles.summary: EU’s carbon rules enter implementation phase, putting Indian MSMEs under pressure  Down To Earth
articles.full_text:
When European buyers stop ordering steel, the consequences for an Indian manufacturer can begin well before a carbon bill arrives. For Chandan Steel Limited, a stainless steel manufacturer based in Gujarat, some smaller European customers have already disappeared as the European Union’s (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) adds a new layer of costs, emissions data and paperwork to cross-border trade.
“Some smaller European buyers that previously purchased one or two containers, typically 20 to 25 tonnes, have disappeared. Even the number of inquiries has gone down because of the additional cost burden and additional paperwork the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) demands,” Chaitanya Chandan, director of Chandan Steel, tells Down To Earth (DTE). “Those small buyers are switching to finished steel goods instead of purchasing raw materials from India as it leaves a hole in their pockets.”
The company exports around 40,000 tonnes of steel annually out of total production of about 60,000 tonnes. Its products include precision bars, profiles, flanges and forgings, seamless tubes and pipes, wires and wire rods. Chandan says it is still too early to quantify CBAM’s impact on the company as the EU’s rules and compliance requirements continue to evolve.
CBAM entered its definitive phase on January 1, 2026, moving beyond the reporting-only transition period that began in October 2023. The mechanism covers imports of selected iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, electricity and hydrogen products. EU importers must account for embedded emissions in covered goods. The purchase of certificates for emissions associated with 2026 imports is scheduled to begin in February 2027, with the first annual declarations and corresponding certificates due by September 30, 2027, according to the European Commission.
For Indian exporters, the immediate challenge is not limited to the carbon price. They must also establish the emissions associated with production, obtain data from suppliers, arrange verification and provide the information European customers need to comply. Although the legal obligation to purchase and surrender CBAM certificates rests with the authorised EU importer, exporters may bear part of the cost through lower prices, renegotiated contracts or lost orders.
Paperwork behind a carbon bill
For small and medium manufacturers, demonstrating compliance can be a challenge in itself. Aditya Garodia, managing director of Corona Steel Industry, tells DTE that the company is facing difficulties obtaining the data and certifications required to establish the emissions embedded in its products. “We have been consulting experts for months to get everything in place so we can get necessary compliances and certifications done as early as possible if not immediately, and stay ahead of our competitors.” Based in Kolkata, Corona exports to developed markets, including the US, Canada, Western Europe, the UK and Australia.
Manufacturers often buy steel and other materials from outside suppliers, including secondary mills. Garodia says, “Collecting the required certifications for these inputs and assembling the documentation for a CBAM assessment can be difficult. Consultants are available, but many are still learning the requirements and are not readily accessible across the country.”
He estimates that compliance and certification could cost a company Rs 5-10 million, depending on the manufacturing capacity. He also says the price difference between steel sourced from large producers and secondary producers could be around 15-20 per cent, making it difficult for smaller and medium manufacturers to switch all their inputs to more expensive material from large producers.
“CBAM has not yet significantly affected the industry,” Garodia says, adding, “The impact will become more visible as the payment system takes effect. Smaller firms have limited resources to assess the emissions of every product and component used in manufacturing.”
The requirements can extend beyond emissions generated inside a factory. A manufacturer may need information on the carbon intensity of steel, components and other inputs, as well as the electricity used in production. If a supplier cannot provide verified information, the exporter may have to use applicable default values or find another way to meet the reporting requirements.
October is typically when Binayak Hi-Tech Engineering, a West Bengal-based manufacturer of fabricated iron and steel products for construction and agricultural applications, begins receiving orders from European customers for the following year. But this year, some buyers are holding back. “Normally, we start getting orders for the next year in October,” managing director Atul Jhunjhunwala tells DTE. During a conversation on October 3, he said three to four customers had asked to wait until the end of the month before placing orders, as they sought greater clarity on CBAM.
Describing CBAM as a “grey area”, Jhunjhunwala pointed to uncertainty over its implementation and reporting requirements. Some customers were delaying orders or considering pausing shipments until the rules became clearer, he says, adding that it is too early to estimate the effect on orders. The uncertainty also extends to emissions reporting across supply chains. More than 90 per cent of Binayak’s production is exported, including to Europe and North America. Calculating product-level emissions is challenging when manufacturers depend on suppliers for information about the raw materials and components they use. “Only part of a product’s emissions can be controlled directly by the manufacturer. Much of the information needed for a product-level emissions calculation depends on raw materials and components sourced from other suppliers,” Jhunjhunwala says.
Binayak uses both solar power and conventional electricity supplied by Calcutta Electric Supply Corporation (CESC). Jhunjhunwala says, “Obtaining the emissions data needed from electricity suppliers has been difficult, despite writing several times over the past 8-9 months to CESC. Even when we, manufacturers, are willing to calculate our own emissions, we cannot complete the exercise without information from other parts of the supply chain, and we don’t know how clear their sources are.”
The company has been consulting specialists to understand the documentation and verification required under CBAM. Manufacturers, particularly micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), often lack the technical staff and resources needed to interpret the requirements independently, Jhunjhunwala highlights. The process also raises concerns about disclosing commercially sensitive information on suppliers, costs and production.
For companies exporting to Europe, compliance could also help distinguish their products from those of competitors. Jhunjhunwala says Europe is a growing market for Binayak and that the company is working towards CBAM compliance, with the intention of expanding its European business if it can meet the requirements ahead of competitors.
Garodia says the effect of CBAM on exports remains uncertain. “Bottlenecks and hurdles will persist for the first 2-3 years, the industry might figure things out by 2028 as the industry does not yet know the extent of the disruption,” he said, when asked whether the compliance hurdles could affect India's trade with Europe.
Steel exports face most immediate exposure
India’s exposure to CBAM is particularly significant in iron and steel. Eurostat data show that the EU imported €3.9 billion worth of iron and steel from India in 2024, making India its largest source of such imports that year. Between 2019 and 2024, imports increased by 89.2 per cent.
Indian government data show that finished steel exports to the EU reached 4.03 million tonnes in financial year 2023-24 (FY24), compared with 1.95 million tonnes in FY20, according to the Union Ministry of Steel.
The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) estimates that India’s steel and aluminium exports to the EU had already fallen 24.4 per cent in FY25, before CBAM certificate payments began. The research services institute attributes part of the decline to reporting and compliance requirements. In a December 2025 report, it estimated that Indian steel and aluminium exporters could face pressure to reduce prices by 15 to 22 per cent to remain competitive once the payment phase began.
An industry specialist from one of India’s leading integrated steelmaking companies tells DTE that exports to Europe account for only around 4-5 per cent of the company’s production. The company will continue supplying the market only if its margins remained comparable with those available domestically, the specialist says, adding that it will not absorb the CBAM cost.
The impact is likely to vary by production route, emissions intensity, product mix and the share of exports going to the EU. A June 2026 study by the Centre for Responsible Business finds that coal-based technologies account for more than 80 per cent of Indian steel output. It estimates the sector’s carbon intensity at around 2.55 tonnes of carbon dioxide per tonne of steel, compared with a global average of around 1.85 tonnes.
India’s steel industry includes large integrated producers as well as secondary manufacturers that rely on different combinations of raw materials, electricity and production processes. This diversity makes company-level emissions data important in calculating the potential cost of CBAM.
A June 2026 working paper by the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations (ICRIER) estimates that India’s iron and steel exports to the EU could decline by 23.94 per cent at a carbon price of $86.01 per tonne of carbon dioxide. The corresponding estimated decline for China was 22.45 per cent.

articles.title: Nobel economics prize rewards the theory behind ECB rate decisions - Brussels Signal
articles.summary: Nobel economics prize rewards the theory behind ECB rate decisions  Brussels Signal
articles.full_text:
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences has awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences to Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford for “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”. The two Americans have spent their careers explaining how the decisions of households and firms add up to inflation, unemployment and the slumps that governments try to cushion.
Hall teaches at Stanford University and Woodford at Columbia University. They share a prize of 12 million Swedish crowns, about €1.1 million, announced in Stockholm on October 12.
The academy said the pair had built models that allowed governments and central banks to time fiscal and monetary measures more precisely. John Hassler, who chairs the prize committee, said economies were now “better equipped to deal with shocks” such as energy crises.
That is close to a description of the European Central Bank’s past year. On June 11 the bank raised its three key interest rates by 25 basis points, the first increase since September 2023, after the war in the Middle East drove energy costs up and pushed euro area inflation above 3 per cent.
The deposit rate now stands at 2.25 per cent. ECB President Christine Lagarde presented the move as a signal meant to stop the energy shock from spreading into wider prices.
Woodford’s 2003 book Interest and Prices became the standard text for inflation targeting and he has advised the Riksbank, the Swedish central bank that funds the award. Much of his later work concerns expectations, which is why central banks now treat their own communication as an instrument of policy.
Hall, a senior fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, long chaired the committee at the National Bureau of Economic Research that decides when American recessions begin and end. His research on consumption undercut the assumption that household spending moves predictably with income.
The theory has not settled the European quarrel over who should do the stabilising and with whose money. The European Commission rejected Italian and Greek requests for more room under the EU fiscal rules on October 8, with the bloc’s deficit projected to reach 3.5 per cent of GDP this year and average 10-year borrowing costs at 4 per cent.
Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis argued that adding exemptions would damage the credibility of the rules themselves. Eurogroup President Kyriakos Pierrakakis said ministers agreed that support measures should stay temporary and targeted.
The economics prize is not part of Alfred Nobel’s bequest. It was created by the Riksbank in 1968 to mark the bank’s 300th anniversary and first awarded a year later to Ragnar Frisch of Norway and Jan Tinbergen of the Netherlands.

articles.title: Two Kent stores to close as major chain announces it’s leaving the UK - Kent Online
articles.summary: Two Kent stores to close as major chain announces it’s leaving the UK  Kent OnlineMajor stationery chain to close all UK shops in huge blow to high street  AOL.co.ukFull list of 10 stationery and card stores closing across UK by 2027 as chain shuts ALL locations  The SunWell loved Newcastle store closing down as shoppers grab last-minute bargains  Chronicle LiveMajor stationery chain to close ALL UK stores as high costs make business 'unsustainable' &...
articles.full_text:
Shoppers in Kent are set to lose two Typo stores after the stationery and gifts retailer announced plans to pull out of the UK.
The chain has branches at Canterbury's Whitefriars and Bluewater shopping centre in Greenhithe.
Typo says all of its UK shops and online trading will end by early 2027, although exact closure dates for individual branches have not yet been announced.
It comes at a time when high streets and shopping centres across the country are facing continued pressure.
Typo is known for its colourful and quirky range of stationery, cards, gifts, accessories and lifestyle products, and has operated in Britain for around a decade.
The retailer, which is owned by Australian fashion group Cotton On, currently has around 13 stores across the UK.
It has blamed high rents, rising operating costs and softer sales for the decision to leave the British market.
In a statement, the company said it had made the decision after “careful consideration” and that its priority was to support its UK staff through the transition.
It said there was “no sustainable path today” for Typo in Britain despite efforts by its teams.
The Canterbury and Bluewater closures come as retailers across the UK continue to announce store closures and restructuring plans.
Claire's shut all 154 of its standalone UK and Ireland stores earlier this year after entering administration, while stationery retailer TG Jones is undergoing a major restructuring that could see a large number of former WH Smith stores close.
The department store sector has also been hit, with Harvey Nichols undergoing major changes following its takeover by Frasers Group.
The Newcastle branch of Typo has already closed following a clearance sale, but the remaining stores are expected to continue trading until their individual closure dates are confirmed.
Typo will continue operating outside the UK.
The company said: “After careful consideration we are closing Typo’s operations in the United Kingdom, with all stores and online trading to close by early 2027.”
It added: “Despite the efforts of our teams, ongoing high rent and operating costs, combined with softer sales, mean there is no sustainable path today for Typo in the UK.”

articles.title: Germany’s battle to break its economic addiction to China turns existential - The Telegraph
articles.summary: Germany’s battle to break its economic addiction to China turns existential  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
For decades, Germany seemed immune to the China shock that has wreaked havoc on Western manufacturers.
After Beijing joined the World Trade Organisation (WTO) in 2001 and flooded markets with cheap goods, Germany’s carmakers and chemicals producers not only stood strong but benefited from selling to the new Chinese market.
However, German policymakers and industrialists became complacent as China pursued closer business ties. Cue what economists have coined the “China Shock 2.0” and Germany is suddenly one of the most vulnerable countries in the world.
Now, German-China relations are undergoing a sea change as Chancellor Friedrich Merz wakes up to how Beijing’s new era of global dominance is hammering the German economy.
As recently as 2020, Germany had a trade surplus of nearly €20bn (£17bn) with China. This is now a deficit of €21bn.
Analysis by the Global Public Policy Institute shows that while many countries, including the UK, have reduced their exposure to China in recent years, Germany has become increasingly vulnerable. Since 2013, Germany has moved from the 10th most exposed country to China to the third, behind only South Korea and Russia.

articles.title: European Utility Stocks Facing Fresh Grid Risk Investors Should Watch - Simply Wall Street
articles.summary: European Utility Stocks Facing Fresh Grid Risk Investors Should Watch  Simply Wall Street
articles.full_text:

That mix of potential calm and ongoing risk keeps pricing power, asset safety and cash flows firmly in focus for anyone watching integrated and renewable-focused stocks. articles.title: Teen wounds headmaster and teacher after opening fire at French school - France 24
articles.summary: Teen wounds headmaster and teacher after opening fire at French school  France 24Teenager arrested after two teachers shot in French school  BBCFrench 14-year-old ‘shoots two teachers with hunting gun’  The TelegraphStaff shot at school in France - as pupil detained  Sky NewsFrance school shooting: Police detain pupil after two injured  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
Two teaching staff were shot and wounded by a 14-year-old boy armed with a hunting rifle at a school in Aubagne near Marseille Monday morning, French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said. Authorities said the teenager's father had been taken into custody and that there did not seem to be any link to the student protests that have swept across the country in recent weeks.
A 14-year-old boy opened fire with a hunting rifle at a middle school in France on Monday, injuring the headmaster and a teacher before being disarmed by a member of staff, local authorities said.
The shooting took place at Joseph-Lakanal middle school in the southern town of Aubagne, near Marseille, where a third person was grazed by gunfire, police said.
Authorities said there did not appear to be a link with high school protests that have rocked France in recent weeks.
"The middle school was not affected by the high school students' protest," police told AFP.
The suspect "came in carrying a bag which was a guitar case. He clearly removed a weapon from this guitar case – a long gun, a hunting rifle," said Marseille's deputy public prosecutor Audrey Jouaneton.
He fired at least four shots, including inside a classroom occupied by teachers and pupils, leaving a mark on a blackboard, she added.
The headmaster, 53, and teacher, 37, were not in critical condition, according to authorities.
"The suspect, for reasons as yet unknown, fired at the headteacher, who was hit by a shower of pellets in the thighs and lower back," said Jacques Witkowski, prefect of the wider Bouches-du-Rhône region.
He then fired at a second teacher, who was hit by buckshot in the thigh before a member of staff disarmed him, he said.
The suspect "is not known for any history of delinquency or radicalisation," Witkowski added.
Read moreFrench students vow to keep up protests as UN voices 'concern' over violence
Sarah, a pupil at the school, told AFP she heard the fire alarm go off during her Spanish lesson and went into the corridor, where she and her classmates "bumped into" the gunman.
"He started shooting and said: 'I've only come for the teachers, not for the pupils,'" she said.
An investigation into attempted murder has been opened.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who visited the scene, said the suspect's father had been taken into custody.
Investigators were "trying to understand how this young person ended up in a position with this gun", Nunez told reporters.
'Prevent the worst'
French President Emmanuel Macron on X praised the teaching staff for their quick reaction.
"I commend the composure and exemplary response of the teaching staff, which helped to prevent the worst from happening," he said.
Nunez and Education Minister Édouard Geffray, arrived at the scene Monday afternoon.
Geffray called for action against such violence.
"This unacceptable act is yet further evidence of the rise of unchecked violence in our society, against which we must all take a stand," Geffray said on X.
There has been a spate of violent incidents at French schools in recent months, prompting bag checks on entry in some establishments.
Read moreArt teacher critically injured by student in southern France school stabbing
In February, a 14-year-old stabbed an art teacher in southern France at least three times, leaving the 60-year-old in critical condition.
A 14-year-old student in June last year fatally stabbed a teaching assistant in eastern France.
In another, a student carried out a stabbing spree in several classrooms in April last year, wounding a girl and three other pupils.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Chinese car makers increasingly rely on overseas markets as September exports surge - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Chinese car makers increasingly rely on overseas markets as September exports surge  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
China exported around 919,000 passenger vehicles in September, lifted by overseas demand for plug-in hybrids and pure electric vehicles, data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers showed. In the first nine months of 2026, China exported more than passenger cars, up more than 70% compared with the same period last year.
Meanwhile, domestic passenger car sales in China have fallen for most of the year as they face weaker consumer confidence at home and scaled back government subsidies. They declined 27% in September year-on-year to over 1.6 million units, according to the association.
In recent months, Chinese automakers have more aggressively targeted rapid growth in overseas markets such as Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia and Africa. Canada is also opening its doors to Chinese EV exports under a tariff cut deal with China.
The industry is increasingly relying on overseas markets for sales and profit growth as players seek to offset the weakness in the domestic market, said analyst Stephen Chan with S&P Global Ratings.
Chinese car exports to Europe focused also on the rapidly rising sales of Chinese hybrid vehicles. As pressure on the EU to rebalance trade with China grows, EU trade chief MaroS Šefcovic said Friday that China and the EU reached an interim deal that could cut Chinese hybrid vehicle exports by around half.
Analysts said protectionist measures will likely continue to cloud Chinese automakers' overseas outlook.
"You can't expect BYD or the other OEMs (manufacturers) to export too many cars without facing tariffs or pushbacks from the foreign governments," Xiao Feng, head of the Hong Kong and China Industrials Research at investment group CITIC CLSA, told reporters recently.
Geopolitics is the biggest challenge in its overseas expansion, Stella Li, executive vice president at Chinese EV giant BYD who drives the car maker's global growth, acknowledged at an event this month.
As a result, BYD has been expanding its capacity to make cars locally in overseas markets including setting up manufacturing plants in Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil and Hungary, she told the Milken Institute ?Asia Summit in Singapore.
Chinese automakers will likely continue to increase production overseas to help avoid risks such as tariffs, said Ming Lee, head of Greater China automotive and industrial research at BofA Global Research of Bank of America. "More and more volume will be made locally," he said.
The US, meanwhile, has effectively barred Chinese EVs from entering its market with hefty tariffs. US President Donald Trump's meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping during his state visit to Washington in September did not result in a deal on allowing Chinese EV exports to the US, and experts say the U.S. market is probably not on top of the agenda of Chinese automakers due to ongoing political uncertainties.

A "do not eat" warning has been issued to consumers and businesses after Salmonella was identified in certain eggs imported from Ukraine.
Food Standards Scotland (FSS) and the Food Standards Agency (FSA) said the eggs originate from Yasensvit Ltd, Kyiv, Ukraine, and are stamped with the code 3UA1012066, which is printed directly onto the shell.
The eggs may have been supplied to catering businesses or sold through smaller retail outlets.
The eggs may have been repacked by UK businesses and sold under different business names or packing centre details on the outer packaging, making the egg stamp code the most reliable way to identify affected products, FSS said.
“The FSA’s advice is that if people have bought any of the affected products, do not eat them and instead, dispose of them at home, as they may be unsafe,” it said.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) detected Salmonella Enteritidis in samples of eggs and carried out whole-genome sequencing, which showed that the strain did not match the outbreak strains currently under investigation.
Salmonella infection can cause symptoms including fever, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps, which usually resolve without treatment after a few days. However, the infection can occasionally cause more serious illness, including sepsis.
Anyone experiencing symptoms should avoid attending work, school or nursery until they have been symptom-free for at least 48 hours to help prevent the spread of infection.
Food businesses that have received eggs stamped 3UA1012066 should immediately stop selling or using them, withdraw affected stock from sale and, where products have been sold directly to consumers, undertake a recall, FSS said.
FSS added that while most affected eggs are believed to have been supplied through the catering sector, some may also have been available through smaller independent retailers and convenience stores. They are not sold through major supermarket chains.
Eggs that are thoroughly cooked and handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk. Infants, young children, pregnant people and older adults should continue to only eat raw or lightly cooked eggs if they are produced in the UK and are part of a recognised assurance scheme, FSS said.

articles.title: Euro hovers near 17-month low against the British Pound as debt woes weigh - FXStreet
articles.summary: Euro hovers near 17-month low against the British Pound as debt woes weigh  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
The Euro (EUR) depreciates further against the British Pound (GBP) on Monday after dropping about 1.7% over the previous two weeks, as ongoing concerns about France's fiscal health keep investors on their toes. The EUR/GBP pair trades just above 0.8450 after rejection at the 0.8490 area on Friday, with the 16-month low of 0.8447 just a few pips away.
Investors are staying away from the Euro as the spread between the 10-year French OAT yield and the safer German Bund escalates to 137 basis points, its highest level since the 2012 financial crisis. The political deadlock in France, ahead of the presidential elections next year, and the social unrest spreading through the country are a toxic cocktail for investors that has crushed the Euro over the last few weeks.
ECB's Lagarde and UK GDP are the highlights this week
In the Calendar on Monday, the focus will be on the European Central Bank (ECB) and Bank of England (BoE) speakers. Trading volumes, however, are likely to remain at low levels amid a long weekend in Japan and a partial holiday in the US.
In the Eurozone, on Wednesday, ECB President Christine Lagarde is expected to speak at a central bankers’ meeting in Bangkok, Thailand, and might provide some hints about the timing for the next interest rate hike.
In the UK, the highlight of the week will be August’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and Industrial and Manufacturing Production figures, due on Thursday. These numbers might attract particular interest this week, with investors looking for confirmation of the hawkish comments by BoE policymakers, including Governor Andrew Bailey in previous weeks.
Analysts at Commerzbank argue that the UK’s “improved growth outlook should make it easier for the Bank of England to raise rates further in order to lean against inflation.” Regarding the EUR/GBP's near-term outlook, Commerzbank points out that they expect "EUR/GBP to trade broadly sideways over the coming months.”
Central banks FAQs
Central Banks have a key mandate which is making sure that there is price stability in a country or region. Economies are constantly facing inflation or deflation when prices for certain goods and services are fluctuating. Constant rising prices for the same goods means inflation, constant lowered prices for the same goods means deflation. It is the task of the central bank to keep the demand in line by tweaking its policy rate. For the biggest central banks like the US Federal Reserve (Fed), the European Central Bank (ECB) or the Bank of England (BoE), the mandate is to keep inflation close to 2%.
A central bank has one important tool at its disposal to get inflation higher or lower, and that is by tweaking its benchmark policy rate, commonly known as interest rate. On pre-communicated moments, the central bank will issue a statement with its policy rate and provide additional reasoning on why it is either remaining or changing (cutting or hiking) it. Local banks will adjust their savings and lending rates accordingly, which in turn will make it either harder or easier for people to earn on their savings or for companies to take out loans and make investments in their businesses. When the central bank hikes interest rates substantially, this is called monetary tightening. When it is cutting its benchmark rate, it is called monetary easing.
A central bank is often politically independent. Members of the central bank policy board are passing through a series of panels and hearings before being appointed to a policy board seat. Each member in that board often has a certain conviction on how the central bank should control inflation and the subsequent monetary policy. Members that want a very loose monetary policy, with low rates and cheap lending, to boost the economy substantially while being content to see inflation slightly above 2%, are called ‘doves’. Members that rather want to see higher rates to reward savings and want to keep a lit on inflation at all time are called ‘hawks’ and will not rest until inflation is at or just below 2%.
Normally, there is a chairman or president who leads each meeting, needs to create a consensus between the hawks or doves and has his or her final say when it would come down to a vote split to avoid a 50-50 tie on whether the current policy should be adjusted. The chairman will deliver speeches which often can be followed live, where the current monetary stance and outlook is being communicated. A central bank will try to push forward its monetary policy without triggering violent swings in rates, equities, or its currency. All members of the central bank will channel their stance toward the markets in advance of a policy meeting event. A few days before a policy meeting takes place until the new policy has been communicated, members are forbidden to talk publicly. This is called the blackout period.
Author
Graduated in Communication Sciences at the Universidad del Pais Vasco and Universiteit van Amsterdam, Guillermo has been working as financial news editor and copywriter in diverse Forex-related firms, like FXStreet and Kantox.

articles.title: The European Union (EU), which enacted the world's first comprehensive artificial intelligence (AI) - 매일경제
articles.summary: The European Union (EU), which enacted the world's first comprehensive artificial intelligence (AI)  매일경제
articles.full_text:
Spain has institutionalized its experience in operating AI-regulated sandboxes into 16 guidelines to help companies comply with laws and regulations. The regulatory grammar is different, but the essence is the same. It does not tie norms to isolated obligatory provisions, but creates an ecosystem where companies innovate under clear rules and link their performance to market opportunities.
Does our legislation support this ecosystem. In January, we established a comprehensive legal foundation by implementing the "Basic Act on Artificial Intelligence Development and Trust Foundation (Artificial Intelligence Basic Act)." Now, it is necessary to check the effectiveness based on whether a company can clearly understand and comply with its responsibilities and whether the support system is in place so that its efforts can lead to innovation and growth. It is worth paying attention to three tasks.
First, it is necessary to reorganize the obligations and responsibilities between the subjects of the follow-up and the application relationship with individual laws. While the current law defines the targets of follow-up by dividing them into "development business operators and user business operators," the responsibility regulations of high-impact AI operators impose obligations on the general "artificial intelligence business operators" covering them, making it unclear who will follow them. The content and scope of responsibilities should be specified according to the role of each subject and the possibility of risk control in the value chain leading to the development, provision, operation, and use of AI. In addition, high-impact AI for recruitment and loan screening may overlap with the duty of explanation as it corresponds to automated decisions under the Personal Information Protection Act. The scope of application and implementation method of each law should be clearly summarized to reduce the burden of overlapping and confusion in interpretation. It is necessary to substantiate the process of preliminarily reviewing legal consistency by utilizing the regulatory deliberation and inter-ministerial coordination function of the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy Committee. Now is the right time for the Ministry of Science and ICT to operate a research team to improve the artificial intelligence law system.
Third, regulations and industrial policies should be linked so that AI safety and reliability investments can lead to competitiveness. The current law requires state agencies and others to prioritize products and services that have undergone basic rights impact assessments when introducing high-impact AI, and has also provided a basis for supporting small and medium-sized enterprises to fulfill their responsibilities. Now it is time to embody this principle as a basis for actual purchase and support. SMEs should support test and evaluation costs and computational resources from the development stage, and use sandbox verification data for follow-up evaluation and public purchase to reduce the burden of compliance, expanding opportunities to enter the market. When corporate capabilities support the level of trust required by the state and the market evaluates its performance, regulation and promotion become an industrial strategy.
The leap to the third round of AI will be accelerated when rational regulations and industrial policies interlock like cogs. Korea has effectively implemented its high-impact AI obligation for the first time in the world, becoming the first mover in AI regulation. Although it is a meaningful achievement, it is also the starting point for the international community to verify regulatory design and enforcement capabilities. If the density, rationality, and international consistency of regulations suitable for preemptive legislation are not met, the previously prepared system could rather be a "Galapagos regulation" that hinders Korean companies. Now is the time to rewrite the regulatory grammar so that the results of preemptive legislation can lead to industrial competitiveness.
[Kang Hye-kyung, a Pacific expert at law firm]

articles.title: China Agrees to Cap Hybrid Car Exports to EU at 350,000 a Year - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: China Agrees to Cap Hybrid Car Exports to EU at 350,000 a Year  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
China will cut the number of hybrid vehicles it ships to the European Union to about 350,000 a year. The EU will impose an import quota on hybrids and China has accepted it, allowing the two sides to avert the immediate risk of a full-blown trade dispute.
EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao met in Beijing on the 8th and 9th of this month and agreed on 16 items including the hybrid export restrictions, trade and investment, export controls and intellectual property rights, Bloomberg reported on the 11th.
Under the agreement, the EU will move to cap hybrid vehicle imports at 350,000 units in the first year. The quota takes effect Dec. 1 and will rise 6% each year from the second year, running for a total of four years. To comply with the World Trade Organization's non-discrimination principle, the import limit will apply not only to Chinese-made hybrids but also to those from other countries.
Markets responded with relief to news of the agreement. Shares of Chinese automakers broadly gained on the Hong Kong exchange that day, with BYD, China's largest electric vehicle maker, rising as much as 2.7% at one point.
The agreement came ahead of an EU summit on the 15th and 16th of this month. Germany and France had pressed the European Commission for strong trade countermeasures, arguing that China's overcapacity and subsidy policies were threatening European manufacturing and jobs.
After the EU imposed countervailing duties of up to 35.3% on Chinese-made battery electric vehicles in 2024, Chinese automakers expanded exports of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and conventional hybrid electric vehicles, which were excluded from the duties. As a result, Chinese automakers' share of Europe's hybrid market had risen to about 25% as of August this year.
Trade experts say the agreement favors China. Beijing avoided tough EU trade measures while making few concessions on the structural issues behind its vast trade surplus with the bloc, they said.
Joe Peissel, senior economist at Chinese research firm Trivium China, told Bloomberg that China had scored a diplomatic win, saying it offered various agreements and memorandums of understanding while leaving largely untouched the fundamental problems driving the trade imbalance. Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University, said China, already embroiled in a trade conflict with the United States, sought to avoid letting trade friction with Europe escalate as well.
China's dominant leverage over the global rare earth supply chain is also cited as a reason the EU would find it hard to take a hard line. Christopher Beddor, an economist at global research firm Gavekal Dragonomics, said that if the EU were to build large-scale tariff barriers, China could use restrictions on rare earth exports as a retaliatory tool.
